World.title: Haley Cavinder's Cowboys tight end husband caught her eye with a DM, couples that pole dance together & more
World.content:
Welcome to a Thursday in the middle of October. Or I should say, welcome to the latest edition of True Romance. Today is all about pushing back on the notion that romance has been defeated and it no longer exists.

For those buying in on that, and I'm sure for some it's the case, I present to you several examples that, despite a possible downward trend overall, there are those making it work. If nothing else, there's hope.

We have a full slate from the smooth athlete to influencer DM that landed to couple that pole dance together and even a couple of actors who covered their workplace in romance. Light a candle, relax and let’s get into it.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Long before the lucky pregame butt squeezes or the messages written on the back of Haley Cavinder's pants or even taking the heat for Jake Ferguson's bad game, there was the classic shooter taking his shot.

The Dallas Cowboys tight end slid into the former college athlete and influencer's DMs with a line that ended up working and anyone can use.

Haley said on an episode of People's WAG World, "He just DMed me and asked how my golf game was."

And there's this idea floating out there that you can't meet people. Firing off a wild DM usually doesn’t work. A "How's your golf game" is smooth. The two hit it off, and now they're married, with a story to tell their grandkids one day.

Grandpa was in the NFL and grandma used to dance on TikTok. They met after he sent her a message on social media. A love story as old as time.

"I don’t like to get high or too low when it comes to that stuff. I wasn’t looking for anything, and I don’t know if Ferg was at that time either," she continued.

"But then we spent 10 days together straight, and he’s just a good, down-to-earth human being."

If you're having trouble finding someone, maybe you're just looking in the wrong places and sending DMs that aren't landing. There is hope. Fire off one about golf to a TikToker and see what ends up playing out.

JOE BURROW'S GIRLFRIEND SHARES CHEATING HOT TAKE, WOMAN'S SISTER HOOKED UP WITH HER DATE & REGAINING THE SPARK

Before we move on, let's find out the results of the poll from last week. The "Do you go through with the wedding if your husband-to-be calls you your sister's name at the altar?" one.

In a stunner, given that the woman who this happened to did go through with the wedding, an overwhelming 72.5% said no, you leave that jerk at the altar. An unforgiving bunch of hopeless romantics, I suppose.

Go follow True Romance on Twitter and Facebook and keep sending your emails here: sean.joseph@outkick.com (anonymously if you prefer).

Couples that pole dance together, stay together

I bet, had that couple been pole dancing together, the husband-to-be wouldn’t have said the name of the bride's sister at the altar. Because if you didn’t already know, couples who pole dance together are weirdos.

Let me finish. Weirdos who "strengthen their bonds and keep the spark alive." Take it from Los Angeles newlyweds Misha and Sam who, if they need pole dancing or anything as newlyweds to keep the spark alive, might be doomed.

But that will be something they'll never be confronted with as long as they keep hopping on the pole together. And that's what we're here to focus on. The positive aspects of what these two are doing.

Their first dance featured "saucy flips and splits on the polished pole," according to the NY Post. It turns out hitting the pole can be done in front of others. That's an interesting twist to this that I didn’t see coming.

I was thinking this was more of an in the privacy of your own home activity. But why not something for everyone? Who needs movie nights or long walks when you have this and all of its options?

"There’s a lot of stigma around pole dancing, some people might think, ‘Oh, that’s just for strippers,’" Misha told The Post.

"Yes, it has sensual roots. But there’s so much athleticism that go into it. It’s a lot harder than it looks. We love it."

Sam, who is the one who suggested they get into pole dancing, said, "A lot of people think pole is just for women. It’s strange for them to see a guy do it, especially with his [female] partner. I just don’t feed into the negativity."

He added, "There are times I have to hold all of Misha’s weight while we’re doing a move, or she may have to position herself in a certain way to accommodate me. It’s like a metaphor for marriage."

There really is something out there for everyone. If you're willing to take a chance, you could be one of those who finds the person you want to pole dance with for the rest of your life. That's a lovely thought, isn't it?

If you think about it, pole dancing together really is just a metaphor for marriage.



This Week In True Romance

Follow True Romance on Twitter and Facebook .

Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys were 'having sex all the time' in their disguises on set of The Americans

As much as I'd like to believe that couples pole dancing will work for people, and I'm sure it will for some, I can tell you a relationship built on having sex all over the set you're working on does work.

At least it has for Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys. They've been together since late 2013 after starting their relationship while working on the series "The Americans".

We now know that when they weren't filming they were busy on set having sex in their disguises. Why do we know that? Well, because it's 2026 and everyone tells everybody else everything.

Which reminds me, I'll have to tell the story sometime of a graveyard at night and the back of a Nissan Pathfinder. Anyway, back to Keri and Matthew making a mess of their workplace.

"We were falling in love and staying up all night and having sex all the time and just wearing disguises, like, I’m f---ing [in] crazy wigs and wearing pearls," Russell said during a podcast appearance, reports Entertainment Weekly.

"When have you ever worn pearls and [been] f---ing in trailers and f---ing everywhere. I mean, it was insanity. It was so fun and sneaky, and sexy, and so good."

If that doesn’t say true romance, I don't know what does. Congratulations to the happy couple for both their extracurricular activity on the set and for extending hope for others. Well done.

What's the male equivalent of a woman wearing sexy underwear expecting them to be seen by her date?

We've done a ton of these, and I don’t know that we've come across a more important question. She puts on her sexy underwear and he does what?

If you were expecting a lot of effort here, you're going to be disappointed by the folks weighing in on Reddit, although something tells me that won't be a first.

Sure, there are those who put in some work, but go ahead and set your expectations appropriately. Not that slipping on special underwear is a heavy lift.

Some guys do that too. A blown out waistband could ruin the mood. On the other hand, a lovely Borat-style mankini could get the evening going.

Wearing the underwear without the blown out waistband

When my girlfriend and I started dating, she told me that it was attractive that I visit my dad every week (he's in his eighties and lives alone).

Him pulling out his big ... thick ... fat wallet filled with money.

Actually cleaning their house/apartment and any room mates being gone

Doing 10 pushups before the date as if that makes up for not regularly working out.

Trimming the sasquatch

I've been told my work clothes.

Borat mankini

Planned out date, super clean car and apartment that don't smell like dudes. Bathroom must be clean as fudge.

As someone who's married I can't really understand the female gaze because all of the mundane things I do she tells me is incredibly hot/sexy. So what I've learned over the years is to just pay attention to what she finds hot and it usually works out for me, even if I can't really understand what she finds hot about it.

If the question is, what menswear exist that is equivalently sexy or a 1 to 1 to lingerie we don't really have that. If the question is what do men do when they expect to get some play, I'd say it's put actual effort into their hygiene and fashion. It's a low bar.

I put on my robe and wizard hat

Wearing boxers/ briefs on outside of pants

Build something sick like a deck, or maybe cut down a tree with a chainsaw. Execute a big complicated house project and make it sexy as hell like a bathroom renovation.

Wearing sweatpants with no underwear. Uhmmpphhhffff

Song of the week

- MP from Staunton, Virginia writes:

Sean, this week’s True Romance column about the guy who boldly announced his love for his best friend’s girlfriend reminded me of a classic song by Ral Donner (that was originally recorded by Elvis). It’s called The Girl of My Best Friend. Unlike the guy in the column, the guy in the song had the good sense to keep his feelings to himself and just pine away for her. Hope this song is named Song of the Week. All the best.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

-------------

We did it. We successfully made it through another week of romance. Let's do it again next Thursday before I log off for an entire week.

Keep the song recommendations and anything else you want to share coming my way. If you were on the receiving end of a smooth DM, I want to know about it.

Hayden Panettiere’s final moments were captured in a frantic 911 call as the brother of her on-and-off boyfriend desperately tried to revive the actress after finding her unconscious at a South Carolina apartment Aug. 16.

"​​Oh, God, oh, my God — you do like CPR or something?" Zach Hickerson asked the dispatcher in the newly released audio obtained by ABC News and CBS News.

The seven-minute call reveals Hickerson performing CPR on Panettiere while Brian Hickerson administered Narcan.

Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive at the Greenville residence Aug. 16. Zach told the 911 operator that he had arrived at the apartment after returning from church and discovered his brother and Panettiere inside.

The operator then instructed Zach to lay Panettiere flat on her back and begin CPR while emergency crews rushed to the scene.

World.title: Was your identity stolen? What to do in the first 24 hours
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Discovering that your identity has been stolen can leave you feeling angry, frightened and unsure where to begin. Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage.

The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. Fortunately, you can take several steps right away to protect yourself and begin recovering.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT

Why the first day is so important

Identity theft can quickly spread beyond the account where you first discovered the problem. Someone who gains access to your email, for example, might use it to reset passwords for your banking, shopping or other accounts. That's why acting quickly can make a difference.

However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened.

What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft

The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour.

Hour 1: Stop the immediate damage

Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information.

Contact your bank or credit card company. If someone accessed your account or made unauthorized transactions, call the number on your card or the institution's official website. Report the fraud and ask whether the account should be locked, frozen or replaced. Also ask about disputing unauthorized transactions.

If someone accessed your account or made unauthorized transactions, call the number on your card or the institution's official website. Report the fraud and ask whether the account should be locked, frozen or replaced. Also ask about disputing unauthorized transactions. Change compromised passwords. Start with the affected account and your primary email address if it may have been exposed. Use strong, unique passwords and a trusted device.

Start with the affected account and your primary email address if it may have been exposed. Use strong, unique passwords and a trusted device. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an authenticator app or passkey when supported.

Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an or passkey when supported. Check for unauthorized account changes. Review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, forwarding rules and active sessions. Sign out of unfamiliar devices.

Important: If money has been stolen, report it to your financial institution immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary by account and transaction type.

Hours 2 to 4: Protect your credit

Next, make it harder for criminals to open additional accounts using your personal information.

Place a fraud alert on your credit file. Contact Equifax, Experian or TransUnion. The bureau you contact must notify the other two. An initial fraud alert is free and generally lasts one year.

Contact Equifax, Experian or TransUnion. The bureau you contact must notify the other two. An initial fraud alert is free and generally lasts one year. Freeze your credit with all three bureaus. A credit freeze is free and restricts access to your credit reports, making it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. You must contact each bureau separately.

A credit freeze is free and restricts access to your credit reports, making it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. You must contact each bureau separately. Review your credit reports. Visit AnnualCreditReport.com to check reports from all three bureaus. Look for unfamiliar accounts, inquiries and incorrect personal information.

You can freeze your credit even if you expect to apply for a loan or credit card soon. Simply lift the freeze temporarily when necessary.

Hours 4 to 8: Report the identity theft

Creating an official record can help you dispute fraudulent accounts and recover your identity.

Report identity theft to the Federal Trade Commission . Visit IdentityTheft.gov to create an identity theft report and receive a personalized recovery plan.

. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to create an identity theft report and receive a personalized recovery plan. Contact local police when appropriate. A police report may be helpful if your identification was stolen, you know who committed the theft or a creditor requests additional documentation.

A police report may be helpful if your identification was stolen, you know who committed the theft or a creditor requests additional documentation. Save your report information. Keep copies of your FTC report, police report if applicable and confirmation numbers.

An FTC identity theft report can help you exercise certain rights under federal law, including requesting that credit bureaus block fraudulent information. However, you generally do not need to file an FTC report before notifying a bank about unauthorized transactions.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?

Hours 8 to 16: Secure your other accounts

Identity thieves sometimes try to use stolen information across multiple services.

Review other important accounts. Check email, banking, retirement, shopping and payment accounts for suspicious activity. Replace any reused passwords.

Check email, banking, retirement, shopping and payment accounts for suspicious activity. Replace any reused passwords. Contact your mobile carrier. If you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized phone number transfer, report it immediately. Ask about account PINs, number locks and additional verification.

If you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized phone number transfer, report it immediately. Ask about account PINs, number locks and additional verification. Notify your employer when necessary. A compromised work email, payroll account or employee benefits account may expose additional information.

A compromised work email, payroll account or employee benefits account may expose additional information. Check your devices. If malware or phishing may have caused the theft, update your software, run a strong antivirus software scan where supported and remove suspicious apps or browser extensions.

If malware or phishing may have caused the theft, update your software, run a where supported and remove suspicious apps or browser extensions. Protect your tax identity if necessary. If someone used your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return, contact the IRS. You may need to complete Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit. You can also request an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) at IRS.gov to help prevent fraudulent federal tax returns using your information.

Hours 16 to 24: Document everything

Once you've addressed the most urgent threats, organize your recovery efforts.

Create a fraud recovery record. Write down dates, times, account numbers or case references, representatives' names and the steps you've taken. Store sensitive details securely.

Write down dates, times, account numbers or case references, representatives' names and the steps you've taken. Store sensitive details securely. Make a follow-up checklist. Identify remaining accounts, disputes and organizations you still need to contact.

Identify remaining accounts, disputes and organizations you still need to contact. Schedule additional credit checks. Continue reviewing your credit reports and financial statements because suspicious activity may appear later.

Continue reviewing your credit reports and financial statements because suspicious activity may appear later. Save copies of important documents. Keep correspondence, dispute letters and identity theft reports in a secure location.

Common identity theft recovery mistakes to avoid

Even when you're moving quickly, certain mistakes can create additional problems.

Trying to handle everything at once. Focus on active fraud and the most sensitive accounts first. Other tasks can follow.

Focus on active fraud and the most sensitive accounts first. Other tasks can follow. Assuming a credit freeze fixes existing fraud. A freeze helps prevent certain new accounts from being opened, but it doesn't remove fraudulent accounts or stop unauthorized transactions on existing ones.

A freeze helps prevent certain new accounts from being opened, but it doesn't remove fraudulent accounts or stop unauthorized transactions on existing ones. Calling numbers from suspicious messages. Always contact institutions through independently verified phone numbers or official websites.

Always contact institutions through independently verified phone numbers or official websites. Failing to document conversations. Keep records of who you contacted, what they said and any deadlines they provided.

Keep records of who you contacted, what they said and any deadlines they provided. Stopping after securing one account. Review other accounts that may share passwords or recovery information.

9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

What can wait beyond the first day

Some recovery tasks will continue beyond the first day, including disputing fraudulent accounts, correcting credit reports and following up with creditors. However, report unauthorized financial transactions immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary depending on the type of account and transaction. Your initial priority is to stop additional fraud and secure your information.

How identity theft protection can add another layer of security

Recovering from identity theft often involves contacting multiple financial institutions, disputing fraudulent charges and keeping track of important paperwork. An identity theft protection service may help simplify the process by offering recovery assistance, ongoing monitoring and guidance when suspicious activity appears.

What an identity theft protection service can help with

Identity recovery support: Some services provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through disputes, paperwork and communication with affected institutions.

Some services provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through disputes, paperwork and communication with affected institutions. Financial protection: Depending on the plan, certain services offer reimbursement for eligible stolen funds, recovery expenses and legal assistance. Coverage limits and exclusions vary.

Depending on the plan, certain services offer reimbursement for eligible stolen funds, recovery expenses and legal assistance. Coverage limits and exclusions vary. Ongoing monitoring: Alerts can help identify suspicious activity involving your personal information, financial accounts or credit reports.

Alerts can help identify suspicious activity involving your personal information, financial accounts or credit reports. Recovery guidance: Some services offer access to identity theft specialists who can explain next steps and help you navigate the recovery process.

Keep in mind that no identity theft protection service can prevent every type of fraud or guarantee that stolen money will be recovered. You can also take important steps for free, including freezing your credit, placing fraud alerts and reporting identity theft at IdentityTheft.gov.

See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

If you're helping someone else through this

Many people go through this first-24-hours checklist not for themselves, but for an aging parent, a spouse or another family member. If you're the one helping, the same steps apply. Start by securing compromised accounts, freezing credit, reporting fraud and documenting what happened. Keep in mind that you may need permission or legal authorization to speak with financial institutions on someone else's behalf.

Patience is important, too. Identity theft can be frightening, especially for someone who isn't comfortable managing financial accounts online. Helping them make phone calls, organize paperwork and track important deadlines can make the recovery process easier.

In the days that follow

Once the first 24 hours are behind you, continue working through your checklist. Dispute fraudulent charges and accounts, follow up on your identity theft report and request that fraudulent information be removed from your credit reports. Keep monitoring your financial accounts for suspicious activity, since criminals may attempt additional fraud using stolen information.

Recovery timelines vary depending on the type and extent of the theft. Some problems can be resolved quickly, while more complicated cases may take months.

Consider asking a trusted family member or close friend to help you stay organized. Having someone review documents, take notes or track deadlines can help prevent important details from slipping through the cracks.

The most important thing is to stay focused on what you can control. Secure your accounts, report suspicious activity promptly and follow through on unresolved disputes. You may not fix everything in the first 24 hours, but taking these steps can help limit further damage and put you on the path to recovery.

Kurt's key takeaways

When someone steals your identity, it's easy to feel like you've lost control of your financial life. I've seen how quickly one compromised account can lead to bigger problems, especially when criminals get access to email or other personal information. My advice is to focus on what you can control right away. Contact your bank, secure your most important accounts and freeze your credit with all three bureaus. Then report the theft and keep a record of every conversation. You don't need to pay a company to take these initial steps. I also recommend keeping an eye on your accounts long after the first day. Identity thieves may try to use stolen information again, even after you've addressed the original problem. A little extra attention now can help you catch suspicious activity before it causes more damage.

World.title: Suspicious white powder sent to election offices in 3 states
World.content:
Secretaries of state’s offices in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma were sent packages this week with mysterious powders, just weeks before the offices are set to oversee the midterm elections.

Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.

The national groups representing secretaries of state and state election directors expressed concern about the suspicious letters in a letter Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement.

“Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities,” the statement added.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday echoed the sentiment that election officials should “never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties,” adding that his office was working with state and federal law enforcement following the mailing targeting it.

“Fortunately, delivery of the letter was preempted by investigators at the U.S. Postal Service, who are dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states,” LaRose said, while thanking the Postal Service.

Ohio is one of a few states facing tight elections in just a few weeks.

The election bodies of Oklahoma and Louisiana, facing fewer contested elections, were threatened Tuesday, when each state announced it had received packages with suspicious powders.

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections,” Oklahoma State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said in a statement.

Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams said in an email Wednesday that an employee in the office’s Election Division opened a package containing a white powder and was taken uninjured to the emergency room “as a precaution.” Williams added that law enforcement did not find evidence of “harmful substances.”

“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Williams said.

Louisiana State Police said in a statement that it responded to reports of a white powdery substance found in a package at the secretary of state’s office.

“LSP is working with the FBI to identify the substance, which was successfully recovered and submitted for testing at the FBI’s crime lab. No employees have reported injuries or adverse health effects related to the incident,” state police spokesperson Jacob Pucheu said in an emailed statement.

NBC affiliate KTAL of Shreveport reported Tuesday that the Baton Rouge building was evacuated.

The FBI declined in an email to confirm specific instances or locations. The agency said in a statement that it and the Postal Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the FBI’s national press office said.

It is not the first time that states’ election officials have faced threats near an election. In 2024, at least 20 states were targeted with letters containing suspicious powders. In one instance in Utah, a mailing with a suspicious powder was intercepted, with a letter signed by a so-called United States Traitor Elimination Army.

The mailings prompted several agencies, including the Justice Department, to release guidance about protecting personnel against hazardous materials.

World.title: DOJ threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizen individuals on their voter rolls.

Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter on Tuesday sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan with a list of names of possible noncitizens identified by the federal government. The letters demand they review the list by noon on Thursday.

“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in the letters, which was obtained by NBC News.

McCotter wrote that the DOJ provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that county election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined.

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”

Reuters first reported on the letters.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said the federal government has no authority supporting its demands.

“They can send the letter,” he said. “California doesn’t have to do anything about it.”

Federal law prohibits systemic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election. At this point, less than three weeks out from Election Day, the only changes to the voter rolls can come from individualized information, like notification from the Social Security Administration that someone has died.

A DOJ spokesperson said the department is asking California to sequester ballots, not change their voter list.

In a statement Wednesday, Logan said his office had not accessed the thumb drive the DOJ provided “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” He added, “We do not consider the device a secure medium.”

“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Logan said in the statement. “Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”

Weber said in a statement Wednesday that the DOJ did not provide a list of purported noncitizens to her office and that the administration lacked the legal authority for its request.

“The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said in the statement. “California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election.”

All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5.

The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizen individuals. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud.

Election officials in several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records.

Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections.

“What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for postelection challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington state. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.”

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.”

“You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.”

Levitt agreed with the election officials’ conclusions.

“Are they laying the groundwork to say that voting was fraudulent? Of course they are, 100% they are,” he said, referring to the Trump administration. “Is the boy who cried wolf going to cry wolf? Yes, that’s what the boy who cried wolf does.”

Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by noncitizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

During the second Trump administration, the DOJ has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.

World.title: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market, as doubts grow about AI investments
World.content:
Just one week after hitting fresh all-time highs, U.S. stocks are showing signs of strain as investors begin to fret about returns on the trillions of dollars that have been put into AI.

For U.S. consumers, it could mean a shakier economy moving forward.

As of Thursday morning, the S&P 500 was off more than 1% from its week-ago record, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen about 4% below its peak last week.

Driving the declines: Quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic has slowed, the Financial Times reported Wednesday. The AI giant is expected to be worth more than $1 trillion when it goes public, and at nearly $17 billion, its revenue is still massive and the company said it is profitable.

There are also rising concerns about whether China-based memory technology companies could undermine, or even overtake, their Western rivals. And even though the AI data center buildout has created a global shortage of processing chips, there are fears that Chinese mass production of memory chips could flood the market with an oversupply.

Meanwhile, investors have begun selling off the bonds backing some data centers, primarily over fears that AI revenues won’t be sufficient to cover the massive sums that have been borrowed to finance the building of the centers.

On Thursday, economist Ed Yardeni, a widely respected market commentator, lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 target to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates. The S&P 500 currently sits at about 7,600.

Most Americans don’t directly own tech stocks, let alone work in AI, which a growing number of studies show may have begun to limit job opportunities. Still, the AI buildout has been a massive part of what’s bolstering the economy, at least on paper.

Nearly half of all U.S. economy growth this year is attributable to tech-related spending. Those investments have also lifted the stock market even as a growing swath of other companies have experienced sharp declines in their share prices.

The tech-driven gains have in turn created a wealth effect that has helped propel steady U.S. consumer spending and, by extension, the job market. The result has been sturdy economic growth, even as lower-income and even middle-income households have continued to struggle under stubborn inflation and declining earnings.

“While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said earlier this week.

But other economists say consumers are already contending with a host of stressors that stand to weaken their position. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that inflation among businesses reached its highest rate since December 2022 — price growth that could eventually trickle down to consumers.

If tech spending — and stocks — show any sign of sustained declines, broader U.S. economic growth would likely be at risk.

“Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices, slow job growth and the sell-off in equities (if it continues) are all downside risks to consumer spending,” analysts with Citi wrote in a note Thursday.
