World.title: Make a 'sick day' kit for cold and flu season before your household gets hit
World.content:
Make a 'sick day' kit for cold and flu season before your household gets hit

Andee Tagle/NPR

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. 

Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?

Life Kit How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season How to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season Listen · 20:57 20:57

In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin .

Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed . That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.

Sponsor Message

Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.

Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.

You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated, wearing masks and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.

What to include in your cold and flu prep kit

Over-the-counter medications

When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.

But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.

These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.

Sponsor Message

Reed and Amin suggest these medications:

Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.



For kids: Don't use children's ibuprofen for children under 6 months old; naproxen is only approved for children 12 years and older.

Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers .



For kids: Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow this dosing chart when using children's acetaminophen.

Look for a children's version for 12 years and under. Be sure to follow when using children's acetaminophen. For pregnant people: Acetaminophen is the recommended OTC pain reliever for pregnant people , according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.

Antihistamine. Yes, the same thing you take for spring allergies! Colds and allergies have similar symptoms like sneezing, runny noses and watery eyes, which is why they can both be treated by a histamine-blocking medication that can help dry up your sinuses.



For kids: Some OTC allergy medicines are approved for children as young as 6 months, but not all — and some have more side effects than others, says Amin. Check in with your care provider first if you have questions.

Decongestant. Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages.



For kids: Pills are not recommended for kids under 4 and medicated sprays are not recommended for kids under 6.

Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan — often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — can temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed.



For kids: Not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Cough expectorant for a congested cough. Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.



Sponsor Message

For kids: Cough medicine is not recommended for children under 4; do not use for children under 2, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.

Honey

Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."

Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.

Thermometer

This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.

Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)

Nasal saline treatment

The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.

One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.

Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days .

Other comfort items

Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.

Sponsor Message

Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub, for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.

Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.

Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.

Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says.

When to call your doctor

As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.

However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.



A fever in infants younger than 3 months; above 102 F for children; 103 F for adults; or any high fevers that last longer than 1-2 days and/or don't respond to fever-reducing medicine.

Shortness of breath or erratic breathing

Extreme thirst, inability to drink liquids, trouble urinating or producing tears, dark urine, severe or persistent vomiting

Confusion, disorientation, extreme irritability or weakness

These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.

Sponsor Message

This digital story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

World.title: These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices
World.content:
These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices

toggle caption i Megan Varner/Getty Images

📲Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App

Some key voters say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.

NPR observed two online focus groups Tuesday night with 12 Georgians who voted for President Biden in 2020 and then supported Trump in 2024.

Almost every voter — 11 out of 12 — said they were disappointed with the overall job Trump has been doing. And 10 said they regret voting for him.

"I've been disappointed," said Charles P., 43, who identified as a Democrat. (The voters participated under the condition their last names would not be used.)

Sponsor Message

"I just don't feel like there's any positive to this administration at all," he continued. "Inflation has only gotten worse, there've been more wars. The tariffs haven't done anything. It seems like we have more enemies now than ever. I just don't see anything positive with his tenure."

Richard A., a 56-year-old Republican, said he's been out of work for 10 months and there is a long list of problems he sees with the direction of the country under Trump.

"Food crisis, starting the war with Iran, inflation," he said. "ICE immigration has just torn families apart, has caused deaths. ... It just seems like everything has gone downhill."

The comments align with Trump's faltering approval rating and a darkening midterm outlook for Republicans. Trump has picked up his campaign travel in recent days, touting his record and arguing for the GOP to retain control in Washington.

These focus groups with swing voters are conducted every month in battleground states across the country. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project.

Focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, but they do provide insight into what voters are thinking. And in this case, they provide some insight into how voters are deciding who they are supporting this fall.

Sponsor Message

Swinging to Democrats

Rich Thau, president of Engagious, moderates these focus groups. He said for the first time this year, a majority of swing voters said Trump was going to influence their midterm decisions.

"In previous months, when we asked people whether President Trump would influence how they vote, they would say things like, 'Well, I'm looking mainly at the candidates themselves,' or 'I'm looking at the overall sort of environment in the country,'" Thau said.

"This month, seven out of 12 said that he would influence them to vote for Democrats. And that was new."

Karla S., a 49-year-old Democrat, was one of those seven.

"I did vote Republican for 2024," she said. "I made up my mind. I've been so disappointed that I'm just going to go straight and just do Democrat, Democrat, Democrat. Because I'm so disappointed with how this administration has been doing."

Cedric, a 41-year-old independent, said he won't be voting for any politicians that are closely aligned with Trump.

"I think we're not going in the right direction, so I don't want to vote for a candidate that's not going to stand up to him or they're going to go along with his policies," he said. "I'm looking for something different."

Ten out of the 12 participants said they plan on voting for Georgia incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Some voters said they wanted to keep him in office specifically because he wouldn't be aligned with Trump.

Restoring order

Thau said some voters felt that if Democrats take control of Congress, it could provide some needed stability to the country — and the economy, in particular.

"There was some sense that Democrats could restore some semblance of order, and that they'd be able to control a bit of what the president is trying to do or has been doing, to the point where that might restore some of their confidence in the economy," he said.

Sponsor Message

That's what Thomas M., a 65-year-old independent voter, said is his expectation of a Democratic-run Congress.

"I think there would be more controls placed on Trump with people who are not afraid to stand up to him," he said.

In contrast, if Republicans retain power, Thau said "some respondents told us they thought that the president would have even more control over what goes on because Republicans are afraid to stand up to him."

Jennifer W., a 43-year-old Republican, said she worries "Trump would have free rein."

World.title: Carney says Albertans should vote ‘No to the Nine’ in referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans should vote against the nine referendum questions focused on immigration and constitutional reform as he visited Calgary on Thursday.

“I just wanted to come here, thank you for what you’ve already done, thank you what you’re going to do in the next few days,” Carney told the crowd in the city's northeast.

“Make sure everyone’s out there marking their ballots ... including, ‘No to the Nine.’”

“No to the Nine” is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine ballot questions on Oct. 19, in addition to voting to remain in Canada.

Carney was meeting with volunteers and others at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary.

Earlier, he appeared to discuss the campaign with a person holding a sign tied to a campaign from Public Interest Alberta, an education advocacy group.

“‘No on the Nine’ … that’s good,” Carney said.

WATCH | Carney says 'No to the Nine' while campaigning in Calgary: Carney says 'No to the 9' while campaigning for Canadian unity in Calgary | Duration closed caption 3:06 Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Calgary Thursday to rally Albertans to choose Option 1 to stay in Canada in Alberta's referendum on Monday. While here, he also voiced his support for the 'no' side on questions 1 to 9 that deal with immigration and constitutional changes.

The prime minister has previously spoken out on the separatism question. In a Thanksgiving message delivered from a classroom in Edmonton, Carney highlighted various federal initiatives, such as the Pacific Link pipeline.

“We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines,” Carney said.

Carney is scheduled to join former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for his "Forever Canadian" group later today, while Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver a pro-unity message at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Friday.

Carney is also expected to attend rallies on Friday in Edmonton and Red Deer.

Volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park hold placards for Alberta's referendum during a visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, while saying she has voted to remain in Canada, has advocated for Albertans to vote yes on the other nine questions.

Speaking to CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault during a one-on-one interview in Calgary last week, Smith said the nine questions are those which she “wants a mandate” on.

“I haven’t been neutral on that,” Smith said. “I’ve been persuading people that this is what we need to do.”

Earlier this week, three former Alberta premiers urged voters to say “no” to the five immigration-related questions on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot.

CBC News has requested additional comment from the Prime Minister’s Office and a spokesperson for Smith.

Liberal MP says he's voting against questions

Liberal MP Corey Hogan, who represents a Calgary riding, spoke to the Calgary Eyeopener on Thursday about the nine other questions.

Hogan said he was voting “no” to the entire process.

“We should be asking ourselves, do we want to reward this kind of behaviour? And I don’t think that we should,” Hogan said.

“I don’t think that we should use our country as a bargaining chip … I think the questions are quite manipulative, they’re written in ways to get certain answers.”

LISTEN | Liberal MP Corey Hogan talks to the Calgary Eyeopener ahead of the referendum: Calgary Eyeopener 10:05 Referendum 2026: Corey Hogan While Prime Minister, Mark Carney, is in town tonight for a pro-Canada rally at the BMO Centre, Calgary-Confederation Liberal MP, Corey Hogan, joined the show to voice his own thoughts ahead of Monday's referendum.

Although he said he’d vote “no” to all nine questions as a sort of protest to the process, he was more open to ballot question seven, which involves abolishing the federal Senate.

“With all love to my senator colleagues, I love senators, I don’t love the Senate,” he said.

World.title: Arizona university to 'part ways' with coach who oversaw training where Matthew Mayich collapsed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Arizona State University (ASU) says it will "part ways" with the hockey coach who oversaw the training at which Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on a hot day this August.

ASU has “reached a mutual agreement to part ways with hockey coach Greg Powers,” officials said in a statement Thursday, adding that former NHL coach Dave Hakstol will replace him.

Mayich, an NHL prospect drafted by the St. Louis Blues, remains in hospital in serious condition, his family’s lawyer, Robert Carey, said Thursday.

In an initial review released last month, ASU official James Rund wrote that Mayich collapsed at a training at ASU’s Tempe campus just before 8:30 a.m. Aug. 20. The review also said coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

ASU then said it would commission an independent review, to be conducted by former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales.

Mayich's family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances around the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to his collapse. Mayich's parents say he was healthy prior to the workout. The family's lawyers said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

WATCH | Mayich family demands answers: Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout | Duration closed caption 2:26 The parents of Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old NHL prospect from Stoney Creek, Ont., speak to CBC News after their son collapsed after 'military style' training at Arizona State University. Mayich is in critical condition and unlikely to recover, says his lawyer.

Family says Powers should cooperate with investigation

"Our focus remains where it has been since August 20, on Matthew, and making sure what happened to him is fully understood and never happens to another player," the Mayich family said in a statement through Carey Thursday.

They said Bales's investigation must continue "with its full scope, gathering all digital evidence and covering everyone involved in that morning’s workout and in approving it, and its findings must be made public."

"Coach Powers’s departure should not limit his cooperation or anyone else’s, and the players who have spoken up must be protected," the family added. "We wish Coach Hakstol, his staff, and the players a safe and successful season."

Seven of Mayich's teammates anonymously sent a letter to ASU's president Michael Crow on Sept. 28, disputing some findings from the school's review of the workout that led to his collapse. Players alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

It urged that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."

Powers had been ASU’s head coach since 2015 and, in 2022, signed a five-year contract extension through the 2026-27 season. He was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 30, ASU said in a statement. ASU assistant coach Mike Corbett was appointed to lead the team.

University hires Colorado Avalanche assistant coach

Before ASU announced hiring Hakstol on Thursday, he had been working as an assistant coach for the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche. He previously worked as a head coach with the Philadelphia Flyers and the Seattle Kraken, as well as an assistant for the Toronto Maple Leafs.

In a post to X on Thursday afternoon, ASU said the staffing shakeup was a "new chapter of Sun Devil Hockey" and shared a statement from Hakstol which said, in part, "I couldn't be more excited to return to college and bring a winning culture to Arizona State Sun Devil Hockey."

ASU Athletics Director Graham Rossini also announced that former NHL player Matt Greene, who played for the Los Angeles Kings and Edmonton Oilers, would join the team as an assistant along with current assistant, Jimmy Mullin. Corbett’s status was not announced.

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

World.title: The 'leap second' is no more. How a minor time adjustment became a major problem
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth.

On Thursday, an international timekeeping body in France voted to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour, which could take centuries or even millennia.

The precise atomic time we use to track our days — developed in the 1950s and measured by tracking the natural vibrations of atoms — is slightly out of sync with solar time, which is based on the position of the sun in the sky relative to a specific location on Earth, because the planet's rotation has been gradually slowing.

The leap second was introduced in 1972 as a way to correct the discrepancy. Ten seconds were added immediately, says Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre.

Since then, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, which tracks the difference between the solar day and atomic time, has monitored the discrepancy to determine when an extra second is needed.

When that threshold is reached, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures adds a second at either the end of December or the end of June. Leap seconds have been added 27 times, most recently in 2016.

Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, says leap seconds are becoming increasingly difficult to manage as more systems rely on precise timekeeping. (National Research Council Canada)

If we didn't make those tiny adjustments, nothing would perceptibly change in our lifetimes. But eventually, Beattie says, "you might get the brightest part of the day at midnight and the darkest part of day at noon."

The concept is similar to leap years, whereby a day is added to the end of February every four years to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons because the Earth's orbit around the sun takes about 365¼ days.

Without leap years, our hottest months would eventually fall during what is now winter, and the colder months during summer, Beattie says.

What's the problem?

But the time has come when leap seconds seem to be causing more trouble than they're worth.

"The basic global agreement is that we want to do away with these abrupt leap seconds," Beattie said.

That's because the small adjustment can be a headache for tech and telecommunications companies and infrastructure that relies on precise timekeeping.

WATCH | Potential issues with the trend toward permanent Daylight time: Sleep experts say permanent daylight time could negatively impact kids | Duration closed caption 2:07 Manitoba clocks won't spring forward or fall back anymore, after the province announced it's doing away with the twice-a-year time change. But some experts say choosing daylight time rather than standard time could cause health issues and will be more of a burden for school-aged teens.

Companies also have different ways of implementing leap seconds, such as changing their clock rates to stretch the extra second over several hours or an entire day.

Beattie says that variation among networks creates a risk of system failures.

The leap second was blamed for Reddit and LinkedIn crashes in 2012, for example, and brief outages at Cloudflare in 2016.

"The problem is that the needs for timing and network synchronicity are just going up and up, they're ever increasing," Beattie said. "And so the risks are just increasing along with them, because all you need is for some system to not implement it properly and then you could have a cascade effect that could cause quite significant problems."

Negative seconds?

There's another complicating twist.

Over the last six years or so, the Earth's rotation has actually sped up, raising the possibility that a "negative leap second" — in which a second would be taken away — could be needed in the future.

Tech giant Meta said in 2022 that a negative leap second could have a "devastating effect" on software, adding, " In any case, every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures."

The fix, passed Thursday by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, is instead to let those extra seconds add up to 3,600 — a full hour — before adjusting the clocks, pushing the issue many generations down the road. The change will take effect in May 2027.

Not everyone is impressed by this approach.

Paul Delaney, a York University physics and astronomy professor emeritus, says he was "surprised" to hear the proposal.

"It is a problem for an increasingly computerized, AI-oriented economy, and that's obviously what we have," he said. "But that said, gosh, don't we still hire computer programmers to sort these sorts of things out? Some part of me says that we're throwing in the towel and saying, 'Oh, it's too difficult to do, and what the heck, it is just a second.'"

'Not a perfect system'

Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, says many factors affect the Earth's rotation speed, but it has tended to slow over time, in part because of the moon's effect on Earth's tides.

But complex variables, including climate change and glacial melting, can cause changes in that trend.

She says there is no perfect system for our clocks to account for these shifts and "we'll be fine" without leap seconds.

"This is a real human problem that we've been struggling with forever, as long as we've been watching the stars move across the sky and tracking when the sun rises and sets, and trying to get the patterns right," Lawler said.

"It's always going to be a little bit wrong, and I think we just have to accept that."

World.title: 'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski blamed his kidnapping for the fact he's currently representing himself at his own trial in a victim impact statement he read at the sentencing submissions hearing for his kidnapper on Thursday.

"I have had to forego any normal routines, like having a steady job, as a safety precaution, which has spiralled into significant financial difficulties which have had far reaching consequences," said Pleterski in Superior Court in Toronto.

"The most significant is my inability to pay for a lawyer to defend me against the false allegations that this individual and others have made against me."

Pleterski's jury trial is currently underway in the same courthouse. He's pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. So far Pleterski has only cross-examined the first of a dozen witnesses called by the Crown.

Deren Akyeam-Pong pleaded guilty to nine charges related to Pleterski's 2022 kidnapping in October of last year. Those charges include kidnapping, assault and various gun charges.

This photo of Pleterski during his December 2022 kidnapping was entered as an exhibit during the guilty plea of his kidnapper Deren Akyeam-Pong. (Ontario Superior Court)

Pleterski, now 27, thought he was meeting with a potential investor on Dec. 5, 2022, when a gun was pressed into his ribs in the backseat of a pickup truck in Toronto. The abduction was the beginning of a three-day-long kidnapping during which Pleterski was threatened and tortured.

The torture included waterboarding, cigarette burns and getting beaten with golf clubs as his captors drove him between several locations in southern Ontario, according to the agreed statement of facts from Akyeam-Pong's guilty plea.

Three other men have also been charged in Pleterski's kidnapping. Their trial is expected to start later this year.

'Cannot sleep at night': Pleterski

"The thought that I may soon end up sharing a jail cell with my kidnappers has completely debilitated my ability to think clearly through this," read Pleterski in court Thursday.

"I cannot sleep at night. I come to court alone and am being asked to represent myself, but all I think about is being locked in a prison for an extended period of time with the same people who kidnapped, beat and threatened me."

Pleterski also spoke about the "emotional consequences" of his kidnapping, which he said are "difficult to explain to those who have not lived through it."

"Fear, stress, uncertainty and the continuing effort to process what happened consumes my thoughts and affects my well-being on a continuous basis."

The Crown in Pleterski's fraud and money laundering trial is alleging he spent investor money on himself, including on flights on private jets. (aiden_pletersik/Instagram)

The Crown in Pleterski's trial is alleging he guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.

"Whatever opinions people may have of me, my financial affairs or the circumstances that preceded these events, no financial dispute justifies kidnapping, violence or intimidation," Pleterski said in his victim impact statement.

"Ultimately, I want to be able to move forward with my life without being defined by these events. I just hope that the time will come that I don't have to look over my shoulder or worry about the safety of my family."

Tracey Vogel, the Crown prosecutor in the kidnapping sentencing, is asking for a 23-year sentence for Akyeam-Pong related to the kidnapping conviction and a separate conviction for eight gun and drug-related offences.

Craig Zeeh, Akyeam-Pong's lawyer, is asking for a 12-year sentence. Sentencing submissions are expected to continue Thursday and Friday.

Pleterski's fraud trial is expected to continue Friday.

World.title: Céline Dion is the latest Barbie doll, but fans quibble over likeness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Already a bestselling recording artist, Grammy and Juno award winner and musical icon, Céline Dion is adding a new accolade to her shelf: Collectible Barbie doll.

But toymaker Mattel's salute to the famed Canadian singer has rankled some fans, who say the likeness doesn't resemble their queen of the power ballad.

Mattel announced the Dion doll on Monday as part of its Barbie Signature Series, the toy company's premium line of collectible dolls celebrating famous faces from the worlds of fashion, the arts, sport and more.

Previous figures honoured with specialty dolls include Miley Cyrus, Whitney Houston, Marilyn Monroe, Venus and Serena Williams, and Dr. Jane Goodall.

WATCH | Céline Dion is now a Barbie doll: Céline Dion finally gets her very own Barbie doll — and yes, there's a Titanic throwback | Duration 0:26 Retailing for $92 Cdn, the limited-edition doll is a nod to the international star’s 1998 performance of My Heart Will Go On at the Academy Awards.

Dion's limited edition doll recreates her look from the 1998 Academy Awards, when the historical romance Titanic scored 11 Oscar wins, including best original song for My Heart Will Go On, which the Quebec-born singer performed during the ceremony.

"It is a true honour to join the Barbie legacy with a doll inspired by one of the most meaningful moments of my career," Dion said in a statement.

"I hope this doll inspires everyone to express themselves with confidence, follow their dreams and believe in the power of their own voice."

The doll is based on Dion's look from the 1998 Academy Awards, where she performed My Heart Will Go from the film Titanic and the soaring ballad won the Oscar for best original song. (Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)

A wave of initial fan reactions expressed dismay on social media; though happy with the tribute, they shared disappointment about the likeness of the doll, which retails for $90.

"So sorry but she doesn't look like our Céline," a fan with the username celinedion_amour noted on the Barbie Instagram announcement, offering praise for the "iconic dress and the necklace" but unhappiness with the doll's face.

"Why did you all do Celine like that?!" added commenter duchess_rizzy. "I thought it's old lady Rose from Titanic."

A host of fans gave the doll thumbs down, saying its face did not resemble the Canadian singer. (Barbie/Instagram)

Others noted that rather than Dion, the doll appeared to resemble actress and former Real Housewives of Beverly Hills cast member Lisa Rinna. Others noted a closer resemblance to Catherine, the Princess of Wales .

Recent concert comeback

Last month, Dion made a momentous return to performing in the Parisian suburb of Nanterre at Plenitude Arena, Europe's largest indoor concert venue, where she kicked off a series of more than two dozen highly anticipated shows that will stretch into 2027.

WATCH | Céline Dion returns to the stage: Celine Dion marks triumphant comeback at Paris residency opening | Duration closed caption 3:27 Tens of thousands of Celine Dion fans gathered to watch the French-Canadian singer return to the stage in Paris, after a diagnosis of stiff person's syndrome in 2022 forced her to take a break from performing.

It marked her first concert in six years, following a brief public performance closing out the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

The Grammy and Juno-winning singer had stepped away from the spotlight in 2022 after revealing she'd been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a progressive neurological autoimmune disorder that causes pain, stiffness and muscle spasms.

World.title: Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been wagered on Ontario municipal races via prediction markets
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Betting on the outcome of elections isn’t allowed in Canada — but that’s not stopping prediction market websites like Polymarket and Kalshi from taking hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of wagers on who will win Ontario’s municipal races this October.

On Polymarket, for example, close to $400,000 has been spent so far on bets about who will be the next Toronto mayor, while about $43,000 has been spent on Kalshi.

Similar wagers have been set up for places like Oshawa, Oakville and Mississauga, with total accumulated bets ranging from about $5,000 to about $40,000. There is also some betting happening on the online "social prediction game" Manifold, which uses play money instead of real currency.

Though there's nothing illegal about a non-Canadian prediction market taking bets on Canadian elections, Ontarians themselves aren't allowed to participate.

Prediction markets, which allow users to bet on nearly any kind of event, are regulated here, with wagers limited to predictions on climate, financial markets or economic indicators, and available solely through dealers authorized by the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO).

Polymarket is also currently riding out a two-year ban in Ontario, after the Ontario Securities Commission argued that the website broke provincial securities law in 2025.

Using VPN’s to hop over digital fences

Even though it’s not allowed here, it wouldn’t be difficult for Canadians interested in betting on municipal elections to do so, says Cristie Ford, an associate professor at the University of British Columbia who focuses on financial regulation.

“You can use a VPN to conceal your physical location, or the location of your computer in Canada, to make it look as though you're outside of Canada,” she said.

Polymarket spokesperson Connor Brandi told CBC News the platform “strictly prohibits the use of VPNs or similar tools to bypass geographic restrictions,” adding that it carries out monitoring and reviews to detect users doing so.

Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever says the platform has seen "no evidence" of the use of VPN's to bet on Ontario races.

"We restrict election markets in Canada. Because we verify every user’s identity and residency at signup, using a VPN does not get around that restriction," she wrote.

WATCH | When prediction markets arrived (legally) in Canada: Controversial prediction market betting coming to Canada | Duration closed caption 2:05 Toronto-based online investment giant Wealthsimple is bringing prediction market betting to Canada through its new app, Wealthsimple Predict. Prediction markets allow users to wager on the outcomes of real-world events, but critics warn they're just another dangerous form of gambling.

The real risk with the betting, and the reason it's not allowed, says Ford, is the possible skewing of public perception of the candidate’s chances in a way that could impact election results.

“By making it look as though there's momentum behind a particular candidate, you can potentially affect whether or not people show up to vote,” she said.

Nelson Pang, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto who studies risk-taking behaviour among young people, says that group is particularly at risk of making unwise betting decisions on the platforms, with a lot of industry marketing and advertising targeted toward young men.

CBC News asked both of Toronto's leading mayoral candidates — Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford — about their reaction to the wagers.

“I am certainly not engaged in any of that,” said Bradford. He encouraged people to vote, not bet, saying it's the “only way” to make political change.

Chow, speaking at a campaign event promoting libraries, said that she hasn’t looked at the platforms but that it’s up to other levels of government to finetune their regulations.

“That’s a whole lot of money,” she added. “Maybe that money could be donated to the library foundation.”

Who’s in charge?

While the risks of this kind of wager may be clear — it’s trickier to identify which Canadian authority should be ultimately tasked with enforcing the rules.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), which banned Polymarket, says it expects all parties subject to its orders and settlement agreements to comply with their obligations.

Ultimately, though, the OSC says the regulation of prediction markets is up to the Canadian Securities Administrators, an umbrella organization that represents provincial government agencies, and the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, a non-profit that allows the investment industry to self-regulate.

The Canadian Securities Administrators, meanwhile, said it's CSA members that are tasked with using their "rule-making and enforcement powers to help safeguard investors" using prediction markets.

LISTEN | Prediction markets, manipulation and global geopolitics: Day 6 8:51 Wagering on war: Prediction markets net millions and spawn allegations of insider trading Prediction market platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi are apps where anonymous users can place bets on just about anything. When several users cashed in big this week on bets about the timing of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, there were allegations of insider trading and calls for regulation. Sarah Mills, a Professor of Human Geography at Loughborough University in England, explains how prediction markets work and why they’re ripe for manipulation.

In its response to CBC News, CIRO spokesperson Ariel Visconti reiterated its rules around which topics and investment dealers are authorized, but didn’t describe any further steps to improve regulation enforcement.

“If an investor uses a VPN or other means to circumvent geographic restrictions to access these platforms, they are not protected by the regulatory safeguards that apply when trading through a CIRO-regulated investment dealer,” wrote Visconti.

World.title: Pentagon will not livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter: Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice-President JD Vance said he wouldn't watch it.

Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."

But, he continued, "any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."

The Pentagon has said Hasan's execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose."

The announcement earlier this month from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan's execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.

It also came as capital punishment already faced renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived an execution attempt by Tennessee that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalization.

The Pentagon on Thursday declined to elaborate beyond Trump's statement.

Livestream decision backlash

Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things."

When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.

But he continued: "Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration's decision to livestream Hasan's execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered."

WATCH | Pentagon previously said execution would be livestreamed: Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says | Duration 1:49 Former U.S. Army psychiatrist Nidal Malik Hasan is set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, the first military execution in the U.S. in more than 65 years. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a planned attack at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. The Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed.

Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, in Louisiana, voiced similar sentiments.

For his part, the U.S. president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth's announcement that it would be public.

"Well, they're making a determination about that," Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream.

As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: "He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

The cancellation comes less than three weeks before elections to determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress, as voters increasingly register disapproval of Trump's policies in opinion polls.

Sen. John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called the cancellation "the right move" in a statement.

13 killed in Fort Hood shooting

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, at a military base in Fort Hood, Texas.

An Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, Hasan walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment.

He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.

Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, but it's not clear whether or not he will. An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment by Reuters.

The U.S. military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since the Second World War. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

World.title: We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know aren't the healthiest choice.

A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.

But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.

Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health, and could even be linked to some types of cancer.

But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University, published Thursday by JAMA Network Open, signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.

The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.

People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.

But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.

WATCH | Food costs, literacy factors in reliance on unhealthy ultra-processed products: Why it can be hard to avoid ultra-processed foods | Duration closed caption 2:01 Research has shown how bad ultra-processed foods can be for people’s health, but factors including the cost of fresh foods and food literacy can make them harder to avoid for some Canadians.

Feeding the furnace

De Souza and co-author Dr. Sonia Anand, a vascular medicine specialist, examined the diets and brain MRI scans of more than 8,700 Canadian adults, with a median age of about 58, and broke them down into four groups, from those with the lowest intake of UPFs to those with the highest.

The latter cohort was made up of people who consumed nearly 45 per cent of their calories from UPFs, or the equivalent of 16 servings a day, which they self-reported in a survey listing 150 to 170 food items consumed in the past year.

By comparison, the group with the lowest consumption got 15 per cent of their daily calories from UPFs, equal to three servings.

Anand, a professor of medicine and epidemiology at McMaster, says they analyzed the scans of higher-risk participants and found that their UPF-heavy diets were associated with increased body fat and visceral fat — the kind stored deeper in the body and around organs.

"Fat tissue in the wrong places can be almost like a furnace spewing out a whole bunch of inflammatory proteins that then affect our brains," she said.

Ultra-processed foods like instant noodles are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives, preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours, rather than minimally-processed ingredients. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

Anand says the MRIs of the higher-risk group showed changes to the brain similar to silent strokes, a type of stroke that doesn't present any noticeable symptoms but damages the tissue.

These injuries add up over time and make it more likely that people could develop neurological problems, such as vascular dementia, says Dr. Michael Hill, a neurologist and professor at the University of Calgary who is not affiliated with the study.

"The more injuries you accumulate, the more likely you are to have neurological problems later in life, most commonly vascular dementia," he said.

While the damage a UPF-heavy diet may do can't be reversed, Hill says dietary changes can reduce further progression.

"Feed your brain," he said. "It's not just about your gut, right? It's about your whole body."

He says the findings are consistent with a growing body of evidence about the health impacts of UPFs.

LISTEN | About 1/3 of Canadian adults are obese. Ultra-processed foods are a major culprit: The Dose 21:34 What's the harm in eating ultra-processed foods and what can I do about it?

'Eat foods that rot, not rotten foods'

De Souza notes that not all processed foods are ultra-processed and, in fact, many processed products in grocery stores have a lot of nutritional value.

"Some degree of processing is absolutely necessary in the food supply," he said. "It helps keep food safe and shelf stable."

But a can of beans, a bag of frozen vegetables or a container of yogurt are all different from a fast-food meal or a box of sugar-coated cereal.

Foods are classified using what's known as the NOVA system, where foods are determined to be ultra-processed if they are mostly or entirely made from substances derived from plant and animal sources and combined with additives like salt, sugar, fats and oils, as well as preservatives, stabilizers, dyes and artificial flavours.

They also tend to be lower in fibre, vitamins and minerals that benefit overall health, de Souza says.

Hill says that while "one Snickers bar isn't going to hurt you," ultimately, ultra-processed food isn't going to benefit your health — especially if you're eating it regularly.

And even when people want a sugary or salty treat, he says it's going to be better if they make it at home from whole or minimally-processed foods.

"Eat foods that will rot, but not rotten food," he said.

Anand and de Souza note that their study doesn't provide the full picture of the potential toll UPFs can have on brain health and say more long-term research is needed to determine if dietary changes later in life can make a difference.

The next phase of their research will see 2,000 people who took part in the first round of scans receive a second round to determine if reducing the amount of UPFs in their diets results in changes or improvements to brain health.

WATCH | Ultra-processed foods are cheap, convenient and hard to avoid: 5 tips on how to eat fewer ultra-processed foods | Duration closed caption 3:12 Research shows that pre-prepared, packaged, highly processed food (UPF) is linked to weight gain and obesity, some cancers, dementia and more. It’s also highly delicious and convenient. Dr. Chris van Tulleken offers 5 tips for reducing how much UPF you eat. For more information on ultra-processed foods, how they affect our health and what we can do about it, watch Foodspiracy on CBC Gem and The Nature of Things YouTube channel.

Improving health literacy

Anand notes that not everyone has the time or money to prepare high-quality food, which she says is a systemic issue that would require government intervention to reduce the amount of UPFs available and make healthy food more affordable.

It's also a matter of improving health literacy, which she says would increase awareness about the repercussions of consuming too many UPFs.

Canada, she says, could follow the lead of other countries that have successfully minimized the consumption of UPFs. One such country, Chile, implemented mandatory front-of-package labels for UPFs that are high in sugar in an effort to curb childhood obesity.

She says there are things individuals and governments can do "and we need both to happen to make Canadians healthier."

World.title: Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch

British Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called “humiliating” a proposal by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to offer US President Donald Trump the Chagos archipelago in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating,” she told The Telegraph.

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch, who said it was “mad for someone who wants to be prime minister to say we should give away one piece of British territory just to stop an American president talking about another”. “The Chagos Islands are British. And the Falklands are British and will remain British, irrespective of what the American president says. When Donald Trump is right, we should say so. When he is wrong, we should have the confidence to tell him.”

On the US podcast The Benny Show, Farage had suggested offering Trump Diego Garcia “in perpetuity” in return for his silence on the Falklands. “I give him something. I ask for something back. He’d get that. He’s a businessman,” he said. A Reform UK spokesman said he was referring to US use of the base, “not the Chagos Islands as a whole”, and noted that Farage has opposed handing the archipelago to Mauritius.

The deal to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius while retaining the joint Diego Garcia base was paused in April following opposition from the US administration, although Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to see it through. According to The Telegraph, the White House even considered buying the archipelago as an alternative.

The same newspaper notes that Trump said in August he was reviewing the US position on British sovereignty over the Falklands, amid a dispute over defence spending. Burnham assured him in September in New York that the United Kingdom would defend “the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British”.

World.title: US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly
World.content:
US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:02 UTC Full article

The US Treasury Department on Wednesday removed from its sanctions list Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly and brother of acting president Delcy Rodríguez. The Treasury did not explain the reasons for the decision.

Rodríguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was taken off the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, which entails the blocking of assets in the United States, a ban on entering the country and a prohibition on transactions with US citizens and companies. He had been designated in September 2018, along with his sister, former first lady Cilia Flores and then defence minister Vladimir Padrino. At the time, the Treasury said Nicolás Maduro had given them “high-ranking positions” in the government to help him “remain in power”.

Rodríguez was removed from the list in April, which allowed her to travel to New York in September for the UN General Assembly, where she met US President Donald Trump. Rodríguez took power after Maduro and Flores were detained in a US military operation in Caracas in January; both face charges in New York of drug trafficking and, since last week, of torture and repression.

Since then, the Rodríguez government has negotiated an oil agreement with Washington, announced in August, which according to El País gives the United States majority control over a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, the largest in the world. According to Reuters, the Rodríguez siblings pushed legal changes to further open the energy and mining sectors to foreign companies.

Presidential elections remain without a date. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio received in Washington Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in talks with the Venezuelan government, with no announcements. Opposition leader María Corina Machado is not taking part in that dialogue and has been unable to return to Venezuela.

Badenoch responded in The Telegraph: “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating.” She added that “the Chagos Islands are British, and the Falklands are British and will remain British, regardless of what the American president says”, calling Farage’s remarks “careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security”.

Farage didn't say that Trump/USA could use the Chagos Islands in perpetuity. In his interview he literally said he would trade the Chagos Islands for the Falklands. Reform officials and Farage can deny it all they like, but the evidence is right there and cannot be altered. https://t.co/84HYJw12sf — Thomas Evans @Renewal2030 (@ThomasEvansAdur) October 14, 2026

Farage replied on X that Badenoch “is lying again” and said he would offer the United States the use of Diego Garcia, not sovereignty over the archipelago, in return for America going “quiet on the Falklands”. The agreement signed by the British government in 2025 to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius, with a 99-year lease for the base, is on hold following Trump’s opposition. World.title: What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion
World.content:
What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:45 UTC Full article

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat

Argentina has requested Interpol red notices against individuals linked to the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, and the United Kingdom has asked the organisation to reject them as “politically motivated”, according to the British newspaper The Guardian. Interpol responded by reaffirming Article 3 of its constitution, which prohibits any intervention or activity of a political character.

A red notice is a request to police worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. It is not an international arrest warrant: Interpol reviews each request before circulating it, but each state decides whether to act. According to the newspaper, British officials are concerned that Argentina could persuade other countries that its requests are based on domestic law rather than political motives. It has not emerged how many people are affected or whether any notice has been issued.

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat. “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action,” she said. “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.” Workers in the oil and fishing sectors fear being detained if they travel, particularly to South America.

Argentina has launched criminal proceedings against Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, the project’s partners. British officials quoted by The Guardian describe Argentina’s campaign as the most serious since the 1982 war. On Tuesday, London announced measures to shield its companies from Argentine sanctions, and Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion.

World.title: HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol
World.content:
HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:10 UTC Full article

HMS Protector at Devonport Dockyard, Plymouth

Britain has been left without its Ice Patrol after HMS Protector on Tuesday suffered engine problems and had to be towed back to Plymouth, according to reports in the media. This could speed the Royal Navy’s assessment as to whether the vessel originally built in Norway and now with 25 years of rough seas in both poles has to be replaced.

The breakdown comes at a critical moment, when world powers are rushing to take advantage of navigation opportunities in the Arctic, particularly Russia, and in the southern seas, with as ever aggressive Argentina threatening the Falkland Islands development of its resources.

The Telegraph reports that Royal Navy sources admitted the situation as a “catastrophic failure”. And Commander Tom Sharpe, who commanded HMS Endurance, Protector’s predecessor, said it would be “poor timing” to remove the ship from service.

In March, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, admitted that the Navy was not ready for war. It has five active frigates, six destroyers and two aircraft carriers, alongside a submarine fleet of six Astute-class attack boats and four Vanguard-class subs, which carry the UK’s nuclear weapons.

Both carriers, HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth, have reported mechanical problems since their maiden voyages.

Military chiefs are waiting for the spending review for details about how the Government will meet a long-term Nato pledge of increasing the core defense budget to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035.

HMS Protector underpins the UK’s presence in the British Antarctic Territory, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

In 2008, HMS Endurance, the Navy’s previous icebreaker, suffered a flood caused by “poor engineering standards”. At the time, the Navy insisted that she would be repaired and returned to sea. However, she was not and was eventually replaced by HMS Protector after around three years.

HMS Protector was originally named MV Polarbjørn, meaning Polar bear in Norwegian, before being leased in 2011 by the Navy for £8.7m a year. The UK government paid £51m to own the ship outright in 2013. Later refurbished, HMS Protector should expect to have another decade of use before being withdrawn from service.

With a crew of 88, she is typically lightly armed carrying machine guns, but often carries a detachment of Royal Marines. Although classed as a Royal Navy warship, the vessel has retained her original red and white paint scheme. The Royal Navy website says she is affectionately referred to as the “Swiss army knife – red, versatile, and always there when you need her!”

Last month, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, described HMS Protector as an “essential presence” and confirmed she would be replaced at the end of her service life. He said the Ministry of Defense would replace HMS Protector with “a more modern variant” to ensure support for government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory would continue.

A Royal Navy spokesman said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place. As part of the defense investment plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability.

World.title: A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile
World.content:
A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 07:01 UTC Full article

An electrical storm with hail, unusual in the middle of spring, flooded streets, homes and businesses in Santiago, Chile, on Tuesday and produced a tornado that the Chilean Meteorological Directorate preliminarily classified as EF0, the lowest intensity category. The national disaster prevention and response service declared a red alert in the Metropolitan Region, five days after the mudslide that hit the Las Condes district.

The tornado struck a bus terminal in Estación Central, in the west of the capital, where the gust lifted dozens of zinc sheets into the air. The storm began around 3:30pm, as students and workers were leaving schools and offices, and within minutes flooded avenues, underground car parks and buildings, in some cases with water coming through the roofs. According to regional governor Claudio Orrego, around 20 millimetres fell in about two and a half hours, and districts such as Independencia and Providencia recorded some 18 millimetres in one hour.

Some 22,000 homes were left without electricity, according to the Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels. Classes were suspended at municipal schools in Santiago, Providencia and Ñuñoa, and Las Condes extended its restricted-movement perimeter because of the risk of further landslides. Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said “all emergency institutions” had been activated and that the rain was expected to ease overnight.

“Because of global warming, weather processes are intensifying. And we have just had an electrical storm like none ever seen in Santiago,” climatologist Alejandro Vial told the newspaper El País, linking the episode to El Niño.

Last week, an atmospheric river intensified by El Niño made this the wettest October on record in the Chilean capital and caused the October 8 mudslide in San Carlos de Apoquindo, which left six people injured and around 2,000 homes damaged.
