World.content:
New US Hemp Rules Take Effect December 11, Shifting Demand for South American Exporters

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 00:10 UTC Full article

When new US hemp rules take full effect on December 11, the products with the clearest path forward will be non-intoxicating goods made with THC-free ingredients.

One example: The USDA-certified organic CBD gummies sold by Colorado-based Joy Organics, which uses third-party lab testing to confirm non-detectable THC. For hemp growers and extractors in Uruguay, Colombia, and Argentina, that is where US demand is now likely to concentrate.

The change comes from Section 781 of Public Law 119-37, signed in Washington in November 2025, which rewrites the federal definition of hemp for the first time since the 2018 Farm Bill. Compliance moves from delta-9 THC alone to total THC, which also counts THCA, and finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products are capped at 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container.

The law was due to take full effect on November 12. A short-term funding bill signed on September 2 pushed most of it to December 11, although cannabinoids that the plant cannot produce naturally still lose hemp status on the original date.

Flower shipments face the steepest test

South American exporters have sent raw hemp north for several years. Uruguay recorded its first hemp export in 2020, a shipment to Switzerland, and in 2023 a Uruguayan company sent 10 tonnes of CBD flower to the United States, the largest such shipment from the country to date.

Under the new standard, laboratories calculate total THC as delta-9 THC plus 0.877 times the THCA content. Flower that passed the old delta-9 test can fail the new one once THCA is counted, which makes raw plant material the most exposed part of the trade.

The wider US market faces a similar squeeze. The US Hemp Roundtable, an industry group, has estimated that the new definition would eliminate about 95% of existing hemp-derived cannabinoid products, and stakeholders expect the per-container cap to rule out most full-spectrum CBD products as well.

Where demand is likely to move

What remains is a narrower but steadier category: CBD and other non-intoxicating cannabinoids in finished products that stay under the cap. That favours THC-free inputs, chiefly CBD isolate and broad-spectrum distillate from which THC has been removed, over whole flower and full-spectrum oil.

Paperwork will matter as much as the product. US brands selling gummies, softgels and tinctures already publish lab reports for their own goods, and they are expected to demand the same from suppliers. Joy Organics, for example, makes its THC-free gummies in 10, 25 and 50 mg strengths under USDA organic certification and posts batch lab results online. An organic label in the US depends on certified organic ingredients, so that kind of documentation has to travel back up the supply chain to whoever grew and extracted the hemp, which gives growers with organic certification an opening.

The region starts from different positions. Colombia has permitted hemp production for medical and scientific purposes since 2016 and built a licensing system aimed at export. Argentina passed a law in 2022 creating a framework for medical cannabis and industrial hemp. In Brazil, rules issued by the health regulator Anvisa earlier this year allow authorised companies to grow hemp for medicinal and research purposes, including cultivation aimed at exporting plant material. Brazilian trade press has also reported Uruguayan suppliers turning toward Brazil's import market as the US tightens.

December 11 is not necessarily the last word. The delay is tied to the US funding bill, so the date coincides with the next government funding deadline in Washington, and industry groups are lobbying for a regulated framework rather than a ban.

For exporters, the practical reading is simpler. Shipments built around THC-free ingredients and batch-level testing fit the rules as written, while raw flower depends on what Congress does next.

World.title: Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits
World.content:
Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 23:03 UTC Full article

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28

Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order the United Kingdom to prevent the development of the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands and to refrain from granting new permits to exploit the resources of the disputed continental shelf, according to a statement published by the Hamburg-based tribunal. The hearing will be set “at the earliest possible date”.

The request, submitted on October 13 under Article 290(5) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, lists four provisional measures: that the United Kingdom prevent “the commencement or continuation” of hydrocarbon exploitation through Sea Lion; that it refrain from using information obtained from exploring the disputed areas “to the detriment of the rights” of Argentina; that it stop preventing Argentina from complying with its obligation to protect the marine environment of those areas; and that it refrain from any measure that might aggravate the dispute, “in particular the granting of new permits”.

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28. Before that tribunal, Argentina asks for a declaration that the United Kingdom, by unilaterally authorising the exploration and exploitation of resources in the waters around the South Atlantic archipelagos, is in breach of its obligation to respect Argentina’s “sovereignty and sovereign rights” over those maritime areas; of the obligation to refrain from unilateral measures in areas subject to a dispute “within the framework of the decolonization process” of the UN; of the obligation to protect the marine environment; and of the obligation to settle disputes by peaceful means.

To prescribe provisional measures, the tribunal must consider that the arbitral tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the urgency of the situation so requires. In previous cases, such as Chagos in 2015 and Crimea in 2020, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on questions of territorial sovereignty.

The United Kingdom has said it will engage with the process and challenge any attempt to use it to settle sovereignty. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran said on Tuesday that London’s position is that provisional measures are binding on the parties. Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum with 65% and Rockhopper Exploration with 35%, expects first oil in 2028.

World.title: Human rights commission investigates alleged police brutality in Guadalajara: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🚓 Sheinbaum says CNDH now investigating alleged police abuses at Guadalajara protest : The president said the National Human Rights Commission will examine “the use of water [cannons] and gases in the march” and the arrest of young people who were beaten at Sunday’s protest against water contamination. Police allegedly tortured some of the 39 people detained.

: The president said the National Human Rights Commission will examine “the use of water [cannons] and gases in the march” and the arrest of young people who were beaten at Sunday’s protest against water contamination. Police allegedly tortured some of the 39 people detained. 🚨 Sheinbaum backs protection of citizens after Morelos frees alleged crime boss : Asked about the release of José David Vergara, an alleged leader of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group, hours after his capture Monday, the president said, “The important thing is the protection of citizens.” Morelos authorities freed him to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the decision was taken to save lives.

: Asked about the release of José David Vergara, an alleged leader of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group, hours after his capture Monday, the president said, “The important thing is the protection of citizens.” Morelos authorities freed him to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the decision was taken to save lives. 🛂 Government proposes 17.8% increase in entry fee for foreigners: Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez confirmed the proposal to raise the Derecho de No Residente by 175 pesos in 2027, from 983 pesos to 1,158 pesos (about US $63). The increase, which requires congressional approval, is 50% lower than originally proposed. Of the revenue, 57% would go to the Ministry of National Defense, 15% to the National Migration Institute and 28% to the federal treasury.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Thursday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum weighed in on two significant events in recent days: Abuses allegedly committed by police at a protest in Guadalajara on Sunday and the release of a man identified as a criminal leader just hours after he was captured on Monday in the state of Morelos.

A day after saying that her government “cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum acknowledged that the nation’s human rights watchdog is investigating the conduct of Jalisco state police at Sunday’s protest against water contamination in the Guadalajara metro area.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the government’s confirmation that it is proposing to increase the fee non-resident foreigners pay to enter Mexico by 17.8%.

CNDH investigating possible human rights violations at Guadalajara protest

Sheinbaum told reporters that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) is now investigating alleged police abuses during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday.

Police used water cannons and tear gas against protesters and allegedly tortured some of 39 people who were detained during the demonstration.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum said that the CNDH has to conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations of torture.

“The issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” she said.

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” Sheinbaum asked.

On Thursday, she said that the CNDH will investigate “the use of water and gases in the march” and “the arrest of some young people, who were primarily beaten.”

“CNDH is now doing its work in Jalisco,” Sheinbaum said.

The CNDH said in a statement that it was investigating “possible violations of human rights during a protest for access to potable water in Guadalajara,” where water contamination is a long-running problem.

“The objective is to guarantee an expeditious and impartial investigation … into the alleged acts of repression committed by state security officers,” the commission said.

‘The important thing is the protection of citizens,’ Sheinbaum says after alleged crime boss is freed

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about the decision by Morelos authorities to release an alleged criminal leader captured hours earlier. State authorities freed José David Vergara, an alleged leader of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group, on Monday to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers.

Sheinbaum said she didn’t want to create controversy about the decision, but added that “the important thing is the protection of citizens.”

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that the decision taken by Morelos authorities was motivated by the desire to “save lives.”

“There were a lot of civilian people in the streets,” he said, suggesting that their lives could have been endangered by a violent reaction from the Pueblos Unidos criminal group if Vergara wasn’t released.

The capture and subsequent release of Vergara was reminiscent of the capture and release of Ovidio Guzmán López in Culiacán, Sinaloa, in 2019. The capture of Guzmán López, a drug trafficker and son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera, triggered a hostile response from the Sinaloa Cartel, leading authorities to release him in an attempt to quell the violence in the Sinaloa capital.

Tourist fee to increase by 175 pesos in 2027

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez confirmed that the government is proposing that the Derecho de No Residente (DNR) — an entry fee charged to non-resident foreigners entering Mexico, with some exemptions — increase by 175 pesos next year, from 983 pesos to 1,158 pesos (about US $63).

She noted that the proposed increase — subject to congressional approval — is 50% lower than the hike that was originally put forward.

According to a bill that proposes the DNR increase, 57% of the revenue raised will go to the Ministry of National Defense, 15% will go to the National Migration Institute (INM) and 28% will go to the federal treasury.

According to a Tourism Ministry statement, “173.70 pesos of the additional 175 pesos would be allocated to the INM to strengthen technological infrastructure, border security, and immigration control systems.”

World.title: Mexico and My Money: Borrowing for a property purchase in Mexico
World.content:
As the cost of living rises faster than incomes, paying for everything in cash — especially big-ticket purchases — is becoming increasingly difficult for many people.

In a recent MND financial survey, just 3.6% of respondents said they had borrowed money to make a major purchase in Mexico. Yet more than half said they had lent money to someone while living here, and 22% of those lenders had loaned more than US $3,000.

While the survey was not scientific, the fact that many MND readers engage in private lending suggests plenty of financial need in Mexican society that traditional banks are not meeting.

To be clear, it isn’t all bad. Access to formal credit in Mexico has improved in some areas, particularly with auto sales, but remains much more limited in others, such as housing.

So, what financing options are available for those looking to buy property in Mexico? Below, I’ll explore the possibilities, from conventional mortgages to alternative financing.

Borrowing money for a home purchase in Mexico

It may surprise you to learn that only 10% of home purchases in Mexico today involve a mortgage. The other 90% are paid for in cash or through alternative financing methods.

One reason so few buyers use mortgages is that Mexican commercial banks are very cautious, viewing large home loans to ordinary people as too risky. So, they require large down payments and charge high interest rates. As a result, buying a home with a mortgage is simply unaffordable for many Mexican residents.

At the same time, property prices in Mexico — especially in major cities and popular coastal towns — have risen to levels that are high relative to local incomes. This makes access to mortgage financing more important than ever for people hoping to buy a home.

Who offers mortgage loans in Mexico?

In general, U.S. banks do not finance properties in Mexico. To obtain a mortgage here, buyers must work with a Mexican bank that originates loans.

The most active lenders are some of the nation’s largest banks, including BBVA México, Banorte, Santander México and HSBC México.

Mortgage rates are steep and many applicants get denied

In the first half of 2026, mortgage loans from Mexican banks ranged from 8.8% to 11.35%, depending on the lender, with the total annual cost (CAT) including the rate, bank fees and insurance between 11% and 13.9% per year.

Mortgage rates vary based on the amount requested, down payment size, loan term and the quality of your credit profile. Since loan terms are complex, bank regulator Condusef (National Commission for the Protection and Defense of Users of Financial Services) offers a Mortgage Loan Simulator to help consumers more easily compare offers.

Besides high borrowing costs, down payments are also typically higher in Mexico than in the U.S. or Canada. It’s common on a resale property for the buyer to put 20% to 30% down, though some lenders require 30% to 50% if the buyer is a foreigner. One exception is developer-financed properties, which often accept 5% to 10% down initially.

Mexican banks typically offer mortgage loan terms ranging from 10 to 25 years, with 20 years being most common. The entire process takes anywhere from three to five months — so patience is essential.

Even after a long wait, success is not guaranteed.

According to El Economista, only one in four mortgage applicants in Mexico is successful. I’ve seen these low odds play out firsthand, as my husband and I purchased our home in Guadalajara only when the initial buyer was denied a loan and backed out of the deal.

Getting a mortgage in Mexico as a foreigner

Most Mexican banks offer mortgages only to foreign nationals who hold legal permanent residency. Those with temporary residency — and tourists — though legally permitted to buy Mexican property, cannot secure mortgages here, for lack of credit history.

The application process typically involves review and approval by the bank’s credit department, followed by a property appraisal and legal review.

While requirements differ, most lenders ask for the following documents from borrowers:

Identification: Official ID (passport, CURP)

Proof of income: Usually recent pay stubs, tax returns or income statements

RFC number: Mexican tax ID

Credit history: A good credit score is essential

Credit reference letter: From a financial institution you do business with abroad

Down payment: Anywhere from 30% to 50% of the property value

Medical certificate Confirming that the applicant is in good health

It’s also important to know that Mexican banks require that borrowers hold homeowner’s insurance. This must be secured before your loan can be approved. If you buy property here without a mortgage, the choice of whether to buy an insurance policy is up to you.

Alternatives to traditional mortgages

Developer financing for new or not-yet-built properties

This is another option popular with foreign residents who are unable to pay all cash upfront. To attract buyers, most developers accept staggered payments for the purchase.

For example, you might be asked to put 30% down when you sign a contract, with additional payments required in 6- or 12-month intervals, with those future payments being financed by the developer. Because these loans aren’t done through traditional banks, they may carry higher interest rates.

Because I’ve heard plenty of horror stories about Mexican developers who take investors’ money and fail to deliver the property, I would steer clear of any real estate project not yet built. Legal recourse for property deals gone sideways is slow and arduous — and just not worth the risk in my opinion.

Cross-border mortgages

A newer option in Mexican housing finance is mortgages involving a bank in the borrower’s home country that lends money for property purchase in Mexico. For a U.S. citizen, this would entail taking out a dollar-based mortgage originated in the United States.

One company in the cross-border mortgage business is Moxi, which offers dollar-based mortgages for up to 30-year terms at fixed interest rates. The catch is that the minimum loan size is US $250,000, and borrowers are expected to put at least 35% down on the purchase.

These lenders are generally willing to work with legal foreign residents or visitors on tourist visas. However, those with non-resident status typically pay higher interest rates.

Because cross-border mortgages have such high minimums, they are only useful to those intending to buy luxury properties in Mexico, meaning those valued above US $460,000 or roughly 8,404,265 pesos.

Government-backed loans

For those with formal employment (including foreign residents) in Mexico, public financing is another option for accessing housing credit.

Infonavit, the Mexican federal institute for workers’ housing, is the largest mortgage lender in Latin America with more than 12 million mortgages on its books. There are numerous criteria to qualify, but anyone with a steady employment history whose employer has been regularly paying into the mandatory public housing fund is a strong candidate.

Borrower benefits include lower interest rates than commercial mortgages (3.69% to 10.45% right now), fixed rates over the life of the loan, and loan terms ranging from one to 30 years. An interesting twist with Infonavit loans is that lower earners pay lower rates while higher earners pay higher ones, the opposite of commercial lenders.

The catch with these public loans is that the amount borrowed cannot exceed 2.935 million pesos (US $131,087).

To wrap up, taking out a mortgage in Mexico is a major decision. Before moving ahead with a property purchase in Mexico with financing, I recommend seeking the opinion of a qualified financial advisor.

From tipping and working with local contractors to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Venezuelan food in Mexico City: How immigrants are shaping CDMX cuisine
World.content:
According to the International Organization for Migration, by December 2024, more than 7.89 million Venezuelans had left their homeland in the last 25 years, making it the second-largest population displacement in the world.

While Colombia is far and away the most common destination for displaced Venezuelans, the official INEGI census in 2020 counted more than 52,000 Venezuelans living in Mexico, while Milenio reported in 2025 that, at nearly 26,000, they now make up the largest group of foreign residents in Mexico City, not counting undocumented arrivals. Studies show that most Venezuelans obtain visas and permanent residency cards if they can, suggesting they intend to stay, work and live in Mexico City long term.

A growing presence across the capital

View this post on Instagram A post shared by VENEZUELAN STREET FOOD 📍 CDMX (@ochotrescinco)

While this community is less than 1% of the city’s 9 million residents, you can note their influence if you pay attention — Venezuelan flags fluttering outside of restaurants in Narvarte and Polanco, arepa flour on the shelves of local grocery stores, Venezuelan accents calling out wares for sale along the streets of the Centro Histórico. Most of these immigrants arrived over the last decade, the years of deepest economic and social upheaval in their home country. But a small number of Venezuelans have been in Mexico since the mid-20th century.

In 1948, a small group of Venezuelan exiles came to Mexico fleeing the military coup that toppled democratically elected Rómulo Gallegos. This wave of around 1,000 immigrants and their families was led by Gallegos himself (besides being the ousted president, he was also the country’s most well-known novelist) and Andrés Eloy Blanco, Venezuela’s most celebrated poet and chancellor of the deposed government. It was an era when Mexico welcomed thousands of Europeans escaping World War II and Latin Americans fleeing political unrest in their countries.

Decades of migration and pivotal shifts

From then until the early 2000s, only a small trickle of Venezuelans moved to Mexico, with many working in the oil industry in places like Veracruz and Tabasco. However, when leftist Hugo Chávez was sworn in as president in 1999, many Venezuelans, particularly middle-class professionals who feared his policies, started leaving. They came with visas, passports and degrees, ready to start a new life elsewhere.

That was when Glexsy Abreu arrived in Mexico. She had been introduced to her soon-to-be husband years before, but now she was making a permanent move to Mexico City from Maracaibo. In Mexico, she would have to completely start over when her hematology degree from Venezuela was not accepted, and she couldn’t practice as a doctor. She worked for seven years at the Venezuelan Embassy issuing passports, and she says she watched the flow of immigrants from her country slowly increase into the 2010s.

The influx reached a pivotal moment in 2015, when global oil prices crashed and the quality of life in Venezuela plummeted. The country experienced one of the most dramatic exoduses of its residents to date, with many working-class and low-income residents simply walking out of the country on a treacherous journey north.

Policy shifts and shelter in Mexico City

For many of these migrants, Mexico was not their intended destination. Most had their sights set on the United States. In 2022, Mexico and the U.S. announced a bilateral agreement that the U.S. would accept 24,000 Venezuelans who could prove they had financial support. Those who attempted to enter illegally would be sent back to Mexico.

In the fall of 2025, the population of a government-run shelter in Mexico City’s Tepito neighborhood was almost entirely Venezuelan women and children. Most had walked across the Darién Gap, a harrowing trip that took them through a 60- to 100-mile stretch of dense rainforest, swamps and steep mountains on the border between Colombia and Panama.

The women made it to Mexico just as border restrictions in the United States started to tighten, and so they made the choice to remain in the capital. By 2025, many had been living and working in CDMX for several years. In March 2024, the Venezuelan government offered free flights to anyone who wished to repatriate, and these women took advantage of the program. They moved into the shelter to wait for their flights home. By December 2025, they were all back in Caracas.

Building new lives through regional cuisine

Other immigrants, in particular middle-class professionals, had less dramatic exodus stories. Freddy Soto from the Ocho Tres Cinco restaurant in Roma Norte had already been traveling between Miami and his hometown of Maracaibo near the Colombian border. When his wife was offered a television and film production job, they decided to move to the capital and try their luck in Mexico. A few years later, they opened their restaurant.

Freddy draws the inspiration for the menu at Ocho Tres Cinco from his hometown, a tropical destination that sits next to one of Venezuela’s largest oil reservoirs in Lake Maracaibo. Their specialty is the agüita de sapo, an extra-crispy arepa stuffed with slow-roasted beef and deep-fried cheese drowned in a sauce made from beef broth thickened by hours of slow cooking.

It’s washed down with a refreshing papelón — an iced-tea-like drink made with unrefined cane sugar (piloncillo) and lemon juice that you will find in almost every Venezuelan restaurant on the planet. My personal favorite is at Páramo House in Mercado Roma, where it’s made almost effervescent, with less sugar and freshly squeezed lemon juice.

Staples, flavors and shared traditions

Similar to Mexican cuisine, corn is fundamental to Venezuelan cooking, and foods like arepas (a thick corn patty), hallacas (a regional corn tamal), and cachapas (a type of sweet corn pancake) are common on menus and in kitchens. But there are also lots of tropical flavors like plantains (both sweet and savory), tangy, fresh regional cheeses, tubers like yuca and tropical fruits.

Then there are black beans and rice, common to most Caribbean cuisines, as well as various preparations of slow-cooked meats. One of Glexsy’s favorite dishes to make at home is asado negro — beef coated in a sweet-and-savory papelón sauce.

Some of the country’s most well-known recipes include tequeños (a kind of cheese stick that looks like pigs in a blanket and is sometimes filled with guava paste), pastelitos (a small, savory fried pie), and pabellón criollo, which is the national dish.

Every regional cuisine has its distinctiveness, and those closest to the border with Colombia include a lot of cross-border borrowing of flavors and techniques.

Expanding culinary landscapes across the capital

One of the best Venezuelan flavors is guasacaca salsa — a bright, intense blend of garlic, cilantro, parsley, vinegar and other spices. I had it recently at Comandante Pollo, a new restaurant in Colonia Roma dedicated to the flavors of Caracas. The traditional rotisserie chicken marinated in mojo de ajo and citrus is a bright alternative to the cumin-oregano-achiote-rubbed rotisserie chickens of Mexico, and the yuca fries with guasacaca salsa were unbeatable. The sweet plantains with shredded queso fresco and papelón honey were also fantastic.

These days, Venezuelan kitchens are spread across the city — in Polanco, Narvarte, Del Valle and other colonias. Some are great and some lack sazón.

As the community grows, so do the options, providing the city with yet another delicious culinary addition to all the others we’ve discovered through this series on Mexico City’s immigrants and their food.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: Space debris on Mexico’s Bagdad Beach might be from a launch by SpaceX
World.content:
High tides are slowing efforts to remove suspected SpaceX debris found on Playa Bagdad — a stretch of Mexican coastline in the northeastern border state of Tamaulipas — where environmentalists reported collecting more than 200 fragments in the first 400 meters of a cleanup.

The conservation nonprofit Conibio Global said on Facebook it had delivered another bag of suspected space debris to Mexico’s federal environmental protection agency (Profepa).

🚀 #EsNoticia | ¿Qué está llegando del espacio a las costas de #Tamaulipas? En Playa Bagdad, reportan nuevos fragmentos que presuntamente provienen de cohetes de #SpaceX. La ONG Conibio Global pide investigar su origen y posibles daños ambientales. Mira esto. #OnceNoticias 🔻 https://t.co/TTke3t14Se — Once Noticias (@OnceNoticiasTV) October 10, 2026

The organization suspects the fragments came from SpaceX’s 14th Starship flight, launched Sept. 28 from Boca Chica, Texas — just across the border from Bagdad Beach, which takes its name from a historic port destroyed by hurricanes in the late 1800s.

However, the origin of individual pieces has not been confirmed.

Concerns about the debris harming marine life echo earlier discoveries.

In June 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico’s Environment Ministry (Semarnat) and other ministries would investigate debris reported on Bagdad Beach. At the time, hundreds of metal and plastic fragments had washed ashore following a Starship test flight launch.

In response at the time, SpaceX said tests of Starship materials found no chemical, biological or toxicological risks, and that it had offered Mexico resources and assistance to help recover debris.

As for the most recent cleanup, the newspaper Milenio reported that Conibio Global aimed to survey 50 kilometers of coastline, about 31 miles.

The group said tides had blocked access to some areas and that collection would resume when conditions dictate.

Inspections so far have identified insulation and coating materials. Environmentalists said waves, rain and currents could carry more fragments ashore.

Conibio Global warned that turtles, dolphins, birds and other marine animals could ingest debris or become entangled.

It called on authorities to identify the fragments, investigate potential environmental harm and require those responsible to repair any confirmed damage.

It also sought investigations into reported structural damage to homes and schools and declining fishing catches. However, reports do not establish causal links to SpaceX launches.

Playa Bagdad lies on Mexico’s Gulf coast, south of the Rio Bravo’s mouth. Known as the Río Grande in the United States, the river originates in Colorado and forms the entire 2,018-kilometer border between Texas and Mexico.

With reports from Uno TV, Once Noticias, Milenio and La Razón de Tamaulipas

World.title: Healthcare workers protest in virtually every state over pay, shortages and staffing
World.content:
Listen to this article

Thousands of Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers took to the streets of Mexico City and other cities across Mexico on Tuesday to demand higher pay, better work conditions, increased funding for healthcare and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

In the capital, around 7,000 workers, including doctors, nurses, orderlies, social workers and administrative staff joined a so-called megamarcha (mega-march), which set off from the IMSS-run Siglo XXI National Medical Center in the Doctores neighborhood at 4 p.m. and made its way to IMSS offices on Paseo de la Reforma, the tree-lined boulevard that runs into the historic center.

🔴“¡Presente!” Con un pase de lista, manifestantes mencionan a los estados donde trabajadores del IMSS se movilizan para exigir un aumento salarial, mejores condiciones laborales y el abasto de medicamentos e insumos médicos en las unidades de salud. https://t.co/hOiEVTO42z — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) October 14, 2026

“Don’t get sick because there are no supplies” and “Listen up people, this is your fight too” were among the slogans chanted by the protesting workers.

IMSS workers protested in virtually every state across Mexico on Tuesday, and additional demonstrations were held on Wednesday, including in Mexico City. Among the cities where protests were held on Tuesday were Monterrey, Guadalajara, Tijuana, León and Mérida. Some IMSS derechohabientes (beneficiaries) and other supporters of healthcare workers, including members of various unions, also participated in the protests.

IMSS is a major healthcare provider in Mexico, running hospitals and clinics across the country. Some 78 million people have healthcare coverage through IMSS, a figure that accounts for around 60% of Mexico’s total population. IMSS has more than 520,000 employees, around 80% of whom work in healthcare-related roles.

A 10% pay rise among workers’ demands

Thousands of IMSS workers have made it clear that they reject an offer of a 2.9% pay rise coupled with a 3.9% increase in benefits. Instead, they are demanding a 10% increase to their base pay.

IMSS workers reportedly turned out in large numbers to vote on the proposed pay rise on Wednesday. The newspaper Reforma reported that workers “fear the result might not reflect the will of the voters because the union is the judge” — i.e., members of the National Social Security Workers Union are overseeing the voting process.

At Tuesday’s protest in Mexico City, workers said they were formerly considered “heroes” because of their work during the COVID pandemic, but have now been “forgotten on the payroll.”

In addition to higher pay, IMSS workers have a range of other demands. They include:

The adequate supply of medications and medical supplies in IMSS hospitals and clinics.

The hiring of additional healthcare personnel in order to ease excessive workloads.

The allocation of resources equivalent to 7% of GDP to healthcare. (Mexico’s public and private expenditure on healthcare was below 6% in 2024, according to the OECD.)

Respect for their labor rights, including their right to speak out about problems in IMSS healthcare facilities.

Modifications to the Social Security Law to guarantee the ongoing financial viability of IMSS.

Changes to their pension system.

Additional upgrades to IMSS healthcare infrastructure. (The government has been modernizing hospitals.)

IMSS workers are also calling for the resignation or dismissal of Rafael Olivos Hernández, head of the National Social Security Workers Union. Workers have accused Olivos of pressuring them to accept the 2.9% pay rise on offer and violating union statutes. Some workers also called for the dismissal of IMSS chief Zoé Robledo.

Outside the IMSS offices on Paseo de la Reforma, disgruntled IMSS workers said that their fight for better pay and conditions is just getting started. They pledged to keep up the pressure with future protests if their demands aren’t met.

Vinicio Martínez, a spokesperson for protesting IMSS workers, told Reforma that protests could be “intensified” and that “activities that are a little bit more drastic” could be carried out “until our voice is heard.”

‘There are no syringes, [rubbing] alcohol or diapers. We’re short-staffed, too’

Workers who protested in Mexico City on Tuesday offered firsthand accounts of the conditions they face in IMSS healthcare facilities.

A nurse from the No. 30 General Hospital in the Mexico City borough of Iztacalco told the La Jornada newspaper that no one is called in to cover for staff who are on vacation or off sick.

“We don’t know why,” said the nurse, who asked to remain anonymous.

“We’ve had deficiencies for years and the quality of [medical] supplies has declined significantly,” she said.

The same woman rejected the proposed 2.9% pay increase, saying that it would only increase her fortnightly salary by 109 pesos (about US $6).

“That would be my raise if the union proposal is supported,” she said.

“I’m a single mother, I have a son at university and a daughter at primary school. It’s an insult to the work we do.”

José, a nursing student who works at the No. 32 General Hospital in the capital’s Coyoacán borough, told La Jornada that basic supplies are lacking.

“There are no syringes, [rubbing] alcohol or diapers. We’re short-staffed, too,” he said.

José also denounced the heavy workload medical personnel face, saying that it affects the quality of care they can provide.

América Barragán, a nurse from Jalisco who traveled to Mexico City to participate in Tuesday’s megamarcha, told Reforma that the public healthcare system lacks funds, medicines, medical supplies and personnel. She said that hospitals are overwhelmed by patients, who face long waits to receive specialized care.

“The demand to treat more patients in less time affects both working conditions and the quality and timeliness of medical services,” Barragán said.

She said that the problem won’t be resolved by demanding greater productivity from healthcare workers. Instead, more resources need to be allocated to healthcare, more workers need to be hired and hospital infrastructure needs to be upgraded, Barragán said.

She called on authorities to respond to IMSS workers’ demands with concrete solutions.

Sheinbaum: Workers’ ‘legitimate demands’ are being addressed

Asked about IMSS workers’ protest at her Wednesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum initially responded by showing aerial footage of the Mexico City march.

“We took it from social media; it’s not filmed by the government or anything, but rather …by people who had drones,” she said.

“It’s important for everyone to reach their own conclusions,” Sheinbaum said before presenting footage that showed that the march stretched for quite a distance, but the crowd was relatively thin.

“That was the protest,” she said, adding that everyone could do “their own count of how many people participated.”

Sheinbaum went on to say that IMSS workers’ “legitimate demands” are being addressed. She conveyed the same message at her Tuesday morning press conference, during which she said resident doctors’ salaries would be increased and acknowledged that the government has work to do to improve the distribution of medications and medical supplies to public hospitals.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum said that Robledo, the IMSS director, has been instructed to draw up an “action plan” to “immediately” address “all the legitimate demands of IMSS workers.”

“… When there is a legitimate demand, we’re listening,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that IMSS workers would vote on the proposed pay rise on Wednesday.

“A union consultation is taking place today to see whether [the pay rise] offered by IMSS management is approved or not. It was already approved in Congress, but as there were people who didn’t agree an open consultation is taking place,” she said.

“I asked the Mexican Social Security Institute to ensure that it is totally free,” Sheinbaum said. “… We’re going to wait for the results.”

A day after she outlined a range of government achievements in the area of healthcare, Sheinbaum said that her government is working hard to improve Mexico’s public healthcare system.

“We’re doing better [but] there are still challenges and we have to solve them,” she said.

With reports from La Jornada, Sin Embargo, Reforma, El Financiero and El Economista

World.title: The IMF casts doubt on Mexico’s chances of cracking the top 10 of world economies by 2030
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has thrown cold water on Mexico’s ambitious plan to return to the world’s Top 10 economies by 2030 by declaring in its latest World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, that the goal is unlikely to be reached until at least 2031, if then.

Citing underinvestment as a major factor, the IMF indicated that the expected maximum GDP growth rate over President Claudia Sheinbaum’s first term (ending in 2030) is 2.2%, not enough to reach 10th place among world economies. Sheinbaum had announced that goal shortly after her first 100 days in office two years ago in presenting her Plan México, which has guided Mexico’s economic policy since.

The IMF expects the average annual rate to reach 1.7% during President Sheinbaum’s term, compared with 0.9% under her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador and 1.9% under Enrique Peña Nieto (2012-2018).

On October 2, the IMF revised its projections for Mexico’s economic growth to 1.5% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027. It is projected at 2% in 2029, 2030 and 2031, which is lower than the average for Latin America and the Caribbean, which is is expected to exceed 2.5% in those years.

Mexico had held a top 10 position from 1999 to 2004, but by 2025 it had slipped to 15th. It is expected to rise to 13th this year, overtaking Australia and Spain, and is likely to remain there until 2030, when it will displace Russia to reach 12th place.

What Mexico needs to do to move up

In its report, the IMF stressed Mexico’s need to increase private investment by closing infrastructure gaps, reducing regulatory burdens and uncertainty and strengthening trade integration. It also highlighted the need to improve security, combat corruption and reduce informality.

The director of analysis and strategy at the Mexican financial institution Kapital, Alejandra Marcos Iza, cited a lack of investment, moderate consumption and the ongoing United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations as limiting factors for economic growth, suggesting that ongoing uncertainty surrounding trade fragmentation and U.S. tariffs has hindered new productive projects.

Meanwhile, a Bank of Mexico survey published in July, which assessed the opinions of 42 economic analysis groups from the national and international private sectors, highlighted governance issues as a major hindrance to economic growth, including public insecurity, the lack of the rule of law, internal political uncertainty and corruption.

With reports from El Universal and Puente Libre

World.title: El Jalapeño: US man who applied for Mexican citizenship confirms he now somehow knows the lyrics to ‘El Rey’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Naturalization officials confirmed Thursday that a 34-year-old applicant who submitted his final paperwork for Mexican citizenship was immediately, involuntarily infused with the complete lyrics, pitch-perfect phrasing, and emotional gravity of José Alfredo Jiménez’s ranchera classic “El Rey.”

According to witnesses inside the Secretariat of Foreign Affairs (SRE) office, applicant Mark Miller was signing the final page of his administrative petition when his posture visibly shifted. Miller then closed his eyes, tilted his head slightly backward, and spontaneously articulated the nuanced vocal differences between Jiménez’s original 1971 recording and Vicente Fernández’s iconic 1973 cover version.

“I went to hand the clerk my residence card, and suddenly I was overcome by an absolute certainty regarding the exact moment to hold out the syllable in ‘re-e-ey‘,” said Miller, who had previously required a smartphone display to navigate basic verse structures at social gatherings. “I also felt a deep, ancestral understanding that while ‘Chente’ brought unmatchable vocal power to the track, José Alfredo’s version remains the definitive one.”

SRE officials stated that the phenomenon, colloquially referred to by immigration lawyers as the “subliminal cantina effect,” is a standard bureaucratic side effect of the naturalization pipeline. While native-born citizens absorb the complete national songbook passively during childhood family gatherings, naturalized residents typically receive the entire catalog in a single, concentrated neurological download upon biometric verification.

“It is a completely standard administrative outcome,” said SRE spokesperson Ana Luisa Peralta. “Once the background check clears, the applicant’s mind and body automatically integrate ‘Por Tu Maldito Amor,’ the mandatory world-weary vocal inflections for ‘Camino de Guanajuato,’ and the emotional capacity to belt out ‘Querida’ as though they were personally as heartbroken as Juan Gabriel back in 1984.”

Department sources noted that Miller’s files have been cleared for final processing, provided he can successfully complete the mandatory exit physical, which tests an applicant’s ability to distinctly trill their r’s without warm-up exercises.

World.title: Sheinbaum signs decree blocking violent and hostile content from minors’ social media feeds: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📱 Sheinbaum signs decree to curb harmful online content for minors: Social media sites and online forums will be barred from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Platforms must also verify users’ ages, classify content by age group and offer parental supervision tools. The decree, drawn up after an Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, takes effect one month after its publication in the government’s official gazette today.

🚓 Sheinbaum orders CNDH probe into alleged police torture in Guadalajara: The president said the National Human Rights Commission must conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations that Jalisco police tortured people detained at Sunday’s water contamination protest. “How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

⚖️ Sheinbaum defers to judges on ex-INM chief Garduño’s exoneration: Asked about Francisco Garduño’s exoneration over the 2023 Ciudad Juárez detention center fire that killed 40 migrants, the president said, “It’s what the judges determined.” Lawyers for the victims will challenge the ruling.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum signed a decree that will bar social media sites and other online forums from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation or violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyber-bullying and illegal conduct in general.

The government drew up the decree after a fatal Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, that was allegedly perpetrated by twin 18-year-old brothers who authorities say were exposed to violent content and extremist ideology online.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to allegations that Jalisco state police tortured people who were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday during a protest against contaminated water. One woman said that police beat her and stepped on her bare feet, causing fractures.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 people detained during Sunday’s protest had been released. He said that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.”

He also said that “serious mistakes that must be investigated and sanctioned” were made.

“… No one should have been exposed to violence,” Lemus said.

Sheinbaum signs ‘safe digital environments’ decree

Presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde told reporters that she and other officials met with representatives of social media and other tech companies to discuss the “decree to guarantee safe digital environments for girls, boys and adolescents,” which was presented by the government last Friday.

“Far from demonstrating resistance, they perfectly understood the need for an instrument of this nature,” she said.

Alcalde said that the decree will be published in the government’s official gazette today and take effect one month later.

The decree will oblige social media sites to detect and “immediately” remove “accounts and content that promote or generate violent conduct,” she said.

📲 SHEINBAUM FIRMA DECRETO PARA QUE PLATAFORMAS DIGITALES EVITEN DIFUNDIR CONTENIDOS VIOLENTOS La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum da un mes a las plataformas digitales para avanzar en la regulación de contenidos que inciten a la violencia, contra niñas, niños y adolescentes. ⚠️ Advirtió que, si las medidas no funcionan, se promoverá una reforma legal que establecería SANCIONES. Aclaró que no se trata de censura, sino de garantizar espacios digitales seguros. 📱🫡🫡 — Isabel Uribe (@Isa_Uribe) October 14, 2026

Alcalde said that social media sites will also have to “classify content” by its appropriateness for different age groups, verify the age of their users and “establish supervision tools” for mothers, fathers and legal guardians of minors.

Before signing the decree, Sheinbaum noted that social media and “digital platform” companies agreed with the government’s initiative.

“The only thing they asked for was a month to prepare their platforms so that this is a reality,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the government’s Digital Transformation and Communications Agency will monitor social media sites to ensure that companies are complying with the decree.

“If we see they aren’t complying, we would move onto a law which would involve sanctions for the platforms,” she said.

Sheinbaum orders investigation into allegations of police torture in Guadalajara

Regarding allegations that police tortured people who were detained during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday, Sheinbaum said that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) has to conduct a “very thorough investigation.”

“Yesterday I was asked about the issue of torture in Jalisco. … What happened in Jalisco can’t be allowed,” she said.

“… In addition to the use of streams of water and tear gas [against protesters], the issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” Sheinbaum said.

“A police force cannot torture anyone,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the CNDH investigation should examine “who gave the order” to torture detainees and interview “the victims.”

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to exoneration of former INM chief

A reporter asked the president her opinion about the exoneration of former National Migration Institute (INM) chief Francisco Garduño, who faced a charge of improper exercise of public service in connection with a 2023 fire in an INM detention center in Ciudad Juárez that killed 40 migrants.

“It’s what the judges determined,” Sheinbaum responded.

Garduño, head of the INM between 2019 and 2025, was exonerated at a court hearing in Ciudad Juárez on Tuesday. Lawyers for the victims said they will challenge the decision.

Sheinbaum said that “a very thorough investigation” that examined “the responsibilities of each person” in connection with the fire was carried out. She then reiterated that the exoneration of Garduño was a decision made by “judges.”

According to authorities, the fire started when two detained migrants set a mattress alight to protest poor conditions in the INM detention center. Those two men survived the blaze and face homicide charges.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office began criminal proceedings against Garduño in April 2023, alleging that he failed to fulfill his duty to “supervise, protect and provide security to the people and facilities” under his control.

In September 2025, the former INM chief issued an apology to victims and relatives of the deceased.

There were “human rights violations that never should have happened” due to “omissions by personnel of the [INM],” he said at the time.

The Associated Press reported that Garduño “called for ‘those responsible’ to be punished and for reparations to be made without recognizing his own responsibility in the tragedy.”

To date, no one has been convicted of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the deadly fire.

World.title: Brazil Harvest Hits Record 354.5M Tons
World.content:
BRAZIL · AGRICULTURE

Key Facts — What is happening Brazil’s statistics institute IBGE estimated on Thursday, 15 October, that the 2026 grain, bean and oilseed harvest will reach a record 354.5 million metric tons, up 2.4% from 2025 and 0.4% from its August estimate.

— Why it matters Brazil ships more soybeans abroad than any other country, so a record crop of 175.0 million tons adds to the supply that American farmers compete against in export markets.

— The numbers Soybeans reach 175.0 million tons (up 5.4%), corn 143.3 million (up 1.1%) and coffee 68.0 million 60-kilogram bags (up 18.1%), while wheat falls 24.0% to 5.9 million tons and rice falls 11.4%.

— Who is who IBGE is Brazil’s federal statistics institute and runs the monthly harvest survey; USDA is the US Department of Agriculture, whose global supply outlook American farmers and traders follow closely.

— What to watch IBGE publishes its next monthly harvest estimate on Friday, 13 November, which will show whether the soybean and corn records hold after another round of revisions.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you A record Brazilian soy crop is supply that US farmers must compete with, while a 24.0% smaller wheat crop and an 18.1% bigger coffee crop matter to wheat exporters and American coffee buyers.

Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Brazil’s statistics office expects a record 354.5 million metric tons of grains, beans and oilseeds in 2026. Soybeans, corn and coffee all reach records in its series, while wheat and rice shrink.

The Brazil harvest is on course for a record 354.5 million metric tons in 2026, says IBGE, the country’s statistics institute. The estimate, published on Thursday, 15 October, is 2.4% above 2025’s 346.1 million tons and 0.4% above August’s.

USDA’s 9 October outlook has Brazil shipping 114.5 million tons of soybeans in 2025/26, against 41.2 million for the US. That makes Brazil the top soybean exporter, and IBGE now puts its 2026 crop at a record 175.0 million tons, up 5.4%.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Brazil Harvest Breaks Down

For scale, USDA puts the 2025/26 US soybean crop at 116.0 million tons and the US corn crop at 430.9 million. On those rough numbers, Brazil’s soy crop is half again as big as America’s, and its corn crop a third the size.

Corn totals 143.3 million tons, a record and 1.1% above 2025, with the first crop up 15.5% to 29.7 million tons. The larger second crop is forecast at 113.6 million tons, 2.0% lower than last year on a weaker average yield.

Coffee is forecast at 68.0 million 60-kilogram bags, or 4.1 million tons, up 18.1% on 2025 and 3.0% on August. That is the highest in IBGE’s coffee series, which starts in 2002.

Arabica accounts for 46.3 million bags and canephora, also sold as robusta, for 21.7 million. Minas Gerais state grows 73.4% of the arabica, and Espírito Santo state 66.9% of the canephora.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Wheat and Rice Fall Sharply

Wheat is forecast at 5.9 million tons, down 24.0% from 2025 and 6.2% below the August estimate. IBGE links the fall to a smaller planted area and lower yields.

Rice in the husk drops 11.4% to 11.2 million tons as the harvested area shrinks 12.6%. Beans fall 6.6% and oranges 5.5%, while cotton is down 3.9% and sorghum up 11.0%.

Where the Crop Grows

Mato Grosso, a Centre-West state, grows 32.2% of the total, ahead of Paraná at 13.3% and Rio Grande do Sul at 10.4%. The Centre-West region as a whole grows 50.4% of the national total.

Since August’s estimate, Mato Grosso added the most, 930,020 tons, followed by Bahia with 699,888 tons. Goiás fell the most, by 169,658 tons.

How IBGE Counts the Crop

IBGE’s Systematic Survey of Agricultural Production, known as the LSPA, updates the crop estimate every month. The grain harvest covers 83.2 million hectares, up 2.0%, or about 206 million acres, an area larger than Texas.

Rice, corn and soybeans make up 93.0% of the grain tonnage. Coffee, sugarcane and oranges are counted separately and sit outside the 354.5 million-ton total.

What It Means for US Readers

US growers face a rival: USDA sees Brazil exporting 118.0 million tons of soybeans in 2026/27, against 46.1 million for the US. That outlook covers the 2026/27 marketing year and the crop now being planted, not the harvest IBGE has just estimated.

A bigger Brazilian coffee crop matters to US roasters and cafes, though prices also depend on demand, weather and trade rules. The latest monthly figures on Brazil’s coffee exports to the United States in September are covered separately.

Brazil’s wheat crop is shrinking, and USDA sees 5.8 million tons of output against 7.5 million tons of imports in 2026/27. USDA also says US hard red winter wheat remains uncompetitive in export markets because of higher prices.

The wider picture of what Brazil grows, mines and exports is set out in Brazil’s natural resources. That guide covers soybeans, oil and iron ore with a focus on US readers.

What Is Not Known

IBGE’s soybean figure of 175.0 million tons differs from USDA’s 180.5 million for Brazil’s 2025/26 crop. The IBGE release does not discuss the 5.5 million-ton gap, and the reason for it is not established.

The release covers the 2026 harvest only and gives no price or revenue figures, so the crop’s value is not known. IBGE revises each estimate monthly, so the 354.5 million-ton total can still change.

What Comes Next

IBGE publishes its next harvest estimate on Friday, 13 November. It will show whether the soybean and corn records hold after a month of revisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did IBGE say about Brazil’s 2026 harvest?

IBGE estimated a record 354.5 million metric tons of grains, beans and oilseeds on Thursday, 15 October. That is 2.4% above 2025 and 0.4% above its August estimate.

How big is Brazil’s soybean crop?

IBGE puts it at a record 175.0 million tons, up 5.4% on 2025 and 0.1% on the August estimate. USDA’s own estimate for the 2025/26 crop is 180.5 million tons.

How much coffee will Brazil harvest in 2026?

IBGE forecasts 68.0 million 60-kilogram bags, up 18.1% on 2025. That is a record in its series, which starts in 2002.

Why does Brazil’s harvest matter to US farmers?

USDA’s 9 October outlook has Brazil shipping 114.5 million tons of soybeans in 2025/26, against 41.2 million for the US. A large Brazilian crop adds to the supply American growers compete with.

Which crops are falling in 2026?

Wheat is forecast down 24.0% and rice down 11.4% from 2025. Beans fall 6.6%, oranges 5.5% and cotton 3.9%.

What is IBGE?

IBGE, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics, is the federal agency that produces Brazil’s official statistics. Its monthly harvest survey is called the LSPA.

Sources: IBGE, September 2026 harvest estimate (LSPA), 15 October 2026; IBGE SIDRA, table 6588, monthly harvest estimates by state and region; USDA, World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates, WASDE-676, 9 October 2026 (all accessed 15 October 2026).

World.title: Paraguay Warns El Niño Flood May Match 1983
World.content:
PARAGUAY · EL NIÑO

Key Facts — What is happening Paraguay’s emergency minister warned on Thursday, 15 October, that an El Niño flood could bring river levels comparable to 1983, as the Paraguay River at Asunción stood at 2.29 metres on Wednesday, up 21 centimetres in a day.

— Why it matters The low-lying riverside districts of the capital are the most exposed, and about 3,300 families there could be affected if the river reaches 3.5 metres, while US forecasters rate a strong to very strong El Niño as likely.

— The numbers The river stood at 2.29 metres in Asunción on Wednesday against a record 9.01 metres on 29 May 1983, and the city’s emergency plan carries a G. 7,000 million (about US$1.2 million) budget.

— Who is who Arsenio Zárate runs the National Emergency Secretariat (SEN), Óscar González is the Defence Minister directing troop support, and NOAA is the US weather and ocean agency that issues the El Niño outlook.

— What to watch Watch the daily river readings in Asunción, whether the water reaches 3.5 metres and the Chacarita riverside district, and the next US El Niño update due on Thursday, 12 November.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives 78.5% to a peak of 2.5 or above on NOAA’s RONI index for the 2026 to 2027 El Niño, with about US$97,000 traded (15 October, 12:16 p.m. ET).

— Power Index Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you El Niño winters typically bring a stormier southern United States, so the Pacific event behind Paraguay’s flood risk also matters for US weather, and visitors to Asunción may see disruption near the river.

Paraguay’s emergency minister says an El Niño flood could match 1983 as the river rises in Asunción. NOAA, the US weather agency, rates a strong to very strong El Niño as likely.

Paraguay’s emergency minister, Arsenio Zárate, warned on Thursday, 15 October, that an El Niño flood could reach levels seen in 1983. In Asunción the river peaked that year at 9.01 metres on 29 May, the highest reading in the national hydrology table.

Hoy, a Paraguayan daily, and ABC Color both reported on Thursday that officials expect a rise in the capital. Zárate named NOAA, the US government’s weather and ocean agency, among the forecasters behind his warning.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the El Niño Flood Warning Says

Zárate leads the National Emergency Secretariat (SEN), Paraguay’s disaster relief agency. ABC Color, an Asunción daily, and the regional outlet RCC quoted him saying forecasts point to a very strong El Niño.

He said the river rose almost 1.5 metres in 15 days and now stands about two metres above its reference level. ABC Color said the SEN and the Defence Ministry may move riverside families to Infantry Regiment No. 14 if needed.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How High the River Is Now

The national hydrology service, known as the DMH, listed 2.29 metres at Asunción on Wednesday, 14 October, up 21 centimetres. Its table also shows a record low of minus 1.61 metres on 2 November 2024.

Downstream on Wednesday, Villeta read 2.63 metres and Pilar 4.50 metres, up 22 and 17 centimetres. Pilar’s record is 10.05 metres, also set on 29 May 1983.

These readings are far below the 1983 peaks, but all three stations rose by 17 to 22 centimetres in one day. The Asunción gauge stands about 4 metres above its November 2024 low.

What NOAA Says About El Niño

NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center issued its monthly El Niño update on Thursday, 8 October, with an El Niño Advisory in force. It said a strong to very strong El Niño is likely through January to March 2027, with a chance above 83%.

The Niño-3.4 index, a Pacific temperature gauge, reached 2.1 degrees Celsius above average over the past month. NOAA put the chance of a historic event, stronger than any since 1950, at 83% for October to December.

NOAA’s winter guide says El Niño winters typically feature a strong storm track across the southern United States. The northern states typically see milder conditions, and NOAA’s next El Niño update is due on Thursday, 12 November.

How Asunción Is Preparing

Asunción’s council approved an emergency declaration with G. 7,000 million (about US$1.2 million) budgeted for supplies and repairs, the city said. Conversions use the open.er-api.com market rate of mid-October 2026, about G. 5,711 per US$, not the central bank’s reference rate.

José Jara, the city’s disaster risk director, said about 3,300 families in the bañados could be affected at 3.5 metres. The bañados are low-lying riverside districts closest to the water, and the city is mapping flood zones with Paraguay’s space agency.

Defence Minister Óscar González, a retired general, said on Thursday that a river rise in Asunción is imminent, Hoy reported. He said the Chacarita riverside district worries him greatly, and ABC Color said barracks are open as shelters under SEN coordination.

The Paraná is also in flood near Ciudad del Este, a separate event covered in Paraguay Flood Near Iguazú Uproots Hundreds. Itaipú Dam Explained describes the dam and its spillway.

What It Means for US Readers

The warning leans on NOAA forecasts, so Americans can follow the same El Niño that Paraguay is preparing for. The pattern matters at home because NOAA ties El Niño winters to a stormier southern United States.

Travellers to Asunción may see disruption near the river, and the Paraná flood already affects the Ciudad del Este border area. The city said on Wednesday that no Asunción district was yet affected.

For background, see Paraguay in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances and Paraguay Neighbours Explained. The Asunción city guide covers the capital for visitors.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket’s market on the peak of the 2026 to 2027 El Niño has about US$97,000 traded. It gave 78.5% to a peak of 2.5 or above and 19% to 2.25 to 2.5 (15 October, 12:16 p.m. ET).

RONI is NOAA’s Relative Oceanic Niño Index, and a three-month value of 2.5 or more counts as a historic event. These are bets by traders, not forecasts from NOAA or Paraguay’s government.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

No hydrology-service forecast of the river’s peak at Asunción was found, and the 1983 comparison comes from the minister. NOAA’s outlook covers the Pacific, not river levels.

It is not confirmed when the river will reach 3.5 metres or whether the Chacarita will flood. The total cost of the response is not stated, and the Defence Ministry says it will use existing funds.

River readings differ by source: the city’s port gauge gave 2 metres on Wednesday, while the DMH table listed 2.29 metres. The 3.5-metre threshold for 3,300 families is the city’s own estimate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Asunción flooding now?

Not yet, but officials call a rise in the capital imminent. The DMH table put the river at 2.29 metres on Wednesday, 14 October, and the city said no district was affected.

What is El Niño?

El Niño is a warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that shifts rainfall and storm tracks around the world. NOAA says it is strengthening, with the Niño-3.4 gauge at 2.1 degrees Celsius above average.

How does the 1983 flood compare with now?

At Asunción the river peaked at 9.01 metres on 29 May 1983, the highest reading in the official table. The DMH table put it at 2.29 metres on Wednesday, about 6.7 metres lower.

How much has Asunción budgeted for the flood?

The city’s emergency declaration, approved by the municipal council, includes G. 7,000 million, about US$1.2 million, for supplies, walls and bridges. Final administrative approval of the declaration was still pending on Wednesday.

Is the Paraná River also flooding?

Yes, the Paraná is also in flood near Ciudad del Este, a separate event from the Asunción river rise. The earlier report on that flood covers the families evacuated there.

World.title: Bolivia Holds Colombian, Seizes US$500,000
World.content:
BOLIVIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — What is happening Police in Santa Cruz arrested a Colombian man, Carlos Vargas Ramírez, on Wednesday, 14 October, in the Johan Guzmán murder investigation and found more than US$500,000, four small gold bars and weapons at his home.

— Why it matters Authorities are testing whether he belonged to a network tied to Sebastián Marset, the Uruguayan drug-trafficking suspect now awaiting trial in a US federal court, but they call the link a hypothesis still to be verified.

— The numbers Police list more than US$500,000 in cash dollars, over Bs 130,000 (about US$11,100), four small gold bars, a rifle, handguns and 500 to 550 rounds of ammunition.

— Who is who Interim Attorney General José Armando Urioste leads the prosecution, police commander Adrián Álvarez presented the suspect, and Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo oversees the police.

— What to watch No court hearing or detention order has been announced yet; the open questions are whether he fired the shots or planned the killing, and where the money and gold came from.

— Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you Bolivia carries a US Level 2 travel advisory, exercise increased caution, with the uncommon express kidnappings mostly in Santa Cruz; Marset faces a US trial in Virginia on 11 January 2027.

Bolivian police presented a Colombian suspect on Thursday with over US$500,000, four gold bars and weapons found at his home. Authorities are testing whether he belonged to a network tied to Sebastián Marset, a link they call a hypothesis.

Bolivia holds Colombian Carlos Vargas Ramírez after police found over US$500,000, gold bars and weapons at his Santa Cruz home. Bolivia’s prosecutors say police suspect he may belong to a network tied to Sebastián Marset, now awaiting trial in the United States.

Police arrested him on Wednesday, 14 October, after tracking a phone of the victim, Johan Guzmán Parada, 26. The Fiscalía, Bolivia’s prosecutor’s office, lists murder among the offences under investigation, though police say his role is not yet established.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Police Say They Found

Police commander Adrián Álvarez presented the suspect on Thursday, 15 October, alongside Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo, who oversees the police. The commander said officers identified his home in the La Molina area of northern Santa Cruz, El Deber reported.

Police listed more than US$500,000 in cash dollars and over Bs 130,000 (about US$11,100), El Deber and El Día said. El Deber put the dollars at US$546,500, and El Día’s subheading gives the same figure.

Bolivian amounts here convert at the central bank’s official rate of Bs 11.68 per US$ on 15 October 2026. Bolivia dropped its fixed rate this year, which Bolivia in 2026 Explained covers, so Bs 130,000 is about US$11,100.

Four small gold bars and jewellery were also found, El Deber, El Día and Infobae said. Visión 360 also mentioned small gold bars, and none of the accounts gives a weight or value.

Police described five pistols, a precision rifle and 550 rounds, El Deber and Infobae said. The Fiscalía listed six revolvers, a rifle and about 500 rounds on Wednesday, and the two counts differ.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Bolivia Holds Colombian Suspect Carlos Vargas Ramírez

The Fiscalía, led by interim Attorney General José Armando Urioste, names four offences under investigation: murder, arms trafficking, weapons possession and laundering. Los Tiempos said prosecutors pursue him for arms trafficking, weapons possession and laundering; his role in the killing is unproven.

El Deber quoted Álvarez as saying the case is still being investigated to establish the suspect’s participation. El Diario says investigators are asking whether he planned the attack, as does JuanPastén.bo, citing Sierra Televisión; this is unproven.

The Killing of Johan Guzmán and the Marset Hypothesis

Johan Guzmán Parada, 26, was shot dead on Tuesday, 13 October, at a mechanic’s workshop near the city’s zoo. The Fiscalía describes a contract killing: two men arrived on a motorcycle and one entered the workshop armed and fired.

The Fiscalía says police are testing whether the suspect belonged to a criminal group tied to Marset and alias El Colla. It says the victim allegedly had ties to the same structures, and it calls both points hypotheses still to be verified.

In 2023 the government of the day described Guzmán as a pilot for Marset, El Deber recalled. Lawyer Ángel Veizaga said on Wednesday that no link between Guzmán and Marset has been proved, El Deber reported.

Who Sebastián Marset Is and His US Case

Sebastián Marset, a Uruguayan drug-trafficking suspect, was captured in Bolivia on 13 March and now faces charges in the United States. The OCCRP, an investigative reporting network, says a Virginia federal judge set his trial for 11 January 2027.

Charges there began with money laundering, and a later indictment added drug trafficking and narcoterrorism, the OCCRP said. His defence has signalled it will challenge the handover, which Marset calls an irregular rendition.

El Colla is Erlan Ivar García López, whom a former minister called a trusted man of Marset in 2023, El Deber recalled. The Fiscalía’s statement does not say whether García López faces charges or has any link to this arrest.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department rates Bolivia Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory issued on 18 August 2026. It says express kidnappings, in which victims are forced to withdraw cash at ATMs, are uncommon and mostly occur in Santa Cruz.

Marset awaits trial in a US federal court, so any proven link to him would reach into an American case. For now it is a hypothesis from Bolivian police and prosecutors, and the official statements mention no US role in this arrest.

What Is Not Known

The accounts differ on some details: Vargas Ramírez is 42 in the Fiscalía’s account and 38 in police remarks. Weapon and ammunition counts also differ between Wednesday’s and Thursday’s lists.

The exact dollar total is unsettled: El Deber says US$546,500, while El Día’s text says about US$540,000. No weight or value has been given for the four gold bars.

Whether Vargas Ramírez fired the shots or planned the killing has not been established. Police say they are still checking whether the seized money, gold and weapons relate to the killing.

No statement from Vargas Ramírez or a lawyer for him has appeared in the coverage. The Marset link remains a hypothesis that the Fiscalía says must still be verified.

What Comes Next

El Diario said prosecutor Yolanda Aguilera will seek more checks at the workshop and summon the victim’s mother. El Deber said prosecutor Gary Flores will request pretrial detention, but no hearing date or detention order has been announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the Colombian arrested in Santa Cruz?

The Fiscalía names him as Carlos Vargas Ramírez, a Colombian citizen arrested on Wednesday, 14 October. Prosecutors give his age as 42 and police as 38.

What did police find at his home?

Police list more than US$500,000 in cash dollars, over Bs 130,000 (about US$11,100), four small gold bars, jewellery and weapons. Counts of weapons and rounds differ between the two official lists.

Is he accused of killing Johan Guzmán?

Prosecutors list murder among the offences under investigation, but police say his participation is still to be established. No court has ruled on his role.

Is he linked to Sebastián Marset?

Authorities say he may belong to a network tied to Marset and alias El Colla. They call that a hypothesis that still has to be verified.

Who is Sebastián Marset?

He is a Uruguayan drug-trafficking suspect captured in Bolivia on 13 March and sent to the United States. His trial in a Virginia federal court is set for 11 January 2027.

Is Santa Cruz safe for US travellers?

The State Department rates Bolivia Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory dated 18 August 2026. It says express kidnappings are uncommon and mostly occur in Santa Cruz.

Sources: Fiscalía General del Estado, 14 October 2026; El Deber, 15 October; El Deber, 14 October; El Deber, arsenal report, 15 October; El Día; Infobae; Visión 360; Los Tiempos, 14 October; Los Tiempos, 15 October; El Diario; JuanPastén.bo, 14 October; OCCRP, 1 July 2026; US State Department, Bolivia advisory; Banco Central de Bolivia (all accessed 15 October 2026).
