He also noted the programme’s role in strengthening bilateral relations, promoting mutual understanding and building people-to-people ties. Referring to the vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the Ambassador highlighted India’s guiding principle of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” (the world is one family), emphasising India’s belief in cooperation, shared progress and the well-being of all.

H.E. Mr. Iván Medveczky, Deputy State Secretary for Relations with the South at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Hungary, delivered the keynote address, highlighting the strong historical ties between India and Hungary and the importance of continued cooperation between the two countries. He appreciated India’s efforts to share its knowledge, skills and experience with partner countries through the ITEC Programme, noting its valuable contribution to capacity-building and strengthening bilateral relations.

The celebration highlighted the positive experiences of ITEC alumni and the Programme’s contribution to promoting knowledge exchange, professional collaboration and closer people-to-people ties between India, Hungary and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

World.title: Pakistan brings its rice, and its diplomacy, to a Budapest kitchen
World.content:
Hungarian importers, chefs and food industry professionals gathered at a cooking school in Budapest this week for a different kind of trade promotion: one conducted over a hot stove.

The Embassy of Pakistan held the first Pakistan Rice Festival in Hungary at the KuktaParty Chef Academy, an event built around a single product. Pakistani basmati, the long-grain aromatic rice is among the country’s best-known exports, and the Embassy’s aim was to put it in front of the Hungarian trade in the most persuasive form available: cooked, served and eaten.

The guest list reflected that purpose. Importers and business leaders from the food and agriculture sector made up the bulk of the room, joined by leading Hungarian master chefs, representatives of several public sector bodies and members of the diplomatic community.

Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

A grain with a legal identity

Ambassador Asif Hussain Memon opened the event, telling guests that Pakistani cuisine has considerably more range than international audiences tend to realise, and that spices and rice sit at the centre of it. Much of what is recognised abroad as Pakistani food, he suggested, represents only a fraction of what our kitchens actually produce.

He also drew attention to something that matters more to importers than to diners. Basmati is protected under Geographical Indication, a designation that ties the name to rice grown in specific regions of Pakistan and assures buyers of both its origin and its quality.

Alongside the rice, the Embassy displayed a selection of other Pakistani food products, most notably Himalayan Pink Salt, sold worldwide in both culinary and decorative forms. Guests were invited to sample its different grades, from fine ground to coarse granulated.

Among those attending were Hungarian master chefs István Asztalos and Péter Korpádi, who spoke warmly of the depth and complexity of the dishes on offer and of the quality of the rice at the centre of them.

Ambassador Asif Hussain Memon. Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

Biryani, built in layers

The centrepiece of the afternoon was a live cooking demonstration by the Embassy’s Trade & Investment Attaché, Shehryar Qaisrani, who prepared and explained the process of making biryani in front of the room.

Biryani is among the most celebrated dishes in Pakistani cooking, and also among the most demanding. The rice is parboiled rather than cooked through, then layered over spiced meat with fried onions, herbs and saffron, never stirred, and sealed under a lid to finish in its own steam. The technique, known as dum, gives the dish its characteristic separation of grains and the three-tone colour that appears when the pot is opened.

Each guest left with a sample of Pakistani basmati and a short recipe book the Embassy had prepared in Hungarian, featuring a range of rice-based dishes, so that they could try cooking them at home.

László Asztalos, owner of KuktaParty, said that hosting the event was a source of pride for the school. He described it as a welcome opportunity to contribute to the promotion of Pakistani gastronomy in Hungary while supporting the development of professional and cultural ties between the two countries.

Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

From the kitchen to the trade floor

The food was also a route to business. The Ambassador invited participants to attend FoodAg 2026, Pakistan’s international food and agriculture exhibition, which runs at the Expo Centre in Karachi from 23 to 26 November. The exhibition brings together several hundred exporters across rice, fruit, seafood and processed foods, and offers Hungarian importers direct access to Pakistani suppliers.

The commercial ambition behind the event is not incidental. The Government of Pakistan established a dedicated Commercial Wing at its Embassy in Budapest just last year, as part of a broader effort to build trade relationships in European markets where Pakistan has not traditionally been active.

Mangoes first, then rice

It is not the first time Pakistani produce has made an impression in Hungary. When the Embassy shared Pakistani mangoes earlier this summer, the response was unusually warm, and Prime Minister Péter Magyar posted his appreciation publicly.

Speaking about the wider relationship between the two countries, Ambassador Memon said that food has proved one of the most natural bridges between them.

“Relations between Pakistan and Hungary have traditionally been friendly, built on mutual respect and trust,” he said. “I believe this relationship holds considerable untapped potential, and my aim as Ambassador is to turn our political trust into real economic results and lasting friendships between our people.”

He added that the Rice Festival was an illustration of what that means in practice.

“It allowed us to introduce Pakistani basmati to Hungarian chefs, importers and food professionals in the most direct way possible: by cooking it and sharing it. Diplomacy is often conducted across a table. On this occasion it happened around one.”

World.title: Budapest Christmas market crowned Europe’s most beautiful for 2026! Here’s when it opens
World.content:
Budapest’s Advent Basilica Christmas market has won Europe’s top Christmas market title for 2026, adding another international accolade to its collection. The popular festive attraction opens on 13 November, bringing Christmas cheer back to the Hungarian capital.

Budapest’s Advent Basilica Christmas market has been named Europe’s most beautiful Christmas market for 2026 by European Best Destinations (EBD), beating competitors from across the continent. The award ceremony took place in Monaco on 9 October, with 40 Christmas markets reaching the final.

The latest recognition is particularly prestigious, as Advent Basilica won in the organisation’s ‘All Stars’ category, which brings together previous award winners. The Budapest attraction has already earned the title of Europe’s Best Christmas Market four times, further cementing its reputation as one of the continent’s leading festive destinations.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Why does Budapest’s Advent Basilica stand out?

Set in front of St Stephen’s Basilica, one of Budapest’s most recognisable landmarks, the market combines traditional crafts, festive food and drink, and spectacular lighting to create a distinctive Christmas atmosphere.

According to EBD, the balance between culture, gastronomy and the setting is a key reason for its continued popularity among international visitors. The combination of the historic basilica, carefully designed decorations and culinary offerings makes the market an attraction that draws tourists back year after year.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Maximilien Lejeune, EBD’s managing director, said the event had repeatedly succeeded in delivering the beauty, magical atmosphere and originality that visitors expect from a Christmas market.

He also highlighted how closely the market’s promise matches the experience visitors encounter in person, with Budapest providing the ideal backdrop for the festive event.

The market’s growing international reputation has also attracted attention across the travel media. Forbes included Budapest in its coverage of Europe’s most beautiful Christmas markets for 2026, placing the Hungarian capital firmly on the festive travel map.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Advent Basilica celebrates its 15th anniversary

The 2026 edition marks the 15th anniversary of Advent Basilica. Over the years, it has collected several major international awards, including the title of Europe’s Best Christmas Market in 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024.

In 2024, it also received the distinction of being named the best European Christmas market of all time.

Budapest has enjoyed further success with its other major festive attraction, the Vörösmarty Classic Xmas market. In 2025, it was named Europe’s most popular Christmas market in an analysis by travel experts at Tollwayr, reportedly beating established destinations such as Strasbourg, Vienna and Prague.

The Hungarian capital also secured second place in Travel and Tour World’s ranking of the world’s best Christmas destinations in 2025, behind only New York. Budapest was the highest-ranked European destination, ahead of cities including London, Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Vienna.

Photo: Advent Basilica

When does the Budapest Christmas market open in 2026?

This year’s Advent Basilica Christmas market opens on 13 November 2026, welcoming visitors to the square in front of St Stephen’s Basilica.

The festive attractions will also extend to Vörösmarty Square, where the Vörösmarty Classic Xmas market offers another popular destination for Christmas shopping, traditional Hungarian food and seasonal treats.

For tourists planning a winter city break, the two markets provide an opportunity to experience Budapest’s festive atmosphere while exploring some of its best-known central locations.

Photo: Advent Basilica

What is European Best Destinations?

European Best Destinations has organised tourism competitions involving travellers from around the world since 2009. The organisation works with more than 500 European destinations, including Marbella, Monaco and Madrid, and aims to increase their international visibility and appeal.

Its media partners include Forbes, Condé Nast Traveler and National Geographic. This year’s award ceremony was held in Monaco on 9 October, with Princess Stéphanie of Monaco and Eva Longoria among those attending.

World.title: Drunk driver with no licence accused of fatal hit-and-run in Hungary
World.content:
A 36-year-old woman has been charged over a fatal hit-and-run near Szigetszentmiklós, Hungary, after allegedly drunk driving without a driving licence, killing an electric tricycle rider and leaving the victim without assistance.

Drunk woman with no driving licence caused fatal accident

The Budakörnyék District Prosecutor’s Office has requested an eight-year prison sentence, an eight-year ban from public affairs and a permanent driving ban for the accused. The case will be heard by the Szigetszentmiklós District Court.

According to prosecutors, the woman was working at a car wash near Szigetszentmiklós when the incident happened in February 2025. She allegedly took two customers’ cars without their permission on separate occasions to buy alcohol.

Took customers’ cars to buy alcohol

The woman first drove a car left at the car wash for cleaning to a nearby alcohol shop without the owner’s knowledge. After purchasing and consuming the alcohol, she allegedly took another vehicle – while already drunk – entrusted to the business for cleaning and set off for the shop again.

As she approached the shop’s car park, the woman reportedly turned at speed without noticing an electric tricycle approaching from the opposite direction. The tricycle rider had the right of way. The front left side of the car struck the tricycle, causing it to overturn and throwing its rider to the ground. The victim, reported by local media to have been 41 years old, suffered fatal injuries.

Driver examined victim before fleeing

After the collision, the drunk woman reportedly got out of the car and approached the unconscious woman lying on the ground. When she was unable to lift the victim, she returned to the vehicle and drove away without calling emergency services or providing further assistance.

People who came out of the nearby shop and an adjacent property called an ambulance. However, the victim’s injuries were so severe that she died at the scene. The prosecutor’s office has charged the woman with causing death through drink-driving, two counts of unauthorised use of a vehicle and an aggravated offence of failing to provide assistance.

Join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel.

Prosecutors seek eight-year prison sentence

The prosecution has asked the court to impose an eight-year custodial sentence and bar the defendant from public affairs for the same period. It has also requested that she be permanently disqualified from driving. The accused is currently under criminal supervision, according to the prosecution’s announcement. Local media have also reported that she did not give a statement during the investigation.

The case will now proceed before the Szigetszentmiklós District Court, which will decide whether the defendant is guilty and determine any sentence. The charges and requested penalties represent the prosecution’s position; the court has yet to deliver its verdict.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW OUT NOW: Kosovo’s foreign minister warns of Serbian threats
World.content:
Kosovo’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Glauk Konjufca, has warned that the risk of renewed armed confrontation with Serbia must be taken seriously. In an exclusive interview with Hungary Insider, he accused Belgrade of pursuing territorial ambitions and called for stronger international measures to prevent further instability in the Western Balkans. The minister also addressed NATO’s role in maintaining regional security and the continuing dispute over the deadly 2023 Banjska attack.

Tensions between Kosovo and Serbia remain a significant security concern in the Western Balkans, nearly two decades after Kosovo declared independence in 2008.

The Republic of Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and is recognised as an independent and sovereign state by Hungary and 120 other countries. Serbia continues to reject its independence and maintain territorial claims over the country. The dispute has repeatedly triggered political crises and security incidents, particularly in northern Kosovo, where a substantial ethnic Serb population maintains close ties with Belgrade.

Speaking exclusively to Hungary Insider, Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca argued that recent statements by Serbian officials should be viewed in the context of previous armed incidents and military deployments.

“The threat to the Republic of Kosovo is real, and the international community must recognise the gravity of this pattern,” he said.

Kosovo warns that Serbian rhetoric could signal a wider security threat

Konjufca condemned Serbian Deputy Prime Minister Ivica Dacic’s explicit declaration that the Serbian flag would “sooner or later fly over Prizren”, a city in southern Kosovo, describing it as evidence of Belgrade’s continuing territorial ambitions against the Republic of Kosovo.

According to the minister, such statements cannot be separated from developments on the ground.

He also highlighted the public appearance of Milan Radoicic, former vice-president of the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista and the admitted organiser of the armed group responsible for the September 2023 Banjska terrorist attack, alongside Danilo Vucic, son of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, at a ruling-party campaign rally.

Konjufca described these developments as evidence of a persistent pattern of Serbian territorial revisionism and the political protection afforded to individuals responsible for armed aggression against the Republic of Kosovo, particularly Milan Radoicic, who publicly acknowledged organising the armed group responsible for the Banjska terrorist attack.

The Government of the Republic of Kosovo has consistently maintained that the Banjska terrorist attack was supported by Serbian state structures. The Special Prosecution’s indictment details an organised operation aimed at annexing north of Kosovo to Serbia, including allegations that military infrastructure in Serbia was provided for the group’s training.

Konjufca also pointed to Radoicic’s longstanding political relationship with Aleksandar Vucic, who publicly praised him on several occasions and later acknowledged him as a close political ally. Serbia denies state involvement, while Radoicic maintains that he acted independently.

The Banjska attack continues to fuel tensions

The September 2023 attack in Banjska, northern Kosovo, remains one of the most serious security incidents in relations between Belgrade and Pristina in recent years.

A heavily armed group carried out a terrorist attack against Kosovo Police in Banjska, killing Police Sergeant Afrim Bunjaku. Three members of the attacking group were subsequently killed during the ensuing armed confrontation.

In the days following the Banjska terrorist attack, Serbia amassed tanks, artillery and mechanized infantry along its border with the Republic of Kosovo. The unprecedented scale of this military deployment prompted an extraordinary public warning from the White House, which demanded the withdrawal of Serbian forces. NATO subsequently reinforced its KFOR peacekeeping presence in Kosovo.

In the exclusive interview, Konjufca criticised the lack of accountability for those responsible for the attack, particularly the fact that Radoičić remains in Serbia.

Minister Konjufca called on the European Union to exert decisive pressure on Belgrade to surrender Milan Radoicic and the other indicted perpetrators to the judicial authorities of the Republic of Kosovo. He also recalled the European Parliament’s 2023 call for targeted restrictive measures against Radoicic, emphasising that these demands must now be translated into concrete action.

“Justice for Banjska is essential to preventing further aggression and establishing lasting security in our region,” he said.

How serious is the risk of another Serbia–Kosovo conflict?

Asked whether a renewed armed confrontation was a realistic possibility, Konjufca made clear that his government takes the danger seriously.

Minister Konjufca. Source: Facebook

“We take the risk of renewed confrontation seriously, knowing the devastating consequences of war,” he told Hungary Insider.

He identified a renewed concentration of Serbian combat forces near Kosovo’s borders or another armed attack against Kosovo’s territory and critical infrastructure as developments that would constitute a grave escalation.

Nevertheless, the minister stressed that Kosovo remains committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful relations with neighbouring countries.

According to Konjufca, preventing further violence requires credible deterrence, a strong NATO presence through KFOR, and close coordination with the United States and European partners.

Why Kosovo’s security matters to Hungary

For Hungary, developments in Kosovo have direct regional security implications.

Hungary has long contributed troops to NATO’s Kosovo Force, which is tasked with maintaining a safe and secure environment and freedom of movement in the territory.

The proximity of the Western Balkans also makes regional stability an important consideration for Hungarian foreign and security policy.

Hungary recognised Kosovo’s independence in March 2008 and has maintained diplomatic relations with Pristina since then.

Konjufca acknowledged Hungary’s longstanding contribution to Kosovo’s security in his interview, while also discussing how political developments in Budapest could influence future bilateral relations.

The minister emphasised that Kosovo’s longer-term ambitions remain focused on European integration, international cooperation and membership of NATO.

What else did Kosovo’s foreign minister reveal in the exclusive interview?

Beyond the security tensions with Serbia, Glauk Konjufca addressed several important political and diplomatic questions in his extensive interview with Hungary Insider.

He discussed how Kosovo views Hungary’s political transition under Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whether Budapest could play a greater role in the Western Balkans, and what opportunities exist for closer Hungarian–Kosovar cooperation.

The minister also examined the political connections surrounding the Banjska attack, the measures he expects from the European Union, and Kosovo’s efforts to secure EU candidate status.

He further addressed Kosovo’s ambitions to join NATO, its campaign for wider international recognition, and the message he wants to send to European governments, particularly those in Central Europe.

What does Glauk Konjufca expect from Péter Magyar’s government? How could Hungary influence Kosovo’s European future? And what further action does he want the EU to take towards Serbia?

World.title: Hungarian man wanted over child sexual abuse material arrested in Caribbean nation
World.content:
A Hungarian man wanted under European and international arrest warrants over alleged child sexual abuse material offences has been arrested in Antigua and Barbuda and brought back to Hungary.

A Hungarian man wanted in connection with child sexual abuse material offences and other crimes has been arrested in Antigua and Barbuda, the Hungarian police announced. The suspect, identified only by the initials M. V., was subject to both European and international arrest warrants.

The arrest followed investigative work by Hungary’s International Law Enforcement Cooperation Centre (NEBEK), which helped establish the man’s whereabouts and enabled local authorities to take action.

According to the police statement, the man was suspected of transferring child sexual abuse material depicting the abuse of children under the age of 12.

If you missed it: Bomb threats force two Budapest schools to be evacuated

International cooperation leads to arrest

NEBEK investigators traced the suspect to the Caribbean island nation of Antigua and Barbuda. Information gathered by the Hungarian authorities enabled their counterparts in the country to locate and arrest him.

The case involved an international manhunt, with the warrants allowing law enforcement agencies beyond Hungary to assist in the search. The arrest shows the role of cross-border police cooperation in locating suspects who are wanted in Hungary but are believed to be staying abroad.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Suspect brought back to Hungary

The man was returned to Hungary on 14 October 2026. Officers from the Hungarian National Central Bureau of Interpol and the Rapid Response and Special Police Services took custody of him, according to the police statement.

Hungarian police have not released further details about the other offences the man is suspected of committing or provided additional information about the investigation.

The authorities have stressed the importance of NEBEK’s investigative work and international cooperation in identifying, apprehending and arranging the return of wanted individuals from abroad.

World.title: Croatia Rejects Serbian Accusation of Election Interference
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic in Brussels, 15 October 2026. Photo: EPA/OLIVIER MATTHYS.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic on Thursday dismissed a diplomatic protest note from Belgrade alleging interference in the Serbian parliamentary election as “complete nonsense.”

“It is absolute nonsense to suggest that Croatia, presumably acting as both an external and an internal enemy, is interfering in the political process and the election race in Serbia,” Plenkovic said.

Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s outgoing president and the lead candidate on the “United Serbia” list, said that no country had ever interfered in another country’s elections as extensively as Croatia had done in Serbia’s upcoming parliamentary elections, Serbian news agency Tanjug reported on Thursday.

Vucic welcomed the Serbian Foreign Ministry’s decision to send Croatia a protest note, adding that it should have been done “perhaps a thousand times by now.

“It is important to leave a record that we were aware that Croatia was interfering in our electoral process in the most overt way. Therefore, we have issued a protest note,” Vucic said.

Serbian public broadcaster Radio-Television Serbia said the note stated that attempts to influence Serbia’s electoral processes were unacceptable, as were various aspects of Croatian media coverage of Serbia’s political situation.

“This narrative has been pushed for quite some time. As for the protests regarding coverage by Croatian media, I don’t know what more there is to add. As far as I recall, our media are free – people write what they want,” Plenkovic responded.

“Croatia does not interfere in such matters, nor is this an issue that concerns us. However, there are fundamental values on which Serbia needs to make progress rather than sending us ridiculous notes,” Plenkovic added.

“Unfortunately, we remember Aleksandar Vucic’s role in the [1990s military] aggression against Croatia, and 35 years later, we are witnessing the same rhetoric. This shows there has been no progress towards normalising relations in Serbia,” said Tomo Medved, Croatia’s Minister for Veterans and a member of the ruling Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, on Thursday.

Josko Klisovic, of the opposition Social Democratic Party, described the note as “completely groundless and diplomatically misguided.

“Croatia does not interfere in Serbia’s election campaign. However, it seems that Aleksandar Vucic wants to drag Croatia into it,” Klisovic said, adding that the goal was clear: “Vucic wants to mobilise his electorate to turn out in the largest possible numbers and grant him another term.

“I hope the citizens of Serbia will recognise this manipulation by Vucic and head to the polls with the reality of their current lives, and the lives they wish to lead in the future, in mind,” Klisovic said.

Marijana Puljak, an MP from the Center Party, said the dispute showed Vucic’s nervousness and that the opposition student movement in Serbia was putting him under pressure, prompting him to look for culprits everywhere.

Parliamentary elections in Serbia are scheduled for October 25 with the Student List seen as the main opponent for Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party.

World.title: ‘Family Values’ Row Returns as Kosovo Govt Revives Changes to Civil Code
World.content:
Kosovo MPs during a parliamentary session on September 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Kosovo’s Prime Minister, Albin Kurti, clashed with opposition MP Eman Rrahmani of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, in parliament on Thursday over stalled reforms to the Civil Code and proposed laws on medically assisted reproduction, with disagreements focusing on same-sex unions, reproductive rights and “family values”.

Three bills on these issues are included in the government’s legislative agenda from mid-November until the end of the year.

During Thursday’s session, Rrahmani accused the government of “disregarding traditional family values”.

“Why are you continuing with this agenda? Don’t you think you are offending the citizens who voted for you and disregarding the values of the traditional family?” Rrahmani asked.

Kurti responded that Kosovo needed “comprehensive reform of civil law” to provide greater legal certainty in areas including property, family relations and inheritance.

“These are the areas through which citizens live as individuals and families, and develop and prosper,” Kurti said, adding that legal ambiguities “could leave people uncertain about their rights to use, inherit or sell property”.

Kurti urged Rrahmani to consider the proposed legislation as a whole and not focus on individual provisions.

“The Civil Code contains 997 pages and 1,630 articles,” Kurti said, advising Rrahmani to examine the document in its entirety. “Focusing on just one or two articles risks becoming an obsession and does not help,” Kurti said, causing laughter in parliament.

He added that MPs did not have to agree with every provision but “should consider the broader purpose of the legislation”. He noted that a working group at the Ministry of Justice would meet next week to discuss the matter.

Rrahmani said his opposition concerned two paragraphs of the Civil Code that he believes undermine the family.

“These will not be voted through in this parliament. We will send back those provisions that undermine the family,” he said.

The proposed Civil Code has been stalled since 2022 due to disagreements over provisions that would allow for the adoption of separate legislation regulating civil unions between people of the same sex.

Rrahmani, who in 2022 was a Vetevendosje MP but later switched to the PDK, criticised provisions he said could permit marriages between men, as well as allowing women to become mothers without a father.

Kosovo law currently does not allow same-sex marriages. The constitution, on the other hand, recognises that “on the basis of free consent, everyone enjoys the right to marry and the right to create a family in accordance with the law”.

The government has often declared that it intends to bring the Civil Code before parliament, but the legislation has yet to secure final approval.

The proposed Law on Reproductive Health and Medically Assisted Fertilisation has also faced delays. The government submitted the bill in January 2023 and parliament approved it at first reading in October Attempts to pass it at second reading in 2024 then failed.

Under the draft legislation, women would be eligible for in vitro fertilisation, IVF, regardless of their marital status or whether they were in a same-sex or heterosexual relationship.

Kurti said the desire to become a parent “should be treated with understanding and respect by the state”.

“The desire to become a parent is one of the deepest expressions of human desire,” he said, adding that difficulties associated with parenthood deserved a careful response from public institutions.

The proposed law foresees IVF services and a public bank for reproductive cells. Currently, women seeking these procedures have to turn to private healthcare clinics or somewhere abroad.

World.title: US Convicts Bosnian of Attempting to Buy Arms from North Korea
World.content:
Russian SA-18 and SA-16 Igla missiles with components. Photo: US Government/Wikidata.

The US Department of Justice said on Wednesday that Sasa Micev, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been convicted of collaborating with a co-conspirator from the US and others to violate and evade restrictions on arms sales by trying to buy shoulder-launched missiles from North Korea.

Micev, 43, was described in court documents as “an international arms dealer”. He was sentenced to five years in prison by a court in New Mexico.

A Department of Justice statement said Micev attempted to broker the purchase of SA-18 Igla portable surface-to-air missiles from North Korea without the required licence or approvals from the US Treasury Department Office of Foreign Assets Control.

It stated that on multiple occasions in 2020, Micev and a co-conspirator discussed unlawfully acquiring the Igla missiles. Micev “provided pricing information, participated in efforts to obtain the items through falsified documentation, and worked to procure the weapons from North Korea despite knowing that such transactions were prohibited under US and international laws”, it said.

In late 2020, Micev and the co-conspirator traveled to Ankara in Turkey to complete the purchase of the Igla missiles. However, according to the Department of Justice, the deal fell through after a price dispute with the North Koreans.

Micev pleaded guilty to violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the North Korean Sanctions Regulations.

“Those who knowingly attempt to circumvent US export controls and international sanctions to facilitate the illicit trafficking of military weapons pose a serious threat to our national security and global stability,” said acting special agent in charge Ryan G. McRae of Homeland Security Investigations El Paso in New Mexico.

“Their willingness to profit from prohibited weapons transactions demonstrates blatant disregard for the law,” McRae added.

According to company registries in Bosnia, Sasa Micev was a co-owner of the Banja Luka-based company BSTG (Balkan Security Tech Group), which is currently in bankruptcy proceedings. The company’s website indicates that it offered services in the security sector.

BIRN attempted to obtain a comment, but the contact phone number was unreachable.

NOTE: This article was amended on October 15, 2026 to correct the surname of Sasa Micev in several instances.

World.title: Croatia Sets Eight Conditions for Backing Montenegro’s EU Accession
World.content:
The 100-year-old training ship ‘Jadran’, one of the subjects of dispute. Photo: Ministry of Defence of Montenegro.

Croatia has listed eight demands for supporting Montenegro’s EU accession, all of which are “clearly defined and achievable,” according to a document Zagreb sent to EU member states and the European Commission and European Council.

The document explains Croatia’s position on Montenegro’s accession process in detail. “Croatia seeks to facilitate, not obstruct, Montenegro’s accession,” the text states.

It notes that several issues stemming from Montenegro’s participation in military aggression against Croatia during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s must be resolved. “Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of our shared history and to build a future-oriented relationship with Montenegro,” it says.

Six of the eight demands relate to Chapter 23 in the EU acquis of legislation Montenegro needs to adopt in order to join the bloc, under the heading Judiciary and Fundamental Rights. The remaining two concern Chapter 31, Foreign, Security and Defence Policy.

The first concerns compensation for more than 300 Croatian citizens held at the Morinj camp between October 1991 and August 1992. The second concerns the preservation and permanent visibility of the memorial plaque installed at the former camp. A large metal frame has been erected around the plaque, allowing a movable panel to be placed over it.

“Such concealment would undermine this shared act of remembrance and reconciliation,” the document states.

Croatia also calls for the municipal swimming pool in Kotor, named after Zoran Gopcevic, a former international water polo player who was a guard at the camp, to be renamed. Because of the current name, Croatian clubs refuse to play at the facility.

Fourth, Croatia seeks full cooperation from Montenegro to determine the fate of 14 Croatian citizens who went missing during the aggression against Croatia in the early 1990s.

The fifth demand calls on Montenegro to prosecute those responsible for war crimes committed during the same war, including people who may bear criminal liability under the doctrine of command responsibility.

The sixth demand concerns property disputes dating back to the early 1990s, involving Croatian families who were unlawfully deprived of their property. The document notes that property has been returned to some former owners, mostly members of the Albanian minority, raising concerns about unequal treatment.

The seventh demand concerns the return of the training ship Jadran (Adriatic), which was based in Split before the breakup of Yugoslavia but was in Montenegro for repairs when war broke out in 1991.

According to the document, the Jadran dispute is part of the broader question of the division of the former Yugoslavia’s military assets. It asserts that military equipment belonging to the former Yugoslav federation, which Montenegro continues to hold and which Croatia claims was seized from its territory, has an estimated value of 2.7 billion US dollars.

In its eighth demand, Croatia calls for continued dialogue on the demarcation of the border between the two countries.

Podgorica must confirm the former border between the two former Yugoslav republics, as established by the Arbitration Commission of the Conference on Yugoslavia, commonly known as the Badinter Commission.

According to the document, experts say deviations between the former administrative border and the current situation are minor and do not exceed 220 metres.

Montenegro is currently seen as a frontrunner among Balkan states to secure EU membership and hopes to join the bloc in 2028. But Croatia has repeatedly warned that it requires any ‘bilateral disputes’ to be settled first.

World.title: Albanian PM Blames Opposition After Another Night of Violent Clashes
World.content:
Albanian students protesting on October 14, 2026. Photo: LSA.

Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday accused the opposition of organising student protests that have seen violence erupt on the streets of Tirana for two consecutive days.

Visiting the office of the College of Europe postgraduate institute, which was damaged by fire in the violence on Wednesday, Rama said: “Students are always welcome, and we are always ready to sit down with them to talk, discuss and find solutions to matters that require resolution.

“These, however, are different hands,” he continued. “These are the hands that seek to pull Albania down whenever it tries to rise.”

On Wednesday, the first floor of the Education Ministry was set on fire, while the Prime Minister’s office, the parliament, the Constitutional Court, the Finance and Interior ministries, the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.

Clashes continued until midnight as protesters, some of them masked and throwing stones and petrol bombs, faced off against police who deployed tear gas and water cannons. Police cars and a police station also came under attack.

The Ministry of Health announced on Thursday that 79 people received medical treatment at Tirana’s Trauma Hospital, including 61 were police officers and 18 protesters. Ten other people were receiving treatment at Mother Teresa Hospital.

The clashes led to the cancellation of a parliamentary session scheduled for Thursday. On Thursday morning, students marched towards parliament as the protests looked set to continue.

Interior Minister Ervin Dema on Wednesday accused the opposition and “foreign actors” of inciting the violent clashes, claiming that student discontent had been exploited to destabilise the country.

“Today, all of Albania saw that, in the name of the students, the oldest political element in this country … spoke the language of destruction, flames, and the ransacking of public and private property,” Dema said.

The student demonstrations began outside the Ministry of Education on Tuesday, calling for the government’s resignation, better university conditions and highlighted the high cost of living.

The students were initially called to the streets by the so-called “Flamingo Revolution” protesters. Their daily protests started in June as environmental demonstrations but evolved into an anti-government movement.

World.title: Central Europe Struggles to Square the Circle over Foreign Workers
World.content:
Politics vs economics

That has been a familiar theme across the four countries, where the economic case for foreign labour has not translated into a political consensus for such an influx. Governments and employers might recognise the need for workers, but concerns about wages, competition for jobs and immigration have made recruitment politically contentious.

While having to accommodate the “Czech first” stance of its coalition partner, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) movement, the ruling ANO party of Prime Minister Andrej Babis has vowed to “look for nurses in Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan” and – more generally speaking – bring in 100,000 qualified foreigners by 2030.

“The current 942,000 foreign workers in the Czech Republic are still far below market potential,” ANO stated, with the ruling party planning to reduce the administrative burden, simplify the recognition of foreign diploma and certificates, digitise the entire process, and shorten permit deliveries to 30 days for highly qualified employees and 60 days for medium and low-skilled workers.

And while Czech employers and business associations have overall welcomed such plans, they have also warned of the risks to focus solely on high-skilled labour.

“Speed and predictability are crucial because Czech companies are competing for skilled workers with companies in Germany, Poland and other European countries,” Sotona of the Czech Chamber of Commerce tells BIRN.

“This is not a choice between making better use of domestic labour and labour migration. The Czech Republic needs to do both,” he says. “The objective is not uncontrolled migration, but the opposite: a legal, transparent and predictable system that enables companies to recruit workers whom they objectively cannot find on the domestic labour market.”

Across the border, “foreigners today are not just a supplement, but an essential part of the [Slovak] labour market,” according to Jakub Zagora, an analyst at the Kosice IT Valley in eastern Slovakia. “At the same time, however, we see that the demand for workers still significantly exceeds the supply.”

Obstacles to hiring foreign workers are many, ranging from uncertainty and bureaucratic hurdles to integrating them over the long term, to laborious permits procedures and enduring anti-foreigner sentiment among the population.

About two-thirds of Slovak employees see foreigners as a potential threat to their own jobs, and three-quarters worry their employment hinders overall wage growth, according to a JobsIndex survey. “Employers still see more problems and obstacles than benefits in importing workers from abroad,” assessed Martin Szabo, a labour market expert at Alma Career Slovakia.

Hungary’s restrictions have brought the tension between politics and economic needs sharply into focus. Since the government stopped issuing residence permits to people arriving under guest-worker contracts, employers have warned of difficulties filling vacancies and delays to investment. The door remains open to those applying for a so-called “residence permit for the purpose of employment”, but this is a more complicated and lengthy process, often taking nine to 12 months.

“Companies are already feeling the consequences and complaining about the lack of workers from third countries,” says Kalmar of BusinessHungary.

The organisation has been negotiating with the government to find a solution. Some urgently needed investments are already being delayed as companies are unsure whether they will be able to find enough suitably qualified workers.

The debate intensified during the summer when the owner of Master Good, one of Hungary’s largest agrifood companies, threatened not to proceed with a 120-billion-forint investment, worth about 330 million euros, in a new meat-processing plant if guest workers were not allowed into the country.

Critics accused the company of seeking to keep wages down, arguing that foreign workers, who are often willing to work longer hours than Hungarians, drive down pay. Yet Master Good’s owner, Laszlo Barany, countered that there were jobs for which the company simply could not find Hungarian workers. “There are shifts starting at 02:00 in the night, and the temperature in the processing plant is under 10 degrees Celsius all day,” he told Telex.hu. The company has employed guest workers from the Philippines for years to fill those positions.

Kalmar argues that Hungarian and guest workers are often not alternatives to one another. “In many cases, employing guest workers for certain jobs serves the interests of Hungarian workers,” he says. If there are no food couriers, he explains, a cook’s job could be at risk; if there are no workers at the end of an assembly line, an engineer might also lose their job.

The claims that foreign workers earn more than Hungarians are dismissed by Kalmar and, he says, is legally impossible. He acknowledges, however, that in some cases where a company has had to lay off workers, those dismissed were mostly Hungarian, while workers from third countries were retained. “They simply performed better,” he says.

A survey conducted by HR company WHC found that 70 per cent of medium-sized and large Hungarian companies could not imagine operating without foreign workers. The same survey found scepticism about the government’s plans to bring 300,000-400,000 so-called inactive Hungarians back into the labour market.

The problem with this proposed reserve is that people who are unemployed or economically inactive do not necessarily have the right skills, live in the right places or want the jobs on offer. “The problem is that this reserve usually does not match companies’ needs, either geographically or in terms of skills or motivation,” Kalmar explains.

Poland’s experience illustrates a related difficulty: even when migrants are available, employers cannot assume they will remain in the jobs that are hardest to fill. In research involving employers in agriculture and hospitality, Kaczmarczyk’s team found that businesses had stopped advertising some jobs in Polish altogether because nobody responded.

In agriculture, peak season can mean six or seven days a week and 10- or 12-hour shifts – conditions few Polish workers are willing to accept. Foreign labour has filled much of that gap, but workers who settle and integrate may eventually move into more attractive employment.

World.title: Black Sea Drone Attacks Expose Holes in Bulgarian Security Strategy
World.content:
For Bulgarians, the war in Ukraine this month came closer to home than ever before.

Two drone attacks on commercial ships in the country’s Black Sea zone, on October 6 and October 13, raised difficult questions about Bulgaria’s preparedness for further escalation, and its government’s tendency to avoid direct criticism of Russia.

Each attack sank a ship and damaged another. The exact death toll has yet to be confirmed.

“We don’t have solid evidence to blame either side but logic suggests the strikes have been of benefit to the Russian Federation,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev, himself a former air force commander, said in the wake of the second attack.

He summoned Russian ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who claimed that “a third side” may have been responsible.

Whatever the truth, former deputy defence minister Velizar Shalamanov says Bulgaria’s inaction is dangerous.

World.title: Rising Violence is a Sign that Serbia’s Ruling Party is Panicking
World.content:
During a recent protest against Aleksandar Vucic's visit to the town of Uzice, ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, supporters assaulted and beat several citizens, while police stood by without intervening.

In Belgrade, a group of men attacked and injured an official observer from Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Agency, an independent state institution, while he was documenting campaign activities at a stand operated by the ruling party.

In Novi Sad, SNS supporters led by one of the party’s parliamentary candidates confronted activists and candidates of the opposition student-led electoral list and attempted to seize their banner.

In another incident, Belgrade’s Mayor Aleksandar Sapic was reported to have physically assaulted a female opposition councillor in the street, although he denied this. A week later, an N1 television journalist was attacked and threatened by a prominent SNS supporter while investigating potential electoral fraud. In the city of Nis, a journalist from an independent website was assaulted and injured while filming SNS campaign activities, with police reportedly refusing to intervene.

This week also saw revelations from SNS hired hand Momcilo Marjanovic, who told BIRN that he spent a decade providing ‘security’ for the ruling party, a role that involved buying votes and beating protesters.

These are not episodes scattered across years of political turmoil. They have all been reported in the space of a few weeks, as Serbia gets closer to parliamentary elections on October 25.

World.title: Elisa to shut down 2G network in 2028, competitors hold back for now
World.content:
Phone operator Elisa is to shut down its 2G mobile network in 2028, Sakala reported .

The service will be phased out region by region, and the closure will leave older phones and devices that rely only on 2G or 3G without a connection, as Estonia's 3G network has already shut down.

Elisa spokesperson Toomas Polli said the technology dates from a time when a phone's main job was calling and sending messages, and that the role of networks has changed beyond recognition.

Competitors Telia and Tele2 said they will be closing down their 2G networks too, but not before 2029-2030 – Tele2 spokesperson Tanel Sarri said security devices and gate systems still depend on 2G.

Elisa network services development director Kristo Kork said the 2G closure will happen in phases by region, but the exact timetable and order of regions is still being drawn up and with customers noted in good time - Elisa would not say how many devices on its network are 2G-only, but said most already support 4G and 5G.

The original Sakala piece is here.

Elisa stated on its own website it shut down 3G at the end of 2024, and while most calls and data already run on newer networks, some devices in Estonia still rely on 2G.

Alongside older phones, these include security and alarm systems, electricity and water meters, payment terminals, and industrial and property automation equipment.

Polli said most people won't need to do anything, but devices with a longer lifespan than phones need attention. "Some surveillance, measurement or automation devices may have been installed ten or even more years ago and are still operating on a 2G network," he said.

2G networks, which launched in Finland in 1991, are also being phased out in other North European countries. Sweden and Norway set are to do so in 2027, while Iceland already did so last year. Further afield, G networks have already been shut down in Australia, Japan, and the U.S. Elisa recommends travellers with concerns check whether their device supports 4G and/or VoLTE.

World.title: Estonia mulls allowing dual citizenship in certain circumstances
World.content:
The coalition parties want to allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The opposition questions what problem the change is intended to solve.

On Wednesday, the Reform Party and Eesti 200 parliamentary groups in the Riigikogu jointly introduced a bill that would allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The bill would allow Estonian citizens by birth to apply to have their Estonian citizenship restored even if they had previously lost or renounced it after acquiring citizenship of another country.

Under the Constitution, Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. However, the Citizenship Act stipulates that people who are Estonian citizens by birth but also hold citizenship of another country must choose between the two when they turn 18.

Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said at a government press conference that this was the wrong approach. "There is no reasonable justification for this whatsoever," she said. Pakosta argued that if an 18-year-old receives a letter telling them to choose between U.S. and Estonian citizenship, for example, but wants to retain both, they are fully entitled to do so.

Dual citizenship would be possible only in the case of select countries

According to Pakosta, this is precisely why the law needs to be brought into line with reality. The countries with which dual citizenship would be permitted include European Economic Area member states, as well as the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Switzerland. These countries are home to large Estonian communities.

The opposition does not understand what problem the proposal is intended to solve. Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. Vadim Belobrovtsev, deputy chairman of the Center Party's parliamentary group, suggested that the coalition was trying to push through a proposal ahead of the elections that actually requires more extensive debate.

He said that because the bill applies only to Estonian citizens by birth, it would give some people an advantage over others.

Military service one potential stepping stone

Evelin Poolamets (EKRE) said the bill would create further confusion, particularly regarding compulsory military service. She explained that questions would arise over whether a young person should complete military service in Estonia or another country and which country's military reserve they would be assigned to.

Poolamets noted that the Citizenship Act contains various provisions affecting citizens, including matters related to social security and pensions. "Perhaps the goal is precisely to give dual citizens more opportunities," she said. However, Poolamets added that there was no guarantee a person would contribute equally to both countries.

Valdo Randpere (Reform Party) said times and circumstances have changed, with many young people living abroad and that citizenship is one way to maintain ties with Estonia. Randpere hopes the bill will secure the necessary 51 votes this time.

"I've spoken with both unaffiliated MPs and opposition representatives and I haven't received a firm no," Randpere said. He has not discussed the issue with EKRE representatives. "They would definitely say no," Randpere explained. He hopes at least one opposition party will allow its MPs a free vote.

World.title: Estonian ex-soldier jailed in Russia after visiting his wife
World.content:
A former Estonian Defense Forces member is currently in a Russian prison, accused by the FSB of planning to fight for Ukraine — a charge his family says was forced out of him.

Artur Kirmjõe, 30, is married to a Russian national who is banned from entering Estonia, leaving him to travel to Russia to visit her. He had done so over 10 times before he was detained on April 29.

In a video published by the FSB — Russia's main internal security organ — in the Vladimir oblast in June this year, a man with his face concealed states he got in touch with Ukrainian contacts and asked to join Ukraine's armed forces.

"My attitude towards the war in Ukraine became sharply negative. On my own initiative, I contacted Ukrainian contacts and asked them to help me join Ukrainian military units to fight on their side against Russia," the man is heard to say.

Relatives confirm it is Artur, but say he was induced to say what he does in the video.

"He said what he was forced to say, but it is all lies. It is not true. He was just reading it, I don't know, from a screen or from a piece of paper," said his brother, Jüri.

Artur Kirmjõe served in the EDF'Scout's Battalion. Source: ERR

Artur's mother, Inga Allikas, points out the absurdity of the charges given how and why her son had traveled there. "If a person wants to go and fight on Ukraine's side, they don't take big suitcases and a cat and travel to Russia to their wife," she said.

The "Pealtnägija" report was the first time Jüri and Inga have spoken publicly on the episode under their own names and faces. The family had not drawn attention to the case earlier, hoping it was a misunderstanding which would resolve itself. Now they want international attention drawn to the situation: the 30-year-old Estonian citizen faces 7 to 12 years in prison based on what they call a trumped-up confession.

Artur was born in Tallinn and grew up in nearby Maardu. He is bilingual and studied in Russian for his first eight school years, and in Estonian after that. After high school he studied at the maritime academy, was conscripted, and stayed on as a regular EDF member — serving as a paramedic in the Scout's Battalion at Tapa from autumn 2018 to the end of 2020.

The chain of events leading to his current plight began shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In late March that year, a couple arrived from Russia — a married couple, aged just over 20, referred to in the report as Lina and Sergei. In early April 2022 they applied for international protection in Estonia, saying life in Russia was dangerous for them due to their anti-war views.

"Lina was persecuted because of her political views, which were clearly opposed to the Russian state," said her lawyer, Merili Laansoo.

Indrek Aru, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border guard bureau, said not all circumstances could be commented on, but that the grounds given were checked and no sufficient basis for protection was found.

Artur with his wife Liina (name changed). Source: ERR

When the PPA refused protection, Sergei and Lina appealed. Tallinn Administrative Court found they were not in real danger in Russia: no criminal cases had been opened against them, they were not on any wanted lists, and the likelihood of attracting the authorities' attention was low. The pair appealed to the Supreme Court without success. In November 2023, they were banned from entering Estonia for three years — a detail that matters much in respect of what followed.

"He was quite shocked. You could see he was very uncomfortable, because he started crying. Just uncontrollably," said their friend Lars-Eerik Väina.

While the court cases were unfolding, a romance unfolded too, between Artur and the still-married Lina. The pair were working as security guards at the Kauplus Aasia club in Tallinn. Lina divorced Sergei in summer 2023.

Since Lina had to leave Estonia a few months later, in November 2023, Artur and Lina married in Russia on June 1, 2024, at a registry office in Vladimir, 200 kilometers from Moscow. The couple said they hoped the entry ban would now be lifted, but the PPA refused again — seeing it as suspicious that the application to live in Estonia had come so soon after the marriage, which in turn had followed soon after the entry ban.

As a result, Artur shuttled between Estonia and Russia more than ten times between 2023 and 2026 to see his wife. The lawyer representing them repeatedly pointed out that traveling to Russia could be dangerous, particularly as Artur was a former serviceman, but the PPA downplayed any danger.

"A significant number of Estonian citizens live permanently in Russia. In this case, the specific person has traveled back and forth to Russia repeatedly. Yes, at certain stages our wording may not have been the best. I admit that in hindsight," Aru said. He added that the official information presented at the time was not meant to encourage Estonians to travel to Russia, and that it was an unfortunate choice of words.

"I think those decisions are made en masse; everyone gets the same reply under their application. Nobody looks through the files, nobody looks at the applicant's background, whether it is genuinely safe for them or not," Inga said.

Artur in EDF uniform with his mother, Inga Allikas. Source: ERR

Inga now lives in Helsinki and works as an accountant, but she previously spent years working as a translator for the PPA. She believes official indifference cost her son his freedom. Separation from his wife has caused Artur mental health problems, the family says, and in April this year he traveled to Russia again, after six months apart.

"I lived with him for about 20 years. And the fact that he went there means love told him that it was the only thing worth going for — love," said his brother Jüri.

At the end of April, the FSB arrested the Estonian citizen in Lina's kitchen. Then in June the video appeared on the FSB Vladimir office's Telegram channel and spread to other outlets. In it, Artur appears to confess to anti-Russian activity.

Relatives, who can only communicate with Artur by letter via Lina, believe the video statements are entirely fabricated. "Artur has never been to Ukraine, not even out of tourist interest. To comment on what the charge is based on — some correspondence that was found, maybe. I don't know," said Inga.

Aru said the family's view is now seen differently in light of the arrest and detention. "But in hindsight, would that change anything? We cannot change the past. It is, unfortunately, a tragic story," he said.

Lina says she is currently not facing persecution, but, citing her safety, declined to appear in the report and asked that her real name not be published.

Artur's family has hired a lawyer in Russia and recently appealed to the Estonian Foreign Ministry for help, so that consular officials can assist and diplomats can perhaps pull international strings. "I know Estonia should somehow contact the United States — I don't know which institution — and start negotiations to have Artur added to an exchange list, so he might get home sooner than if he serves all those years," Inga concluded.

World.title: Tartu prison director: Dissatisfaction with prison life hardly out of the ordinary
World.content:
Tartu Prison Director Merle Ulst acknowledged that renting out prison space is a new situation for all parties involved, requiring both the Estonian Prison Service and the inmates brought to Estonia to adapt.

The inmates complained that prison officials did not speak English well enough and that they had been sent to Estonia against their will. Among other things, the inmates were unhappy that the two televisions in their cells were positioned side by side, that the beds lacked guardrails and that they had no privacy when washing.

Ulst noted that the visit by the Office of the Chancellor of Justice took place nearly two months ago when the vast majority of Swedish inmates had been at Tartu Prison for just two days. Most of the issues and concerns raised at the time had already come up in the prison staff's daily work.

"Addressing these issues is part of the prison's day-to-day work. We explain the rules and procedures to inmates, listen to their feedback and make adjustments based on practical experience where reasonable and possible. When new procedures are introduced, it is only natural that some arrangements need to be refined and improved based on initial experience," Ulst said.

She emphasized that inmates cannot expect all the comforts they are accustomed to outside prison and that certain restrictions are an inevitable part of prison life.

"Our task is to ensure humane conditions, respect for inmates' rights and a safe environment for everyone in our custody. These principles also guide us when making changes. We take legitimate needs into account, but not every request warrants changing existing procedures," Ulst said.

The Tartu Prison director noted that the issues raised by Swedish and Estonian inmates regarding everyday living conditions, restrictions and prison procedures are fairly similar.

"Dissatisfaction with certain aspects of prison life is not unusual and addressing such concerns is part of the prison's daily work. Regardless of an inmate's background, we follow the same principles: We ensure their rights and humane conditions while maintaining clear boundaries necessary for the prison to function," she said.

World.title: Eesti 200 to decide Sunday on running with Greens at Riigikogu election
World.content:
Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas is to propose at Sunday's party board meeting that the party run alongside the Greens in the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.

The Greens (Rohelised) will discuss the merger at their own general assembly later in the month. Both parties are polling far below the 5 percent threshold required to win seats, at 1.2 (Eesti 200) and 0.7 percent (Greens), even though Eesti 200 is in office with Reform at the national level.

Media reports that the two parties were considering joining forces emerged late last month.

Kallas, who is also education minister, told ERR she will make the proposal at Sunday's meeting and was unwilling to comment further on the possible merger, or her own political plans before then.

Rasmus Lahtvee, one of the Green party's leaders, said the exact date for their discussions is still not set, but the merger with Eesti 200 will certainly be talked about..

"There is talk [with Eesti 200]. We have been feeling out various possibilities and what the two parties have in common. It is clear that something has to change on the Estonian political landscape," Lahtvee said.

"The merger certainly has to be decided by the general meeting, and that will stay at the end of October," he went on.

Asked whether the parties' possible decisions would be followed by more serious merger talks in November, Lahtvee said some clarity must come soon, as the president will declare the Riigikogu elections by December 6 at the latest. Polling day is set for March 7, 2027.

Eesti 200 has been struggling with very low ratings for several years now. A Norstat poll published this week put support for the party at 1.2 percent, with the Greens at 0.7 percent. The latest ERR-commissioned Emor poll in September put Eesti 200 at 1.9 percent and the Greens at 1.1 percent.

Eesti 200 was founded in 2018 and won 14 Riigikogu seats in 2023, entering government with Reform and, until spring last year, the Social Democrats (SDE). Lauri Hussar, a former Eesti 200 chair, has held the Riigikogu speaker position since April 2023, while Margus Tsahkna is its Foreign Minister.

Eesti 200's rating started to collapse soon after the 2023 election, however, after a donations to Ukraine scandal engulfed a former MP. Another MP, former Green leader Züleyxa Izmailova, who herself had replaced the disgraced MP, returned to her original party, SDE, in 2024. Then in late summer this year, high-profile MP and former Riigikogu Defense Committee chair Kalev Stoicescu quit the party, to join the non-parliamentary Parempoolsed. This left the ruling Reform-Eesti 200 coalition as a minority government.

Eesti 200 has also approached SDE and also the Free Party (Vabaerakond) about mergers, but without success. The Greens in fact have more members now — 705 to Eesti 200's 579 — but their candidates mostly cannot afford the €946 election deposit, which is part of what Eesti 200 could offer.

A party needs a minimum of 500 members to be legally registered.
