World.title: Foreign minister: One must ensure one's own survival when inflicting pain on Russia
World.content:
Estonia's decision to keep a Russian supplier to Silmet off the EU sanctions list was necessary to protect European industry, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said, but stressed that the company must end its dependence on Russian raw materials or face further sanctions.

Estonia has been a leading advocate of sanctions for years. Now it turns out that we have nevertheless been feeding the Russian war machine through Silmet. How is that possible?

Estonia has been and will continue to be one of the most active advocates of sanctions and supporters of Ukraine in Europe. And just on Monday, we imposed sanctions on 1,600 companies and individuals. But my question is rather the other way around: How is it possible that, in the fifth year of the war, Europe remains so dependent on Russia, particularly for rare earth elements, for example? And that is not a question for Estonia. Rather, the question is how actively Europe has been working to eliminate these dependencies. We know that we are buying less energy, but Europe still continues to consume Russian energy.

What we are doing now is setting out our conditions for Silmet. And now that Silmet has also received notification from the European Commission that it has been included on the list of strategic companies, this provides a basis for obtaining European funding. But that funding must come with conditions and one of those conditions must be that the company eliminates its dependence on Russia.

But Estonia has held itself up as a moral beacon in the European Union when it comes to doing business with Russia. How can we now point fingers at others who want to do business with Russia or refuse to impose sanctions?

I would not exaggerate this position of being Europe's moral beacon quite so much. We have simply been very exemplary in our actions and we have absolutely never discussed...

This particular case shows that we have not been exemplary.

Yes, but this particular request also came from the European Commission. We also have to ask the question the other way around: If Russia were to stop supplying these raw materials to Europe altogether, European technology companies, including those in the defense industry, would be in very serious trouble.

So this is not a question of our being a moral beacon. We will continue in that role. Unfortunately, there is still a great deal of lobbying going on in the corridors of the European Commission, not specifically on strategic issues where Europe is dependent, but also purely in the interests of business. This is something that Estonian viewers do not usually learn about.

But we will continue our work as advocates of sanctions and Silmet's owners have also been told very clearly that they have a certain amount of time to eliminate their dependence on these raw materials. And this particular company will be added to the sanctions list at Estonia's own initiative.

How exactly did Silmet's supplier, a Rosatom subsidiary, end up on the proposed sanctions list? Who put forward that proposal?

We do not know how this particular company ended up on the list. Estonia has also made a great many different proposals concerning both companies and individuals. And in a sense, that is the problem with the European Commission's procedure: Before a draft reaches the member states' ambassadors, quite a few names and companies disappear during the process.

That happened this time as well. In fact, of those 1,600, I estimate that more than 50 have disappeared. We do not know who made those proposals, which is not even such a big problem. But we do not know at whose request those individuals and companies were removed from the list.

Now, Estonia acted very honestly and clearly. When the draft was already complete, the Commission pointed out that this particular magnesium plant was very directly connected to Silmet's supplies and that Silmet accounts for a very large share of what Europe needs for its industry. They asked us to look into it and it turned out that Silmet was dependent on this particular plant in its supply chain.

Did Estonia ask for Silmet's supplier not to be included on the list?

On the Commission's recommendation, we said that this particular proposal should be removed from the draft until the supply problem involving Russia had been resolved.

Did that proposal come from the Estonian government or from Silmet?

No, the proposal came to us from the Commission and I, as foreign minister, acting under the existing government mandate, confirmed that this would indeed have real consequences for European industry and that, until the supply problem was resolved, this company would not be included on the sanctions list.

We have been working for several years to find some kind of solution, but Silmet is not a state-owned company. Silmet is a private company. Silmet's owner is Neo Group, which is listed on the Canadian stock exchange.

Now that we have a real means of leverage, for example through funding, we can set our conditions directly for Neo Group. And that is what we have done.

I hope this problem will be resolved next year and that this particular company in Russia will also be on the sanctions list. It is not that easy to change the mines from which these raw materials originate. The issue is not only that there is enormous global competition, but, according to Silmet, it also requires changes in technology, and that is precisely why investment is needed.

Four and a half years have passed since the start of the war. Have you previously spoken with Silmet's management about the fact that importing these materials from Russia is not a particularly sensible thing to do, given that they would inevitably be sanctioned at some point?

We have discussed this repeatedly and we have also discussed how to attract investment here so that this specialized industry can develop in Estonia. Our goal, in fact, is to bring rare earth production, magnet manufacturing and the entire research, development and innovation center to Estonia. There is enormous competition for this around the world.

Silmet and Neo are the world's largest producers of rare earth elements outside China. So, for example, we are currently negotiating with the United States to conclude a memorandum of understanding. The European Union has already done so with the United States.

And we have been working to get Silmet and Neo included on Europe's list of strategic companies, which happened last week, and to bring European Union investment here.

Incidentally, a Neo magnet plant opened in Narva last year and the European Commission has already invested in it. So there are enormous opportunities here for Estonian industry and for our own economy.

But one specific problem that remains unresolved in Europe is this dependence on Russia and it must now be addressed as quickly as possible. It certainly will not be easy, but the only thing the Estonian government can do is apply pressure. We do not actually want to lose our own industry either.

By the way, are raw materials still being shipped from Russia's Solikamsk Magnesium Plant to Estonia today?

We are in contact with Neo's representative and my understanding is that another shipment still needs to be made. They have already factored that in. This morning (Wednesday — ed.), they also issued a public press release announcing their intention to use the available opportunities to end Russian supplies and eliminate this dependence.

Four and a half years after the start of a war that everyone has long known about. Can we trust them? And what happens if they still have not found a new supplier by the end of this year or the beginning of next year? Will national sanctions be imposed or what happens then?

If Europe has taken the necessary steps to make this technological change possible and Silmet, for example, still does not make that change, then it is no longer our responsibility. In that case, this particular company must be added to the list.

We have simply provided an opportunity for this change to take place. And this is not something that began because the company appeared on a proposed sanctions list. Work on this issue had already been underway.

Let's clarify one more thing about the timeline. Did the prime minister know that Estonia did not want to impose sanctions on a Rosatom subsidiary?

This was part of the normal working process and it was handled at my level. We bring individual decisions to the government when, for example, we are going to block a sanctions list.

That is what almost happened with the sanctions against individuals when two oligarchs were removed at France's request. If we had decided, for example, to be the only country to vote against the list and the entire list of 3,000 individuals headed by Putin had ultimately been left without sanctions, decisions of that kind would go through the government.

The prime minister is certainly aware that Silmet depends on Russian raw materials or that European industry depends on Russian raw materials. But this particular process is managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

But the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee did not know about this either?

That Europe depends on Russian raw materials? I think that...

Were they aware that Silmet imports raw materials from Russia?

I think the entire Estonian public knows that because, as far as I know, Silmet's story has been discussed for more than 10 years.

As for the working process, this is actually how it operates because there is constant work going on between the member states and the Commission on these sanctions lists, proposals and everything related to them. That is precisely the work of our diplomats.

Why was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' initial reaction that this information should not have become public?

I do not know where the idea comes from that this information should not have become public.

That initial reaction, suggesting that this was some kind of retaliation against Estonia, that we had done something and now information had become public about which company in Russia might face sanctions?

Everything that happens in the Committee of Permanent Representatives, or Coreper, is not some kind of state secret. In that sense, I cannot say what the big secret here is.

Perhaps it is even a good thing that this has become so public and that Estonian society as a whole and Europe more broadly are recognizing that we still have a very significant strategic dependence on Russia.

What is even worse is that Europe is actually dependent on China, and, to be frank, I do not see any solution whatsoever to that problem.

We will resolve this Russian problem, or rather, the company must resolve it, not the Estonian state. But I think Europe's dependence on China will remain for a very long time.

In your assessment, did the Ministry of Foreign Affairs act correctly? Was its reaction in the first few days exactly what it should have been?

I think the reaction of the Estonian public was entirely...

The ministry's reaction.

The Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs is doing its job and we have never concealed what we are working on.

If I were in the same situation I was in a few weeks ago, I would make exactly the same decision because we are talking about European industry, we are talking about Estonian industry and we are talking about the need to eliminate our strategic dependence on Russia.

So there is no need to look for any conspiracy theory here. Communication has been very open.

But perhaps we should openly acknowledge that, in certain cases, we have no other choice. This company is so important to our economy that, in some cases, exceptions have to be made and imports from Russia have to continue.

In certain cases, when supply problems have not been resolved and these are existential issues for us, then inevitably that is how things are.

But that does not mean we should in any way abandon our support for Ukraine or stop applying additional pressure on Russia, which we have no intention of doing.

In a sense, I am even pleased that Estonian society is so uncompromising that we do not accept any such deviations or alternative interpretations.

Unfortunately, that is not the case across Europe. Increasingly, we are seeing that it is becoming harder and harder to agree on new sanctions packages. In fact, when you start working on something, you often have to take several steps back.

How can Estonia demand that other countries adopt these sanctions packages when we ourselves seemingly cannot even comply with them very well?

We can comply with them very well. Estonia has called for a complete trade embargo. Just today, at my decision-making meeting, I approved new proposals and this changes absolutely nothing about our course.

This is completely normal work for other member states as well. When issues like these come up, they are raised. This is not just about Estonia's interests or anyone's business interests. It is actually a European problem.

These matters must be discussed openly and, as foreign minister, I have no problem explaining them because any reasonable person in Estonia can understand this.

This is not some kind of moral competition. We are talking about how to inflict as much pain as possible on Russia while also ensuring our own survival.

And the question should rather be asked the other way around: How is it possible that Russia holds such powerful leverage over the whole of European industry?

What do you think the answer is? Why has Europe backed itself into a corner when it comes to raw materials?

It is not just Europe. This is actually a broader global issue and it is not just about Russia. China's influence is even greater.

In this context, perhaps what is unfamiliar to Estonia is that this particular rare earth industry and magnet industry are of such enormous importance to the entire world, especially Europe.

Europe has simply been unable to respond in the way many other countries have. And if we look, for example, at what President Trump is doing in this field today, the sums of money involved are enormous and so is the political influence.

We will get to Trump, but I want to ask one final question on this subject. You met with your Ukrainian counterpart on Monday. How could you look him in the eye in light of all this?

I looked him in the eye the same way I always do.

They are facing a very difficult winter, during which they will need very substantial assistance from Europe.

By Monday, it was also already clear that Trump had once again put Ukraine under pressure.

So I think we should focus on what the truly existential issues are and how we can help Ukraine survive this winter.

Those are the issues we actually discuss with our colleagues from Ukraine and Europe.

Eesti Ekspress reported today that there are 22 kilometers of spare gas pipeline in southeastern Estonia intended for Russia. Should Estonia maintain a gas pipeline intended for Russia in working order?

If that is what you mean, then it can be kept in working order, but not open.

Keeping it in working order also costs money.

Well, that is some kind of international obligation, since it is an international gas pipeline. But the question is whether the pipeline is open. It is not open.

It has been open on certain occasions?

Exactly, and that is why I met with the prime minister this morning and our climate minister has also been given the relevant instructions.

In fact, the valves are located in Latvia and a large part of the infrastructure is in Lithuania.

This is a European Union issue, but it is certainly one of the ways, let's be frank, that we could put pressure on Russia at some point because gas and gas transit are not subject to EU sanctions.

Let's talk about Trump and Putin. As we know, the U.S. president struck a so-called diesel deal with Putin. Why has the U.S. president begun bringing Vladimir Putin out of isolation?

First of all, this is not the first time that many people who sympathize with Ukraine have suffered what you might call a nervous breakdown, gone gray or lost a few brain cells.

But I think these questions should, of course, be put first and foremost to U.S. President Trump.

I think the answers are primarily connected to the midterm elections, which are fast approaching.

What is Estonia's position on this?

We have stated very clearly that this is a step in completely the wrong direction, considering that it allows Putin to earn additional revenue.

But this has now also been accompanied by pressure that goes beyond buying diesel. What is particularly serious is the pressure on Zelenskyy to stop his attacks on oil refineries.

That is actually where Putin and his capabilities can be significantly weakened.

Ultimately, the volume involved is not decisive in terms of either the global market or U.S. consumption.

And this is largely a political game aimed at his own voters, in response to a situation of his own making in which oil and gas prices have risen very sharply.

Has Estonia communicated its position to the United States in any way?

We have stated it completely publicly and our positions are well known.

Going back to the beginning of the interview, we criticize Trump, saying that this move is wrong. Yet through Silmet, we ourselves are feeding that same Russian war machine. Isn't that hypocritical?

These are two completely different issues.

One is whether you go and offer a deal to buy diesel or propose that kind of cooperation.

The other is when you are trying to eliminate your own strategic dependence.

These are not comparable issues.

How has this company been trying to eliminate that dependence for four and a half years without succeeding and now we are hoping it will manage to do so in just a few months?

That is what they say and I think the company's representatives should come on this program and explain to you what they have done over the past four and a half years.

By the way, have you been in contact with Silmet's CEO again over the past week?

I have been in contact with him before, personally.

But not recently?

I have. I spoke with him on Friday and our people are in contact.

Perhaps as a result of this pressure, the company, as a publicly traded company, also issued a press release this morning, which I recommend reading.

Returning to Trump, is Trump now so angry that, for the Ukrainians, this means receiving less intelligence, none at all or receiving it with a delay?

Today, I met with NATO Secretary General Rutte who was visiting Estonia and this was one of the questions we discussed.

NATO is very well informed and as of today, the United States has not restricted its intelligence sharing.

I hope that remains the case.

So this appears to be primarily political pressure, but who knows? Trump is unpredictable.

So, as things stand, at least according to NATO's assessment, the Americans have not started reducing the intelligence reaching Ukraine or causing any delays in its delivery?

Yes. The information our secretary general had was that intelligence sharing has not been reduced.

Military assistance provided through the PURL mechanism has also not been reduced or suspended.

I hope that remains the case.

Finally, a little about Estonian domestic affairs. President Alar Karis criticized the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, meaning you, in his latest speech. Do you accept the criticism?

I think Alar Karis should now move on with his life, just as he appeared to be doing in the photo he posted on Facebook, sitting in a comfortable chair by the sea.

Tomorrow, I am meeting with the new president, Ülle Madise. We have also sat down together since her election by the Riigikogu and our team is working very well with her.

So I would not go down the path of commenting on the views of a president who is already leaving office.

But what will communication between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the presidency as an institution look like now? Will cooperation with Ülle Madise be better?

Just as cooperation was excellent during President Karis' term, it will also be excellent with Ülle Madise.

--

World.title: Estonia still importing Russian food products
World.content:
Estonia's trade with Russia has dwindled since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but imports of food products have continued alongside rare earth metals.

Tespi, a wholesale warehouse store, imports Russian and Belarusian food products that are not subject to sanctions into Estonia. Some of these products are also sold by other grocery stores. The retailers are reluctant to discuss Russian goods.

Apart from certain chemicals and rare earth metals, for which Estonia sought special permission from the European Union to supply Silmet, food products now account for most imports from Russia to Estonia. In August, for example, imports of Russian food products and animal products totaled around €1 million, although last year there were months when the figure reached €3 million. Imports have declined since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but not significantly.

"The fluctuations in food import figures are due to the size of the shipments transported by sea," said Ursula Riimaa, deputy director general for customs at the Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA).

Overall, however, little remains of Estonia's trade relations with Russia.

"Trade with Russia has changed significantly, both in terms of imports and exports. Before the war, Estonia imported approximately €2.2 billion worth of goods from Russia. In the first eight months of this year, imports totaled around €40 million. We're talking about volumes that have fallen more than tenfold," Riimaa said.

The European Union's sanctions policy has primarily targeted sectors of the Russian economy that fuel its war machine, such as exports of petroleum products and mineral resources. Product categories that generate less revenue for Russia have so far largely been excluded from the restrictions.

"Food products and medical supplies have been the two main categories of goods that have largely remained exempt from sanctions so far. However, certain food products classified as luxury goods are subject to restrictions on both imports from and exports to Russia," said Kadri Elias-Hindoalla, director general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' sanctions department.

Compared with prewar levels, EU exports to Russia have fallen by 60 percent, while imports have dropped by 90 percent. Additional restrictions are being introduced with each new sanctions package.

The most significant measure set to take effect next year is a restriction on imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG), which several European countries continue to purchase from Russia.

World.title: Company managing Narva border queue asks city for support after traffic dries up
World.content:
Cross-border vehicle traffic has come to a standstill and the city-owned company is struggling to make ends meet. City officials have not ruled out suspending the company's operations.

Transservis-N, the company that has managed the border crossing queue in Narva, has been struggling financially for two years. In better times, when thousands of vehicles crossed the border, the company paid dividends to the city of Narva. Now it is asking its owner for financial support to stay afloat — €50,000 this year and twice that amount next year. The city of Narva has yet to decide what to do with the company.

"If we shut it down, it will be very difficult to get it up and running again. The buildings will deteriorate and what would we do with the parking lot? We are still finding some use for it today. Cars from Latvia, Lithuania and Finland are parked at the Transservis-N lot, belonging to tourists who cross the border on foot. That brings in some revenue. But the number of Finnish tourists and people crossing the border here in general is steadily declining. We will start discussing this. We may indeed have to make a difficult decision," Narva Mayor Jaan Toots said.

The mayor nevertheless hopes that the border will reopen to vehicle traffic and that the company will not have to close.

Narva's opposition believes there is no point in holding out false hope as border traffic is only likely to decline further during the war, rather than increase. City officials must take this into account. Keeping the company operating solely to provide parking makes little sense.

"These are not even cars belonging to Narva residents and this is certainly not an essential service for us. I think it would make sense to temporarily shut down the company and reestablish it if the border does reopen for some reason. But that can only happen after the war ends," Narva City Council member Katri Raik said.

Narva city officials will decide the fate of Transservis-N as they prepare next year's budget. Vehicle traffic across the border in Narva was suspended in early 2024 when Russia began rebuilding the vehicle terminal at the Ivangorod border crossing. The work is reportedly scheduled to be completed this December.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate slightly rises against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced a slight increase on Thursday in both Baghdad, the Iraqi capital, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,665.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,665 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,670 Iraqi dinars and 1,660 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also increased, fluctuating between 1,664 and 1,663 Iraqi dinars.

US dollar exchange rates rose noticeably in the Baghdad and Erbil markets on October 7, following the cabinet’s decision to revalue the official rate of the local currency, causing turbulence and instability in the parallel market.

Iraq officially depreciated its national currency, with the baseline dropping from about 1,300 Iraqi dinars to 1,500 dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet approved the structural adjustment, which marks a 14.5 percent decline compared to the previous official framework that had been in place since early 2023.

Following the announcement, parallel market rates in Baghdad and Erbil soared, with exchange shops reporting market gains of more than 1,700 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

World.title: Infantino offers apology but ‘no answers’ at FIFA meeting over World Cup plan
World.content:
Zurich – FIFA president Gianni Infantino gave “no satisfactory answers” when grilled Thursday during a meeting to discuss his attempts to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, senior members of football’s global governing body said, but he did offer an apology for the failed project.

“We asked a great many critical questions, but there were no satisfactory answers from my point of view,” said Bernd Neuendorf, the head of the German Football Association (DFB), who is also a member of the FIFA Council.

Neuendorf was speaking after the Council met behind closed doors at the body’s Zurich headquarters, where Infantino’s FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was one of the main topics on the agenda.

Infantino has been under severe pressure since his announcement in late July that he wanted to open FIFA’s premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors.

That plan was ultimately abandoned in the face of widespread criticism, with a rebellion led by European governing body UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and CONCACAF, which runs the sport in North and Central America and the Caribbean.

“I think we had the opportunity to say what we felt, and we spoke a lot about the issues,” Debbie Hewitt, the chair of the English Football Association who is also a FIFA vice-president, told reporters, before adding that Infantino had said sorry.

“I think it is fair to say Gianni apologised at the beginning for what had happened, and he said that with some contrition, and then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what happened.”

Hewitt and Neuendorf are among the 36 members of the FIFA Council, along with Infantino.

Infantino has headed FIFA since 2016 and is running for re-election next March, despite calls for him to stand down in the wake of the FFE plan.

For the moment, no heavyweight candidate has put themselves forward to run against him.

“We were asked to submit our questions” in relation to the plan which was not put to the FIFA Council before the July announcement, Hewitt said.

“One of the disappointing things was we didn’t get answers. We didn’t get answers to anything we had specifically requested, for example getting the papers from FFE, and so we asked the question why and why not.”

– ‘Nothing has shifted’ –

Many leading European national associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino in the upcoming election because of the uproar caused by FFE and other controversies, including his relationship with US president Donald Trump.

Chief among those were Infantino’s decision to create a FIFA Peace Prize and award it to Trump at last December’s World Cup draw, and the decision to suspend a ban for United States striker Folarin Balogun following a red card during the World Cup after Trump intervened directly by phoning Infantino.

“I speak for myself as a Council member — from my position nothing has shifted,” Hewitt added. “I have no new information that makes me feel any differently to how I felt when I went in, other than we do have a president of FIFA who is apologetic about what has happened, and secondly a promise again that we will get the information that we have requested.”

FIFA was expected to put forward a plan at the Council meeting to set up a $6.35-billion development fund for the next four years.

To finance the development fund, which would allow money to be distributed to FIFA’s 211 federations as well as to the regional confederations, it would draw in part on its financial reserves after a commercially successful 2026 World Cup.

The plan would allow for the payment of $25 million to all 211 member federations.

Infantino may hope the latest plan reinforces his position ahead of the election.

The deadline for submitting candidacies is November 18.

World.title: Air routes between Iraq, Kuwait officially reopened
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Air routes between Iraq and Kuwait officially reopened on Thursday following a temporary suspension due to security developments in the region.

The flight corridors resumed operations at 2:00 p.m. Baghdad time, reversing a temporary suspension triggered by regional security developments and escalating geopolitical tensions.

The return of aviation travel is being closely monitored to guarantee civilian flight safety in a challenging regional climate.

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) oversees the new operating arrangements. Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates all participated in technical discussions and official clearances.

Aircraft must follow specific flight patterns and maintain predetermined heights. This enables regional air traffic controllers to maintain close coordination and ensure safe separation of airplanes.

The Iraqi Ministry of Transport mentioned in a statement that the system will be implemented gradually, with the participating Gulf States constantly monitoring operations to respond fast to any unexpected technical or operational issues.

The prolonged conflict in the Middle East has caused significant disruptions to aviation networks across the region.

Before the arrangement, the framework supported by the ICAO was not yet operational, but it is now helping to restore essential transit paths. However, regional aviation authorities are still closely monitoring real-time security risks.

World.title: Three dead as Istanbul sees heaviest rainfall in 80 years
World.content:
Istanbul – Istanbul was battling on Thursday to recover from flooding caused by what officials described as the heaviest rainfall in at least 80 years, as the toll rose to three dead and five missing.

The rain began lashing Turkey’s largest city in earnest on Wednesday morning and intensified throughout the day, causing chaos and flash flooding, with footage showing cars being dragged away by the fast-flowing waters.

“We are talking here about the highest level of precipitation in Istanbul since records began in 1942,” Istanbul governor Davut Gul said.

The death toll from the floods rose to three when authorities found a man’s body near a park in the Kagithane area on the European side, Gul’s office said in a statement.

The storm also claimed the life of a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted when he stepped into a puddle in the Balat area. He was rushed to hospital but medical personnel were unable to save him, officials said.

Five others were missing, officials said.

In Beykoz, on Istanbul’s Asian side, DHA news agency said another man had died after falling into a well while trying to drain the water at a school construction site.

There was no immediate official confirmation of his death.

– Dramatic images –

Istanbul municipal teams and firefighters were carrying out cleanup operations at schools, football pitches, garages and other sites on Thursday, pumping water out of flooded areas and clearing mud, an AFP photographer reported.

On Wednesday evening, the governor said schools would be shut across Istanbul until Monday, urging people to stay home “unless absolutely necessary” and advising those living in basement properties “to spend the night on safer, higher floors”.

Dramatic footage posted online late Wednesday and collated by DHA showed a line of parked cars in the northern Sariyer district being pushed into the torrent of muddy water, where they were swept away.

Another showed people being hauled from the raging waters to safety through a first-floor window, while elsewhere two people with umbrellas were seen stepping into the shovel of a large mechanical digger, which took them away.

Power and water cuts have also hit areas of the city, notably in Sariyer where shopkeepers could be seen trying to salvage their goods from the mud, an AFP journalist said.

– Floods in other cities –

Heavy rainfall in the nearby province of Sakarya caused a two-storey villa on the banks of a stream to collapse in Sapanca neighbourhood. As the house had been evacuated earlier, no one was killed or injured.

And in the neighbouring Kocaeli province, a stream overflowed in Gebze district, sweeping away a driver who was later rescued by emergency workers with ropes. In another district, Basiskele, one man was missing after being carried away by floodwaters, reports said.

Forty-three flights bound for Istanbul Airport had to be diverted Wednesday, as did three flights heading for Sabiha Gokcen on the Asian side, which temporarily suspended take-offs due to strong winds, the transport ministry said.

Turkey’s AFAD disaster agency has set up a crisis desk to manage incidents caused by the heavy rainfall, which by nightfall Wednesday had risen to 1,277 flooding incidents, 15 landslides, 47 people stranded and two roofs blown off.

The heavy rains are expected to continue over the weekend.

World.title: Italian football suffers new blow with Champions League misery
World.content:
Rome – Still reeling from the national team’s failure to qualify for a third consecutive World Cup, Italian football hit a new low this week when for the first time all four Serie A teams competing in the Champions League suffered defeats.

Roma collapsed against Real Madrid at the Stadio Olimpico, conceding three goals in the final seven minutes to lose 4–3 on Wednesday.

“We went from a moment of great euphoria to deep disappointment,” bemoaned Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini.

In their first Champions League home match since 2018, Roma let a famous win slip from their grasp despite leading 3-1.

Inter Milan, runners-up in 2023 and 2025, fell to the most surprising loss for the Italian quartet, stunned by a hat-trick from Italian-German sensation Nicolo Tresoldi in a 4-3 defeat by Club Brugge at the San Siro.

In their first-ever Champions League away match, ambitious Como took an early lead in Rotterdam only to ultimately go down 3–2 to Feyenoord.

A similar fate befell Napoli, who scored first at Villarreal before losing their footing in Spain and being beaten 3-1.

With the exception of Inter, every Serie A team led at some point, yet none managed to hold onto their advantage.

Defending narrow leads was long considered a hallmark of Italian clubs, who have won 12 European Cups and reached 30 finals between them.

Seven-time champions AC Milan and two-time winners Juventus failed to qualify for the competition this season.

– ‘Forgotten how to defend’ –

“Have they forgotten how to defend in Italian football?” asked former Milan and Real Madrid coach Fabio Capello.

With the notable exception of 15-time European champions Real Madrid, the Serie A teams’ conquerors on matchday two of the league phase were relatively modest opposition.

“Knowing how to defend has almost become something to be ashamed of,” said Napoli coach Massimiliano Allegri.

“In the Champions League, opponents make very few mistakes. You have to be patient and stay focused on the ball. All these goals conceded clearly show that much greater attention is required defensively.”

The recent European record of reigning Italian champions Inter has been disastrous, losing seven of their last eight Champions League matches.

Debate regarding the standard of the Italian top flight has reignited.

Serie A clubs spent heavily in the close season, but their financial might is still dwarfed by that of England’s Premier League giants and Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain.

Compared to the golden days of the 1990s, when Italian clubs regularly broke the world-record transfer fee, the country struggles to attract the best players from abroad.

None of the four Serie A sides who competed in the Champions League last season, Inter Milan, Napoli, Juventus and Atalanta, made it past the last 16.

That was the fourth time in six seasons Italy was not represented in the quarter-finals, after a run of having at least one team in the last eight in 15 of the previous 18 years.

The national team failed to reach the World Cup earlier this year, losing a qualifying play-off to Bosnia and Herzegovina as the four-time world champions missed out for a third straight edition.

The Azzurri have not even played a World Cup knockout match since beating France in the 2006 final on penalties.

Since the return of Roberto Mancini as coach in August, Italy have shown signs of a resurgence, holding France to a 1-1 draw at the Stade de France on October 2 and posting two Nations League wins over Turkey.

But in the Champions League, the four Italian clubs have mustered just four points — three for Cesc Fabregas’s Como and one for Roma — and are languishing towards the bottom of the standings.

Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho, however, does not share the prevailing Italian pessimism, despite leading his side to wins over his former club Inter and Roma in recent weeks.

“Both Inter and Roma are truly at a very high level,” insisted Mourinho, the last coach to win the European Cup for a Serie A team with Inter in 2010.

Inter, Roma, Napoli and Como all have winnable home Champions League matches as they look to bounce back next week, against Shakhtar Donetsk, Slovan Bratislava, Bodo/Glimt and a floundering Manchester United respectively.

World.title: US producer prices see biggest jump since 2022 in added challenge to Trump
World.content:
Washington – US wholesale inflation surged past analysts’ expectations in September, marking its biggest jump since 2022 as the war in Iran sent fuel prices rocketing, government data showed Thursday.

The latest numbers, coming a day after hotter-than-anticipated consumer inflation, underscore the challenges that President Donald Trump faces in cooling prices and winning over cost-weary voters in November’s midterm elections.

The Producer Price Index was up 6.3 percent from a year ago last month, according to the Labor Department, significantly above the 5.5 percent expected in a forecast published by MarketWatch.

The acceleration from August was also the biggest year-on-year jump since December 2022, the department said.

On a month-on-month basis, PPI rose by 1.3 percent, the widest advance since March 2022. This was similarly a sharp increase from the 0.5 percent rate in August.

Half of the September uptick for goods costs can be “traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent,” the report said.

“The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose,” it added.

A day prior, government data showed that the consumer price index — a key gauge of inflation — climbed more than expected to 3.7 percent in September.

While price increases may not lock in a second consecutive interest rate hike this month by the US central bank, the odds of higher rates to tamp down inflation have climbed.

With a second straight day of “higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer of Northlight Asset Management.

– Consumers losing steam? –

Even though US consumer spending appears to be holding up, analysts expect household behavior to reflect the growing pinch from rising costs.

A separate Commerce Department report showed Thursday that retail sales grew by 0.8 percent month-on-month in September to $745.0 billion. This was slower than the 1.3 percent pace in August.

The numbers, adjusted for seasonal changes but not inflation, likely reflect the sharp price hikes in energy costs too.

“That headline figure doesn’t tell us much about the health of the consumer, as it was almost entirely driven by a price-related jump in gasoline spending,” said Michael Pearce of Oxford Economics.

He expects consumers will lose steam heading into the year-end holiday shopping season, bogged down by higher prices.

Sales continued to rise at restaurants and bars, by 1.1 percent, likely due to spending by higher-income households, Pearce said.

Sales sharply rose at gasoline stations by 6.4 percent.

Excluding gasoline stations, however, retail sales rose a tepid 0.2 percent.

“The moderation in core retail sales, along with a sharp pullback in auto sales, suggests that real consumer spending was likely flat in September,” Nationwide chief economist Kathy Bostjancic warned in a note.

Stripping out auto sales and that at gasoline stations, overall retail sales was also just up by 0.2 percent from the prior month.

“The key to sustaining resilient spending will be the health of the labor and equity markets. If the unemployment rate remains low, meaning consumers have a job, they will continue to spend, even if more cautiously,” Bostjancic said.

World.title: Ukraine’s Zelensky defies Trump with Russian refinery strikes
World.content:
Kyiv – Ukraine will no longer abide by US President Donald Trump’s demands not to strike Russian oil refineries, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in remarks published Thursday, amid deepening tensions between the two leaders over a US-Russia diesel agreement.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.

Zelensky described the deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to prolong its four-and-a-half-year war with Ukraine, while several of Ukraine’s European allies criticised the agreement.

Addressing the criticism on Saturday, Trump claimed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries were to blame for rising diesel prices and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president”.

“The block (on attacking refineries) is out,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published on Thursday. “We’re done.”

Trump had announced on Sunday a surprise “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, which Zelensky said he knew nothing about.

And earlier this week, Ukraine reported disruptions to a critical US satellite communications system that its army uses on the battlefield.

“We need HONESTY from our partners about this war,” Zelensky wrote on social media on Thursday.

In an interview with British journalist Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s diesel-supply deal with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

He also questioned the advice that Trump was receiving, after senior Ukrainian officials in Kyiv openly accused the United States of helping Russia.

“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said.

“I think his advisors are wrong… This is not (the) right side of history.”

Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages — while Ukraine has hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war.

More recently, Trump’s war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month.

– Satellite row –

The Kremlin accused Ukraine on Thursday of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes.

Russia on Thursday reported that an oil refinery in Ryazan, south of the capital, Moscow, had been hit in a “large-scale attack”.

Kyiv “continues to launch strikes against these facilities,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

“It is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators, who are making vigorous efforts to initiate the peace process,” he added.

Much of the outrage in Ukraine this week has been over restrictions to the Starshield satellite communications system that its military relies upon to detect incoming Russian attacks and to coordinate its frontline response.

Defence officials confirmed that the United States had threatened to withdraw intelligence-sharing if Ukraine continued long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Powerful ballistic missiles struck Kyiv and the surrounding region on Tuesday and Wednesday night, before air raid sirens could sound warning people to take cover.

But tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his SpaceX company was not behind any disruption to the Starshield system.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” he said.

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.

Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.

It is separate from the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations.

Speeds were slower on Wednesday, affecting connectivity, officials said.

Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukraine and its capital in recent months, leading to mounting civilian casualties and disrupting daily life for citizens.

Moscow currently occupies around a fifth of Ukraine, including Crimea, which it annexed in 2014.

World.title: BP to help Iraq produce 450,000 barrels per day from Kirkuk oilfields
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The development plan for four oilfields in northern Iraq has entered a new phase, a move aiming to support Baghdad’s efforts to increase oil production capacity to 10 million barrels per day over the coming years.

The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Thursday that operations for four major oilfields in the northern province of Kirkuk have been transferred to a joint operating body. This initiative aims to consolidate efforts to develop oil and gas assets and to enhance the efficiency of the country’s resources.

Iraqi Minister of Oil Basim Khudair oversaw the transfer of the management of the Kirkuk oilfields from the North Oil Company and the North Gas Company to a joint operating entity. The action is part of the government’s strategy to enhance the nation’s resources and optimize the performance of its production sectors.

These developments are bolstered by British Petroleum’s (BP) participation in a project to develop four oilfields in Iraq, a move that aligns with larger attempts to broaden the base of foreign partners.

The development plan intends to achieve a significant increase in oil and gas output in the next few years.

Khudair highlighted that the transition of operations to the joint operating entity represents a significant milestone in the initiative to develop the four Kirkuk oilfields.

The plan aims to reach an oil production level of 450,000 barrels per day, in addition to 500 million standard cubic feet of gas per day, according to Khudair.

The four oilfields—Kirkuk, Bai Hassan, Jambur, and Khabbaz—are key oil assets in northern Iraq and represent an important part of the government’s plans to increase production.

In 2025, BP reached a deal with Iraq’s North Oil Company to develop oil fields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk, with investments projected to reach $25 billion.

Khudair affirmed that BP is a strategic partner in the oil and gas sectors. He noted that working together as a team will support the project’s implementation and help address any obstacles that may arise during the development phases.

The development plan for the Kirkuk fields includes training Iraqi workers, transferring expertise and technology, and implementing community-focused initiatives, such as building service facilities for the local population.

World.title: NHAI warning prompts IGI T3 parking operator to lift FASTag curbs
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The parking operator at Terminal 3 (T3) of

has removed

-based entry restrictions, bringing much-needed relief to passengers and visitors. The move came a day after Indian Highways Management Company Ltd (IHMCL), under NHAI, warned the acquiring bank associated with the parking facility of action after it emerged that the operator was using FASTag to regulate vehicle entry rather than solely for collecting parking fees.

NHAI had also temporarily suspended FASTag-based parking payments, citing the violation.

Following the intervention of the concerned authorities, restrictions on vehicles with FASTag at Terminal 3 (T3) of Delhi airport have been removed.â

With this, the earlier system has been restored. The parking operator had recently started diverting vehicles without FASTag to the multi-level parking facility, causing inconvenience to users. Vehicles entering this facility often get stuck in queues, exceeding the free parking period and forcing motorists to pay parking fees.

World.title: Government invokes ‘catastrophic event’ clause against 3 highway developers
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a first, the road transport ministry has invoked the newly introduced provision on âcatastrophicâ failure against three highway developers, signalling a tougher crackdown on contractors and concessionaires responsible for poor construction quality and major structural failures on National Highway projects.

The provision of âcatastrophic eventâ allows highway owning agencies to bar the highway developers for two years from bidding for new projects. Such highway builders also face negative ratings that will adversely impact their chances of getting future projects.

TOI has learnt that the road transport ministry recently notified a âcatastrophic eventâ in the case of widening and strengthening of a 45-km stretch of NH-727B in Uttar Pradesh after an accident during construction claimed two lives and left one with grievous injury in March.

The joint venture of VRC Constructions and R&C Infra Engineers has challenged this in the Delhi High Court, and the matter is pending before it.

In the second case, the ministry has notified this penal provision in the contract following a 2-meter settlement of pavement, failure of reinforced earth wall foundation, displacement and tilting of wall blocks and cracking of adjoining ground of a portion of the Poondiyankuppam-Sattanathapuram section of NH-45A in Tamil Nadu.

The concessionaire Poondiyankuppam-Sattanathapuram Section Pvt Ltd (of Oriental) has reportedly moved the court as well.

In the third case, a show cause notice for âcatastrophic eventâ has been issued to JV of Wagad Infra Project and Sorathia Velji Ratna for collapse of a reinforced earth wall at Shahpura on Jabalpur-Hiran river section of NH-12 in Madhya Pradesh.

A catastrophic event in a highway project refers to major failures such as the collapse of bridges, flyovers or tunnels; severe pavement or embankment damage forcing traffic closure; concrete pavement failure beyond prescribed limits; or construction equipment collapse resulting in loss of life. World.title: SC Bar Association files criminal contempt plea against Sanjay Raut, Nikhil Wagle
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) on Thursday filed a criminal contempt petition against journalist Nikhil Wagle and Uddhav Sena leader

over their disparaging remarks against Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant.

Attorney General R Venkataramani has since granted consent to initiate criminal contempt proceedings against the two under the Contempt of Courts Act.

The statements came after Chief Justice of India (CJI) declined a request last week from a delegation of opposition parties to meet him in person. The CJI said the delegation could instead file a petition before the court.

World.title: IGL rolls out AI system to check CNG cylinder safety at pumps
World.content:
NEW DELHI: To prevent CNG vehicles without a valid cylinder hydrotest certificate from refuelling, Indraprastha Gas Ltd (IGL) on Thursday launched an artificial intelligence-enabled vehicle recognition system at 10 CNG stations in the capital.

The system uses station cameras to capture vehicle registration numbers, which are processed through an AI application linked to the online Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO) portal to verify the hydrotest status of CNG cylinders. âIf a cylinderâs certification has expired or is invalid, automated alerts are immediately sent to station staff via handheld devices, LED displays and public announcement systems, enabling quick action before refuelling,â IGL said.

The AI system supplements the existing manual checks carried out by station staff. CNG cylinders must undergo hydrotesting once every three years at PESO-approved testing centres. Following a cylinder blast at a retail outlet in the capital in Aug, PESO had asked all city gas distribution companies to strictly enforce safety norms at CNG stations. The vehicle involved in the blast had additional cylinders illegally mounted on it.





IGL said the system would soon be installed at all its CNG stations across Delhi-NCR and other cities under its jurisdiction. The company operates over 300 CNG stations across 12 geographical areas covering 32 districts in Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan. CNG is also available at nearly 650 petrol pumps operated by oil marketing companies.

The pilot project was launched by PESO joint chief controller of explosives (north circle) Sanjay Kumar Singh at the Shantipath CNG station.

IGL's managing director Kumar Shanker said every vehicle entering an IGL station should undergo prescribed safety checks to protect customers, employees and the public.

IGL said it had also strengthened its safety management plan for CNG station operations, with mechanisms to monitor compliance, identify violations, take corrective action and enforce penalties where necessary.

World.title: Renewable energy expansion needs to be aligned with transmission readiness: Experts
World.content:
NEW DELHI: New Delhi: India needs to align power generation plans with the time required to build transmission infrastructure to meet future electricity demand reliably and affordably, energy sector experts said at RE: DIALOGUES 2026 in the capital.

They flagged right-of-way constraints, the availability of transformers and the distance between renewable energy generation centres and consumption hubs as key challenges for power sector planning.

The mismatch between renewable energy generation and transmission readiness has emerged as a major concern. According to ICRA data for May 2026, about 18.1 GW, or 33% of the 54.8 GW of recently commissioned renewable energy capacity, was relying on temporary grid access because permanent transmission infrastructure was incomplete.

Delays in transmission lines and substations can leave completed solar and wind projects unable to evacuate their full generation capacity.

The constraints are also leading to power curtailment. According to govt, 8,133 gigawatt hour of solar power was curtailed or restricted during April-June 2026 due to transmission constraints and to maintain grid security. The mismatch highlights the need to synchronise the commissioning of generation projects with transmission lines and substations to ensure electricity reaches consumption centres.





The discussion, organised by Policy Perspectives Foundation and Orange Circle Energy, also highlighted the need to strengthen electricity distribution infrastructure, ensure regulatory stability and direct investments towards supporting infrastructure to meet rising demand.

Bhupinder Bhalla, former secretary in the ministry of new and renewable energy, said Indiaâs energy transition must be aligned with its wider development priorities, including domestic manufacturing, technology development, investment and job creation.

He called for coordinated planning between the Centre and states to address infrastructure and regulatory challenges.

Nikesh Sinha, founder of Orange Circle Energy, said India needs to look beyond its ability to generate electricity and assess how much power it will need, where demand will emerge and how reliably it can be delivered.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

âTransmission infrastructure takes time to build, and generation and consumption centres are not always in the same locations.

Anticipating these requirements and aligning transmission planning with generation, while also considering decentralised solutions, will be critical to meeting Indiaâs future electricity needs,â Sinha said.

The experts also discussed the need to channel existing public resources towards priorities such as renewable energy and disaster resilience. Safi Ahsan Rizvi, former adviser to the National Disaster Management Authority and associated with the Policy Perspectives Foundation, said better allocation of existing resources could help unlock investment.

World.title: Is Dhanush ready to make his political debut? Fan club's new avatar sparks buzz
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Actor

's official fan club has been restructured as the 'Dhanush Narpani Iyakkam' (Dhanush Welfare Movement), fuelling speculation about a possible political debut.

The organisation unveiled a new flag and logo and announced plans to build a local network across five assembly constituencies in Coimbatore district.

The restructuring was approved at an executive meeting in Coimbatore on Wednesday, news agency PTI reported. The new red-and-white flag features a large red star, with Dhanush's image at the centre.

The move has drawn comparisons with actor

, whose fan network evolved into a grassroots organisation before he launched the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK).

TVK went on to emerge as the single-largest party in the 2026 Tamil Nadu assembly elections, winning 108 of 234 seats and forming the government with allies.

Dhanush, however, has not announced any plans to enter politics.

The emphasis on constituency-level organisation is a key aspect of the restructuring. The movement plans to establish local welfare units and enroll members across five assembly constituencies in Coimbatore district.





Such networks can help coordinate community activities and build a sustained local presence. However, there is no confirmation that the organisation is preparing for electoral campaigning.

Coimbatore could be a significant testing ground for a new political force. In the 2026 assembly elections, TVK won six of the district's 10 seats.

From MGR to Vijay: The stars in politics

Tamil Nadu has a long history of film stars translating screen popularity into political influence.

MG Ramachandran, popularly known as MGR, founded the AIADMK in 1972 after his association with the DMK and became chief minister in 1977. His popularity helped build a political movement, backed by an organisational network and a distinct political identity.

J Jayalalithaa, who followed a similar path from cinema to politics, also went on to become chief minister.

Vijay is the latest major example. He made a strong electoral debut by clinching the CM chair in the first attempt itself.

What has Dhanush said

The latest restructuring follows Dhanush's appeal to supporters to move beyond film celebrations and focus on community welfare.

At a blood donation camp organised by his fan clubs in Chennai in July, the actor had urged them to use their collective strength to understand local needs and help families facing difficulties.

Reports have also circulated about a possible political outfit named Tamilaga Ezhuchi Kazhagam, but formal registration with the Election Commission has not been confirmed.

In September, when asked about a possible political debut after receiving his National Film Awards, Dhanush laughed off the question.

So, is a political debut on the cards?

The new name, flag, logo and plans for local welfare units give Dhanush's fan association a more structured identity. But these steps do not, by themselves, establish that he is preparing to contest elections.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

A formal political announcement, a declared agenda or confirmation of party formation would provide clearer indications of his intentions.

None has emerged so far.

For now, the Dhanush Narpani Iyakkam could remain a welfare organisation or evolve into something larger. The political speculation is growing, but the actor has yet to signal that he is ready to make the leap from cinema to electoral politics.

World.title: Families await return of 3 Indians killed in Germany fire; Kerala CM assures help with repatriation

Three families in Kerala are awaiting the return of the mortal remains of their loved ones who died in a fire at a residential building in Bochum, Germany, as public representatives seek the Centreâs intervention to expedite the repatriation process.

In a post on X, Satheesan expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families. He said the state government, through NORKA Roots, would bear all expenses related to repatriating the bodies.





Public representatives, including MPs and MLAs, have also approached the MEA, seeking its intervention to speed up the necessary procedures.

Families await return of mortal remains

Lok Sabha MP Benny Behanan visited Sivin Johnyâs home in Kalady on Thursday and met his parents and other relatives. In a Facebook post, he expressed grief over the deaths and said he was in touch with the German Embassy and contacts in Germany to help bring the mortal remains back.

Behanan also urged the Centre and the Kerala government to expedite the formalities.

Johny had travelled to Germany last month in search of employment and was expected to start a job this week, a relative told reporters. His brother, Salvin, is pursuing nursing studies in Germany.

World.title: T.N. govt. to sell parboiled rice at ₹30 per kg through 260 Amudham, cooperative stores: Minister
World.content:
To ease the impact of food inflation and stabilise the prices of essential commodities, the Tamil Nadu government has decided to sell parboiled rice at ₹30 per kg through 211 cooperative stores and 49 retail outlets of Amudham departmental stores run by the Tamil Nadu Civil Supplies Corporation across the State, Minister for Food and Civil Supplies P. Venkataramanan said on Thursday.

Speaking to reporters at the Secretariat in Chennai, Mr. Venkataramanan said the State government has been closely monitoring the prices of essential commodities, such as rice, pulses and cooking oil. He said the increase in the retail price of rice in Tamil Nadu was due to a shortage in the supply of rice from neighbouring Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Further, a section of traders in the State was selling rice at higher prices due to the demand, he said.

He said rice was being sold at an average price of ₹75 to ₹85 per kg in the open market in the State. At present, parboiled rice was being sold at ₹60 per kg and raw rice at ₹46 per kg through Amudham supermarkets and cooperative stores. The State government had now decided to sell parboiled rice at ₹30 per kg and tur dal at ₹130 per kg.

He said 25,000 tonnes of rice would be released immediately for this purpose and a total of one lakh tonnes of rice would be sold at the revised prices. He said this arrangement was in addition to the routine supply of essential commodities through public distribution system outlets. The Minister said demand and prices would be assessed and further measures taken accordingly.

World.title: Jammu and Kashmir High Court bars use of shikara motorboats, jet skis on Dal lake in Srinagar
World.content:
The Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) High Court on Thursday (October 15, 2026) barred the use of motorboats, both shikara motorboats and fuel-driven jet skis, on Dal Lake, and directed the government to explore the possibility of using solar-powered e-engines.

“Taking a comprehensive view of the submissions made, it is directed that the authorities shall ensure that no motorboat, whether it be a shikara motorboat or Jet Ski which operates by fuel, is operated in the Dal Lake until further orders,” held J&K Chief Justice Dr. Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Judge Rajesh Sekhri.

The Division Bench directed the J&K Lake Conservation and Management Authority (J&K LCMA), the Tourism Department, and the J&K Police to implement the order.

“We direct that in case any motorised boat is allowed to ply or is reported to ply, it shall be held as contempt of today’s order of this court, and therefore the officers concerned shall take a strict view by restricting and prohibiting such operations,” held Justice Bhati and Justice Sekhri.

However, the court exempted the boats used by the administration and the authorities for the purpose of emergency services, law and order and disaster management.

“The court is not hesitant to observe that solar boats and electric boats could be a solution for balancing the equities between tourism and the sustenance of lakes,” the judges observed.

The court further held: “On the limited propositions that have been addressed, this court is convinced that in modern times, when lake systems have become a growing concern for civilisation, steps are being taken to exclude activities which would cause pollution, and also it would be important that whatever policy is framed is more reasonable while balancing tourism activities, pollution, as well as the uniformity between the players involved”.

Pleading the case before the court, B.A. Bashir, Senior Counsel, and Falak Bashir, counsel, argued for criteria that are uniform, transparent, and environmental. “Jet Skis, motorboats, or anything motorable which is in the lake is likely to damage the ecosystem of the lake and, therefore, a regulated and protective approach toward the issue needs to be adopted in a uniform manner,” Mr. Bashir and Ms. Falak told the court.

Dal Lake is the central attraction of tourism in Kashmir. However, a report by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) suggested that the lake has witnessed a 10.15% shrinkage in open water area, “dropping from 15.40 square kilometres in 2007 to 12.91 square kilometres in 2020”. The lake is also marred by encroachments and growing construction in its close vicinity.

World.title: JNU harassment row: Women BJP MPs meet LS Speaker, demand action against Akoijam
World.content:
A delegation of the BJP’s women MPs met Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday (October 15, 2026) and demanded action against Congress MP and former JNU professor Angomcha Bimol Akoijam.

Mr. Akoijam was recently dismissed from service by the JNU administration following an internal inquiry into sexual harassment charges.

BJP MP D. Purandeswari told reporters that the delegation sought the Speaker’s intervention for appropriate action. The MPs urged the Speaker to refer the matter to the Parliament Ethics Committee. She said the Speaker had assured the delegation that he would look into the issue.

PTI adds:

"We told the Speaker that the JNU internal committee has found the Congress MP [Akoijam] guilty. We urged the Speaker to consider referring the matter to the Parliament Ethics Committee and also consider whether he should continue as a member of the Lok Sabha," Ms. Purandeswari told reporters in the Parliament House Complex.

"The Speaker gave an assurance that he will certainly look into the matter and also consider if it should be referred to the Ethics Committee," she added.

Mr. Akoijam, a Congress MP from Inner Manipur and a professor at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems under JNU's School of Social Sciences, was dismissed with immediate effect on October 9 following an inquiry into the harassment allegations against him.

He has, however, denied the charges.

At least 11 female students complained about Mr. Akoijam in May this year. The complainants alleged that the professor invited students to his campus residence on the pretext of meetings or gatherings and attempted to harass them sexually. Some students alleged that he also made obscene and inappropriate remarks in class.

Based on a complaint lodged by JNU's chief security officer, an FIR was registered against Mr. Akoijam on Sunday (October 11, 2026) on charges of sexual harassment and insulting the modesty of a woman.

World.title: Land shortage cripples Agriculture Ministry’s weather network rollout
World.content:
An ambitious public-private partnership project by an Agriculture Ministry body to install automatic rain gauges and automatic weather stations in States is proceeding at a crawl, with completion rates in the single digits and at least a year behind deadline. Over 96% of planned sensors are yet to be installed.

The reason, companies tasked with the implementation say, is a paucity of land to install these weather stations and an alleged “retrospective” insistence by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) that these sensors be set up on the ground rather than on rooftops.

The Weather Information Network and Data System (WINDS) is a programme to set up a nationwide network of weather sensors to supply hyper-local weather data. This is mainly to aid in computing insurance estimates and payouts under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY). It is run by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, and executed through the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC).

Over 50,000 sensors planned

Under the WINDS network, the States, through their implementing private partners, are required to set up the sensor network. The Hindu could confirm that three companies — Skymet Weather Services; Ingen Technologies Private Limited, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Weather Risk Management Services; and Azista Industries — were collectively asked to instal 1,197 automatic weather stations (AWSs) and 49,313 automatic rain gauges (ARGs), or about 50,500 sensors in all.

An ARG measures rainfall only, though about 10% of ARGs at the gram panchayat level also carry a temperature sensor. An AWS measures rainfall along with air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction. Data from these sensors flow into data centres run by government agencies, to prepare hourly, daily, and fortnightly forecasts.

Majority of proposed sites rejected

According to documents viewed by The Hindu, Uttar Pradesh was to have installed 27,487 ARGs — over half the ARG target — followed by Uttarakhand (7,983), Odisha (7,286), Assam (2,140), and Himachal Pradesh (about 3,550).

For AWSs, Odisha’s target was the largest at 434, ahead of Assam (196), U.P. (157), and Kerala (148). According to a status update on September 9 — the latest that The Hindu was able to confirm — the network has delivered 113 AWSs (9.4% of target) and 1,730 ARGs (4%), leaving a shortfall of about 48,700 (96%).

The bottleneck is mostly site selection rather than hardware, the documents reveal. Of the 27,644 sites in U.P., 16,478 were rejected. In Odisha, 5,666 of 7,720 sites were rejected, while 524 of 946 sites were rejected in Kerala. The documents also flag hundreds of “duplicate sites” that were approved at the panchayat and block level but need re-checking, sites pending clearances, and those which the States have yet to share with the implementing partners.

Retrospective changes

A representative of one of the private partner companies, who asked not to be named, told The Hindu that the delays stem from a shortage of suitable land and from the requirement that rain gauges be placed on the ground rather than on rooftops. He blamed changes made to the WINDS guidelines “retrospectively.”

The manual published on September 1, 2023 allowed an ARG to be placed on the roof of a single-storey building where siting requirements could not be met or in flood-prone areas, he claimed, adding that the IMD had approved this as a member of the WINDS Committee. About two and a half years later, and after six States had already issued tenders or work orders, the Agriculture Department amended the manual on the IMD’s advice on December 3, 2025, to retroactively limit rooftop ARGs to just 10% to 15% of the total, he said.

‘Height affects weather data’

IMD officials contend that the requirement that ARGs and AWSs be located on the ground is “essential” to ensure that the data collected is accurate.

“The underlying principle – and this is a requirement of the World Meteorological Organisation whose guidelines we adhere to – is that sensors must be on the ground and only in exceptional situations be situated on rooftops. Height significantly affects weather data,” S. Hosalikar, a former senior meteorologist with the IMD and a member of the 2023 committee, told The Hindu.

The 2023 document says: “ARGs shall be located on a level piece of ground, covered with short grass or natural earth,” ideally 4x3 metres in size. “If suitable siting requirements are not met or in case of flood prone areas,” the ARG can go on “the rooftop of the one-story building… rooftop units need a stable foundation and a tamper-proof setup,” adds the document, which was perused by The Hindu.

Cap on rooftop sensors

The manual sets no numerical cap on rooftop units. This only appears in the 2025 amendment which specifies a 10% cap. It also requires that rooftop installations be allowed only if States issue a justification note saying there is no suitable ground space. In flood- or landslide-prone regions, the ceiling is 15%, with prior State recommendation and approval sent to the WINDS Committee.

“Measuring rainfall from the top of the building and from the ground makes a significant difference as some part of falling rain evaporates. Secondly, a consistent network of ground-based sensors is necessary to ensure standardised data, which is difficult to achieve if sensors are on rooftops (with variable heights). India lives in its villages and it should not be that challenging to get small plots of land,” IMD director general M. Mohapatra told The Hindu. He underlined that the IMD was only a technical partner for the project and was not administering it.

The Hindu reached out to Soumya Bandopadhyay, director of the MNCFC, the nodal agency in charge of the project, seeking a comment but did not get any response till the time of going to press.

World.title: Haryana khap plans Oct. 22 sit-in over news anchor’s arrest
World.content:
The Binaian khap in Haryana’s Jind has announced an indefinite sit-in from October 22 to demand the release of news anchor Sudesh Nain, arrested along with four others in a case involving an alleged fake sting operation and blackmail.

The news channel had run a story alleging rise in drug abuse in Chief Minister Nayab Saini’s Assembly constituency Ladwa.

Announcing the decision at a meeting in Jind on Thursday, khap president Raghubir Nain said the agitation would be led by the khap leadership, with participation from khaps across North India, farmers’ organisations, employees’ unions and other workers’ organisations. He said that Ms. Sudesh, a resident of a local village, was their “own daughter”.

Mr. Raghubir said the khap had given the government an ultimatum on October 12 to release Ms. Sudesh by October 14 and cancel the FIR registered against her. However, he alleged that the government has ignored the demand and public sentiment.

Mr. Raghubir also accused the government of attempting to “silence the press”. He said Ms. Sudesh had conducted a sting operation to expose the drug menace and should have been encouraged rather than arrested. “The government says it will eradicate drugs, but when our daughter conducts a sting operation to expose the menace, she is arrested,” he said, alleging that the action was contrary to the government’s stated commitment to tackle drug abuse.

In a press statement following the arrest on October 10, the Kurukshetra police had said that five office-bearers of the news channel were arrested in connection with the alleged broadcast of a six-month-old video, recorded in relation to a personal matter between two individuals, as “fake live sting operation”. Superintendent of Police Chander Mohan said the complainant alleged that the national news channel had presented his old personal video, dated April 16, as a “fake live sting operation” and subsequently blackmailed him.

Questioning the arrests, Congress’ Rohtak MP Deepender Hooda, had in a tweet, said the journalists were “arrested merely because they revealed the truth about the rising drug menace in Ladwa, the CM’s constituency.

World.title: Delhi HC questions delay in setting up open, semi-open prisons
World.content:
The Delhi High Court on Thursday questioned the jail authorities over delays in implementing the Supreme Court’s directions to provide open and semi-open prison facilities in the Capital.

Open and semi-open prisons are less restrictive correctional facilities available to eligible inmates.
