World.title: ‘No person is walang kwenta’: Groups, friends defend Josh Aquino amid podcast controversy
World.content:
The NBI is set to probe the hosts of the 'Machong Chismisan' podcast following public backlash over offensive remarks mocking Josh Aquino

MANILA, Philippines – Podcasts have given ordinary people a platform to speak their minds. Some give us a chance at self-reflection, while others offer comedic relief.

But what happens when the jokes being thrown around in the latter begin to draw more offense than laughter?

In a Machong Chismisan podcast episode published on October 5, Kris Aquino’s son Josh became the subject of mockery as the show’s host, Tito P, referred to him as “walang kwenta (useless).”

While the controversial episode has already been taken down, the Machong Chismisan podcast was not spared from public scrutiny, with groups and newsmakers attesting that the hosts had crossed the line with their remarks.

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag also confirmed to Boy Abunda in a text message on Thursday, October 15, that he has ordered the NBI’s cybercrime division and special action unit to probe the podcast’s hosts and file the necessary complaints.

The Machong Chismisan podcast’s contract has also been terminated by The Pod Network “effective immediately.”

Family friends come to Josh’s defense

Figures who know Josh personally were quick to come to his defense — with Abunda expressing outrage over the incident on an episode of Fast Talk With Boy Abunda. The talk show host said he was puzzled that a group of men who appeared to be intelligent and educated could make such cruel remarks about another young man with a disability.

Abunda recalled that when Josh’s mother, Kris Aquino, was actively seeking treatment in the US, it was his job to gather everyone each morning for a prayer.

“Hindi po walang silbi si Josh. Mali po ang inyong ginawa. Labag sa batas ng Diyos at sa batas ng tao ang inyong ginawa. Napakasakit. Napakasakit, hindi lamang para sa pamilya, pero para sa lahat ng mga pamilya, ng mga bata, ng mga magulang na may kapansanan, na may disability ang kanilang mga anak,” Abunda emphasized.

(Josh is not useless. What you did was wrong. What you did is against the teachings of God and the law. It hurts. It hurts, not just for Josh’s family, but for all the families, children, and parents of those with disabilities.)

Abunda recommended that Kris press charges against the podcast — citing RA 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, which penalizes those who publicly ridicule persons with disabilities.

“Labag sa batas ang ginawa ng mga podcasters na ito. Congratulations, you got the attention of everybody, at hindi dito nagtatapos. Dapat ito’y pag-aralan, dapat tayo’y magreact. Dapat pag-usapan, para maenlighten ang maraming tao. I am sorry for what happened to Josh,” Abunda added.

(What these podcasters did is against the law. Congratulations, you got the attention of everybody, and it doesn’t end here. This should be studied, and we should react. It should be talked about, so we can enlighten even more people. I am sorry for what happened to Josh.)

Meanwhile, Mark Leviste, who was previously in a relationship with Kris, stepped in to publicly defend Josh.

“I love him like my own son, and my children love him like their own older brother. He is one of the kindest, sweetest, most prayerful, and loving people you will ever meet. Sinuman ang tunay na nakakakilala sa kanya ay mauunawaan kung bakit labis na nakasasakit sa aming mga nagmamahal sa kanya ang mga binitiwang salita tungkol sa kanya,”

(Those who truly know Josh understand why it hurts to hear these words be thrown against him.)

Leviste asked that the people behind Machong Chismisan take full responsibility for what transpired, personally apologize to Josh and his family, and ensure that the incident does not happen again.

“You may call yourselves comedians or podcasters, but freedom of expression does not exempt you from accountability! There’s a difference between making people laugh and turning someone into a laughingstock. When your foolish words and slapstick humor demean someone, especially because of his disability, you cross a line that should never be crossed!” Leviste wrote.

Designer Michael Leyva, a longtime friend of Kris, also came to Josh’s defense — personally vouching for Josh’s kindness.

“Making Kuya Josh the subject of your so-called ‘Machong Chismisan’ podcast and mocking his disability is not something that I or any of us should simply let slide,” he said in an Instagram story.

‘Blatant discrimination’

Even the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) had to issue a warning for content creators to be careful about making derogatory statements towards individuals with mental disabilities not just as an act of compassion, but to uphold their human rights.

And for the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA), it no longer becomes comedy when one’s dignity is involved, but instead, it is “blatant discrimination.”

“Creators bear a responsibility to foster respectful and inclusive digital spaces, ensuring that all content is approached with sensitivity and mindfulness. NCDA also calls on the public and social media users to refrain from sharing, reposting, and engaging with any material that demeans, mocks, or exploits vulnerable individuals,” the NCDA wrote.

In the same vein, the Council for the Welfare of Children reminded content creators and media practitioners of the influence they hold over shaping public opinion.

The Down Syndrome Association of the Philippines encouraged Machong Chismisan’s hosts — and in effect, all content creators — to engage with individuals with autism, Down syndrome, and other disabilities for them to hear their stories and use their platforms “to build understanding rather than ridicule.”

“No person is walang kwenta (useless). Every person with autism, Down syndrome, or any disability has inherent dignity and worth. Using their condition as a punchline is not comedy. It is cruelty that hurts thousands of Filipino families who live this reality every day,” the group wrote in its statement.

The Autism Society of the Philippines also advised against patronizing content creators and podcasts “not capable of basic respect.”

“Freedom of expression must never come at the expense of the rights and humanity of persons with disabilities,” the group said.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Raul Daza, longtime congressman of Northern Samar, dies
World.content:
Daza had been president of the Liberal Party and was, at the peak of his political career, the second-in-command in the House of Representatives

MANILA, Philippines – Statesman Raul Daza, the longtime legislator from Northern Samar, has passed away, his family announced on Thursday, October 15.

“He peacefully passed away at 91 years old. He was a devoted husband, loving father, grandfather, great-grandfather, son, brother, colleague, mentor and friend,” read the statement of his widow Teresita Ruiz and their family.

“He leaves a legacy of integrity, courage, humility, empathy and commitment to democracy. He was a man who genuinely put himself in the shoes of others,” it added.

Daza served seven non-consecutive terms in the House of Representatives between 1969 and 2019, and was, at the peak of his political career, speaker pro tempore from 1992 to 1998. He was also governor of Northern Samar from 2001 to 2010.

He served as deputy minister of the Presidential Commission on Good Government, the agency tasked with going after the Marcos family’s ill-gotten wealth.

“A steadfast defender of democracy, justice, and the rule of law, he stood firm in his convictions through the Martial Law years and political exile. He was a member of the Liberal Party (LP) for 61 years, beginning in 1965, and served as its president from 1994 to 1998,” the family’s statement reads.

“Despite the many colors of politics, he firmly believed that we have only one flag and we have only one country,” it added.

Daza was a certified public accountant and a lawyer who graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law. His family said he placed 11th in the Bar exam.

After retiring from politics in 2019, he was succeeded in Congress by his son, Paul, and later his grandson, Niko.

World.title: LIVESTREAM: Maria Ressa, WNYC’s Brian Lehrer discuss democracy in the age of AI
World.content:
RESSA. Nobel Peace Prize 2021 laureate and Rappler CEO at the Social Good Summit 2025, in Pasay City on November 16, 2025.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC's Brian Lehrer for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa will join WNYC host Brian Lehrer for a conversation on democracy in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) on Thursday, October 15, in New York (Friday, October 16, Philippine time).

The event, “Democracy Dialogues,” is co-presented by New York Public Radio (NYPR) and Rappler and will take place at The Greene Space in Lower Manhattan.

Lehrer, host of the Peabody Award-winning The Brian Lehrer Show, and Ressa will discuss the challenges of understanding, defending, and rebuilding democracy at a time when AI is rapidly transforming how people access information and engage with the world.

“Democracy Dialogues” is NYPR’s ongoing live event series examining the state of democracy and the roles of journalism, free expression, and an informed public in sustaining democratic institutions.

The conversation comes as Ressa releases her new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, on October 13.

The event will also be livestreamed on WNYC’s website, C-SPAN, and on Rappler’s YouTube channel. Portions of the conversation will air on The Brian Lehrer Show on Friday, October 16, at 10 am Eastern Time.

Watch the livestream starting at 7 am on Friday, October 16 (Philippine time), or 7 pm on Thursday, October 15 (US Eastern Time). – Rappler.com

World.title: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses
World.content:
Businesses must brace for further risks from transport fares, electricity, wages, El Niño, and a weak peso

September’s 7.2% inflation rate was bad enough on its own. For businesses, the bigger concern is that price pressures could spread beyond the food and fuel shocks that first pushed inflation higher.

Seasonally adjusted inflation accelerated to 1.1% month on month in September from 0.5% in August. In what National Statistician Dennis Mapa described as a relatively “rare” broad increase, 11 of 13 major commodity groups posted faster inflation, while 16 of 18 regions saw inflation pick up. Core inflation also climbed to 4.7%, its highest in three years.

Nerve spoke with three economists to understand whether this is turning into a more persistent inflation problem and what businesses should prepare for heading into 2027. None sees a prolonged second wave as inevitable, but the risk is becoming harder to dismiss.

The September uptick comes as several price increases have yet to fully work their way through the economy. Among them:

Recent jeepney, bus, and taxi fare hikes were barely captured by the Philippine Statistics Authority in September and should show up more clearly in October. Passenger transport by road carries a 3.5% weight in the inflation basket.

Meralco has won approval to raise its average distribution rate from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, its first increase after a rate review in 15 years. Once implemented in November, that increases energy costs for households and businesses.

The P60 minimum wage increase in Metro Manila took effect only on September 26, which means possible cost pass-through could be reflected in later months.

El Niño could add another supply shock into early 2027, with economists warning that a strong drought could cut rice and other food production across the Philippines and the region while also putting pressure on power supply and electricity costs.

The weakness of the Philippine peso is another source of inflation, as it raises the peso cost of imported fuel, food, raw materials, and equipment and could keep feeding into domestic prices.

Mapa pointed to energy, transport, and housing rents as some of the harder pressures to unwind. Electricity inflation was already 14.6% in September, while rents rose 4% and carry more than a 12% weight in the consumer price basket.

READ: [READOUT] What Philippine borrowing tells businesses ahead of 2027

SM Investments Corporation group economist Robert Dan Roces expects inflation to remain a concern, but said much will depend on food and energy prices over the coming months.

“Some businesses may feel the pressure, but demand should remain relatively resilient,” he told Nerve.

RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort told Nerve that inflation may pick up further in the coming months “in view of second-round inflation effects or higher prices of other affected goods and services, or pass-through effects, especially due to higher minimum wages.”

Meanwhile, Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said a second, stickier wave becomes more plausible if higher food, fuel, electricity, and transport costs begin feeding into other prices and keep inflation expectations elevated.

Agriculture, transport, food businesses, and energy-intensive manufacturing face the most direct exposure, while smaller firms have less room to absorb higher costs. Manufacturing may be especially vulnerable given that the sector was already weakening before the latest inflation pressures intensified, with employment falling to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July and 3.46 million in June.

“Small businesses, meanwhile, have less room to absorb higher costs, and retailers could suffer as households spend more on necessities and cut back elsewhere,” Punongbayan told Rappler.

Even as the “ber” months go by, retailers may need to temper expectations for the usual consumption boost. Consider that inflation among the bottom 30% of households reached 9% in September, compared with 7.2% nationally, leaving lower-income consumers with even less room for discretionary spending.

Forecasts vary considerably on how quickly inflation will ease in 2027, with Ricafort taking the most pessimistic view while institutional forecasts generally cluster between 4% and 5.4%.

High inflation also creates a second problem for businesses through interest rates. Here’s how economists think the BSP will react:

Roces expects the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to be more cautious in putting too much additional pressure on growth.

Ricafort is more hawkish, seeing scope for further tightening while inflation remains far above the 2% to 4% target. He also noted that the BSP could partly match future US Federal Reserve hikes to manage interest rate differentials and help stabilize the peso.

Punongbayan said further hikes are possible and easing could be pushed into 2027 depending on how core inflation and expectations go, though higher key policy rates risk further straining borrowing, investment, and growth without fixing supply-side pressures.

The next BSP policy decision is scheduled for October 22, with another Monetary Board meeting set for December 17.

We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.
