World.title: State government corporation axes Brisbane sign’s Indigenous makeover
World.content:
A state government-backed corporation reneged on approval to decorate the tourism hotspot Brisbane sign in Aboriginal artwork during an Indigenous arts festival, the ABC can reveal.

The sign overlooks the city's heart and river, and is described by South Bank Corporation as an "iconic photo stop". Even tennis legend Roger Federer was filmed there.

But the quiet axing of the proposed temporary artwork, despite it having been earlier budgeted and approved by government-backed entities including South Bank, has amplified perceptions that Indigenous voices in state activities are being erased.

South Bank brushed aside questions about culture wars, saying the issue arose because a newly appointed board had to reconsider approving the decoration but lacked time to do so. It would not answer questions including how much time was needed.

A mock-up of the Brisbane sign with artwork that would have been featured during the Clancestry event. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

This year's Clancestry festival took place over 10 days from July 30, involving storytelling, dance, markets and music. Country singer Troy Cassar-Daley was a headline act.

The festival has been run by the Queensland Performing Arts Centre, based at South Bank next to the Brisbane sign, since 2013.

Documents exclusively obtained by the ABC under right to information laws detail this year's plans to temporarily redecorate — or "reskin" — the Brisbane sign for the festival.

It would have been clad in traditional patterns and colours from aqua to brown, designed by Nunukul artist Casey Coolwell-Fisher of North Stradbroke Island. Her work has been used by the festival since 2022.

The sign has proven to be a popular spot for tourists. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The $15,170 cost was "within a festival budget enabled by generous corporate sponsorship of event partners Energy Queensland", a QPAC employee wrote in an email to an arts department bureaucrat in April this year.

"South Bank Corporation (and all three signatories to the deed controlling the Brisbane sign) approved the re-skinning of the Brisbane sign with the Clancestry artwork for the duration of the festival."

The correspondence indicates acute sensitivity at the time about the redecoration.

The Brisbane Sign is located at South Bank in front of the river. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

QPAC was responding to "urgent" queries from the arts department. Those answers were passed on to executive-department levels and even an adviser to Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek.

One departmental bureaucrat wrote: "Can it be publicly said that Energex paid for the sign?"

The department did not answer ABC queries about the urgency, saying correspondence was within "routine responsibilities".

On July 3, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie announced a renewal of South Bank's board, including several appointees with links to Conservative politics.

They included former LNP federal member for Brisbane Trevor Evans and incoming chairwoman Karen Howard, a businesswoman who stood as a NSW Liberal candidate in the 2016 federal election.

Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Within five days, the redecoration approval for Clancestry was in tatters.

Confidential briefing papers say QPAC chief executive Rachel Healy received an email from Julia Scodellaro, her South Bank counterpart, "advising that, due to recent changes to South Bank Corporation's board membership, South Bank Corporation was 'no longer able to provide approval'" for the sign.

South Bank told the ABC the Brisbane sign was a "major asset and the request to reskin it therefore also required consideration by the newly constituted board, which it was unable to do in time for Clancestry".

"South Bank Corporation is committed to supporting all events in the precinct, including Clancestry which was promoted across a range of our channels, including digital and physical displays as well as online."

But Jackie Huggins, a director of partnerships and innovation for Indigenous engagement at the University of Queensland, described the explanation about axing the sign proposal as inadequate.

Jackie Huggins has questioned the motives behind the decision to axe the changes (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Dr Huggins, who is also the ABC's Elder-in-residence and who has served as a director on state-backed entities, said boards "can be very biased in terms of how they serve the government".

"I think this is a broader agenda for the powers that be to simply and deliberately attempt … to erase our culture and our presence," she said.

Dr Huggins pointed to the new state government's cancellation of a Truth Telling and Healing inquiry.

Indigenous figures including Joshua Creamer, a barrister who had chaired that inquiry, have also raised claims of what is called "Project Invisibility", including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders being removed from boards, and programs being defunded.

But a Crisafulli state government spokesman said there was "no such thing as Project Invisibility", that suggesting otherwise was offensive, and that the government was listening to local elected Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander councils to deliver "tangible outcomes".

Decisions about assets, which include the Brisbane sign, were a matter for South Bank, he said.

The Brisbane sign was originally created in 2014 as a temporary landmark for the G20 summit, when world leaders including then-US president Barack Obama and Russia's Vladimir Putin came to the city.

It has since then been refurbished multiple times.

Dr Huggins said of the now-axed Clancestry redecoration: "The design was fabulous … it's very symbolic."

World.title: Weekend storms and showers forecast for parts of Queensland
World.content:
Severe storm activity that has lashed parts of outback and central Queensland this week is set to continue into the weekend as the state's storm season begins.

A high-pressure system in the Tasman Sea will also cause isolated showers in the state's south-east to linger well into next week.

Bureau of Meteorology community information officer Daniel Hayes said an upper-level trough had moved east from Alice Springs, bringing storm activity into western Queensland.

He said the system delivered 30-50 millimetres to the Highlands and Central Coalfields on Thursday, before dumping 120 millimetres in three hours in Middlemount.

SES central region director Andrew Wyatt said that while there were no call-outs, it was a good reminder for the community to be prepared heading into the summer months.

"That rain is very welcome; it's been very dry here for months, as we know," Mr Wyatt said.

" We just need to be mindful that some of these storms that come through might have some very heavy localised rain in them. "

The trough also broke an October wind-speed record in Longreach, where gusts of 111 kilometres per hour were recorded on Wednesday night.

An October wind speed record was broken in the outback town of Longreach. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

Mr Hayes expected the pattern would continue today and into the weekend, with further storms predicted for the central and southern Queensland interior and potentially extending up into the Gulf Country.

"It's likely we'll have showers being more widespread, more likely to see thunderstorms through those areas and hence we'll have probably more widespread falls of rainfall in that 5, 10, 15, 20mm range," Mr Hayes said.

Isolated showers forecast for south-east

The south-east looks set to escape most of the storm activity, with smaller isolated coastal showers expected for the weekend in parts of Brisbane and the Gold Coast.

Mr Hayes said a high-pressure system in the Tasman Sea may see the south-east's isolated showers continue into next week.

"That high does linger in the Tasman Sea for quite a lengthy period into next week and it's not really until the end of next week that it starts to move away, and we see that influence along the coast start to weaken," he said.

Rainy conditions hung over much of central Queensland, including Rockhampton. (ABC: Vanessa Jarrett)

He said the cloudy conditions would cause temperatures to cool across much of the state.

"Persistent cloud and shower activity and storms across large parts of the state will keep temperatures from warming up too much over the next few days."

He said further severe thunderstorm warnings could be issued for the Central Highlands if conditions persisted into this afternoon.

World.title: Council opposes $209m Hindu temple in outer Melbourne green zone
World.content:
A proposed $209 million Hindu temple in outer Melbourne could become the largest of its kind in Australia, bringing in visitors from around the country and generating millions of dollars in economic activity every year.

But the proposal has triggered concerns that the 64-metre tall building could overwhelm local infrastructure and threaten wildlife in the green-wedge zone the site sits in.

Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha Australia Ltd (BAPS) has lodged the application for a Mahā-Mandir place of worship on the Western Port Highway, in Cranbourne South on Melbourne's south-eastern fringe.

Thousands of new residents are added to Melbourne's south-east suburban fringe each year. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

According to the application's economic benefits assessment, the Mahā-Mandir would create 143 ongoing jobs and add more than $12 million a year to the Victorian economy.

It is expected to attract up to 1,200 visitors on a typical weekday, and three times that for special events up to nine times a year.

"With an intricate, high-craftsmanship design, the project is also expected to become a pilgrimage tourist attraction, driving visitation and associated economic benefits," said the report.

It is the second proposal for a place of worship in the green-wedge zone in recent months, exemplifying a pressing issue for fast-growing communities in outer suburban areas with limited land set aside for places of worship.

The Bethel New Life Christian Fellowship had applied to build the two-storey church in a green wedge in Cranbourne South but the proposal was voted down by the City of Casey.

Temple to create 'spiritual home'

Because of its projected economic value, the Hindu temple proposal was lodged under the state government's Development Facilitation Program which means the decision will be made by the planning minister and bypass local council.

City of Casey mayor Michelle Crowther said the council had lodged an objection to the application following an assessment of planning rules.

"The key concerns were really about planning issues," she said.

"Our traffic and road network, the removal of vegetation, impacts on local residents including traffic, noise, lighting and visual amenity and also the inconsistency with the purpose and planning objectives of the Western Port Green Wedge."

Michelle Crowther says the Casey council has objected to the application. (Supplied)

Cr Crowther said the council had asked the state government for clarification on how to assess an application in a green wedge zone — areas outside of urban growth boundaries that are set aside for low-density activities such as farming or environmental purposes.

"It's really discretionary," she said.

"So that's where it makes it tricky for people who are purchasing the land, but also for a council that is considering the applications."

The proposal's economic assessment report argued the temple was important to provide culturally appropriate infrastructure in the area.

Around one in 10 residents of Casey identify as having Indian ancestry, compared to 5.3 per cent of the population across greater Melbourne.

BAPS volunteer Yash Patel said the proposal was about creating a spiritual home for Australian Hindus while being a welcoming part of the wider Casey community.

"We want the Mahã-Mandir to be a welcoming place where people from all backgrounds can visit, learn, connect and experience a part of Australia's diverse cultural and spiritual life," he said.

Other local groups object to temple

David Cole from the Western Port Green Wedge Protection Group said the group also planned to oppose the application.

"Places of worship are an important part of our community, but large urban facilities should be located where the infrastructure exists to support them," he said.

"We encourage governments at all levels to work with faith communities to identify appropriately zoned land within the Urban Growth Boundary to meet their growing place-of-worship needs."

The temple is proposed for a fast-growing area in Melbourne's outer south-east. (Supplied: Peddle Thorp)

Casey Residents and Ratepayers Association president Anthony Tassone said he had concerns about the scale of the development, which he said would be about as tall as a 20-storey building.

"The fundamental planning question is simple: is a development of this extraordinary scale and intensity appropriate on green-wedge land in this location?" he said.

The proposal went to public notice in September.

A Victorian government said the proposal would be considered on its merits.

"Green wedges play an important role in supporting agriculture, jobs, tourism and open spaces around Melbourne, which is why we have a plan to strengthen protections for them," they said.

"Boundaries are being established for regional cities and towns to limit their outward expansion and protect Victoria's natural resources, biodiversity, landscapes and agricultural land."

Victoria's Development Facilitation Program was established to fast-track planning decisions on significant projects to a matter of months.

World.title: Amazon removes ceiling light after it catches fire in safety test
World.content:
This ceiling light, bought on Amazon Australia, catches fire during laboratory safety testing, begins to melt, and keeps burning even after the test is over.

It was one of dozens of products Lighting Council Australia (LCA) warned Amazon Australia about in June.

Yet months later, it was still for sale.

The online retailer removed the listing for the $48 LED oyster ceiling light on Thursday, three hours after receiving questions from the ABC.

Testing of more than 130 lighting products available through online marketplaces has alarmed the lighting industry. (Supplied: Lighting Council of Australia)

The incident highlights a broader concern raised repeatedly by CHOICE, Australia's leading consumer advocacy group: shoppers may assume the law prevents unsafe products being sold on online marketplaces, when it does not.

LCA chief executive Malcolm Richards commissioned the test after purchasing the LED oyster light from Amazon to determine whether it met Australian safety standards.

During one test of its fire-retardant properties, a glow-wire was held to the product for 30 seconds and removed.

Under Australian lighting safety standards, plastic subjected to a flame test must self-extinguish within 10 seconds, without flaming material dripping onto and igniting the tissue paper underneath.

Mr Richards says he warned Amazon Australia repeatedly. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

The light continued burning for more than 30 seconds after the flame was removed and molten drops burnt the tissue paper, prompting an automatic failure and raising concerns about fire safety.

Further tests, conducted by Victorian firm Clevertronics, found live wires were accessible within the product, a safety breach Mr Richards described as "dramatic".

"If you unscrew the cover, which a home owner can do, you can touch the 240V as they're not insulated and be killed instantly," he said.

Do you know more? Have you been injured by a product sold on an online marketplace? Contact Amy Greenbank at greenbank.amy@protonmail.com or amygreenbank.01 on Signal.

More than 130 lights tested

In June, LCA conducted wider testing on more than 130 lights bought through online retailers including Amazon, Temu, AliExpress, eBay and Kogan.

The peak lighting body found seven in 10 failed to comply with Australian safety standards, and nine in 10 lights purchased from Amazon failed at least one compliance check.

Amazon Australia told the LCA in October it had taken steps to remove the products identified as non-compliant.

But Mr Richards said about half of the Amazon products were still available, and others had re-emerged under a different listing or seller.

Amazon Australia removed the lights from sale on Thursday. (AAP: Revere Agency)

The former electrician said Australian businesses could spend $20,000 to $50,000 per product line testing and registering lights to meet local requirements, while some overseas sellers on Amazon were flouting those rules and avoiding the compliance costs.

In a statement, Amazon said it was in the process of removing the non-compliant items and it required all products sold on its platform to adhere to applicable laws.

"We leverage robust seller verification processes, require third-party lab testing to confirm compliance for certain products before they are listed, and employ a variety of additional robust, proactive controls," a spokesperson said.

'Systemic' sale of unsafe products

The problem stretches well beyond lighting.

CHOICE research found 6 per cent of people who purchased products online in the past two years reported an injury or property damage caused by an unsafe product.

It found the sale of unsafe products was "systemic" across major online marketplaces.

Amazon removed the non-compliant products identified by CHOICE in June, but the consumer group has already identified others.

"We urgently need a general safety provision, to ensure dangerous products never reach shelves in the first place," CHOICE senior campaigns and policy adviser, Bea Sherwood said.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said existing product safety laws generally only applied to suppliers who sold their own goods, not online marketplaces.

The ACCC is backing reforms including giving the regulator effective enforcement powers irrespective of the method of purchase, a spokesperson said.

The federal government is currently consulting on product safety reforms, as part of a broader overhaul of the regime.

Submissions close on Sunday, October 18.

World.title: Government urged to do more over Australian's arrest in Vietnam
World.content:
Human rights groups are urging the federal government to ratchet up pressure on Vietnam over the fate of an Australian pro-democracy campaigner who is languishing in jail after disappearing in Cambodia last month.

Melbourne man Hiep Tran vanished after travelling to the region in September to meet Vietnamese human rights groups in Cambodia.

More than a week later, Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security said it had caught Mr Tran and another human rights activist, Norwegian citizen Duc Thuan Nguyen, trying to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".

But that has been furiously denied by Hiep Tran's supporters, who say the two men had no plan to enter Vietnam, and who allege they were likely abducted by Vietnamese authorities and bundled across the border.

Human rights groups have also pointed out that the two men missed other scheduled appointments in Cambodia and left their luggage and personal items in their hotel rooms in Cambodia — suggesting they had no plans to leave the country.

Mr Tran (left) and Duc Thuan Nguyen travelled to Phnom Penh to meet Vietnamese human rights activists. (Supplied)

The two men are members of Viet Tan, an overseas Vietnamese opposition group that the country's ruling party has labelled a terrorist organisation.

Most scholars say that while Viet Tan has roots in armed anti-Communist groups that emerged in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, it relaunched in the 2000s as a political party committed to peaceful change.

Arrest 'outrageous and unacceptable'

Human rights advocate Phil Robertson told the ABC that Hiep Tran's arrest was "outrageous and unacceptable" and another sign that Vietnamese authorities were increasingly determined to target political opponents overseas under its powerful president, former security chief To Lam.

"To Lam has made a point of going after vocal critics whenever he can, and that has included abductions in Thailand, abductions in Germany, abductions now in Cambodia," he said.

Australian human rights activist charged Vietnamese authorities charge an Australian man and two other people with planning to carry out terrorist activities, but a pro-democracy group believes the men were abducted.

Oslo-based lawyers for Duc Thuan Nguyen called his disappearance a "textbook case of enforced disappearance, within a framework of Vietnamese transnational repression".

Cambodia has denied handing over the men to Vietnam, saying they were intercepted at the border crossing.

Vietnam's government has denied targeting critics overseas, saying those allegedly abducted in Thailand were trying to cross illegally back into Vietnam, while the Vietnamese citizen who disappeared in Germany actually returned home voluntarily.

Government making representations

Last week, Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the ABC she would deal with the matter carefully in public.

"I can confirm I'm aware of this case and that Australian officials are aware," she said.

"I can confirm that we have made representations, including from me, in relation to this matter.

"But I'm not in the position, because of privacy considerations, to give you any more information than that."

Mr Tran's supporters say he is currently being detained in the notorious B34 detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, where political prisoners are often held before trial.

Hiep Tran is a pro-democracy campaigner. (Supplied)

Australian officials had not yet been granted consular access to him as of Monday this week — although it was not clear if that has changed in recent days.

His wife, Chloe Dang, said she was "heartbroken" to be separated from her husband, and has pleaded with Vietnam to set him free.

Hiep Tran is not the first Australian member of Viet Tan to be targeted by authorities in Vietnam — Sydney man Chau Van Kham was released in 2023 after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and other Australian government ministers lobbied the government to free him.

Mr Robertson said Australia should be "quite bold" and "be prepared to really push hard, both privately and publicly, for Hiep Tran's release".

"Otherwise, we're going to have him facing, you know, a kangaroo court trial and a long prison sentence, that is going to cause major problems for his family and for Vietnamese Australian relations," he said.

'I've been crying a lot'

The case has also stirred debate in the Vietnamese community in Australia, which includes both government supporters and opponents of the communist ruling party.

My Linh Do says she was interrogated for five days after being detained at the Vietnamese border in 2012. (Supplied)

Brisbane-based community activist My Linh Do, who is a prominent pro-democracy advocate and critic of Vietnam's ruling party, said Hiep Tran's experience reminded her of her own confrontation with Vietnamese authorities almost 15 years ago.

"Since Hiep Tran's incident last week, I got very scared, and I have been losing sleep," she told the ABC.

"I haven't been able to eat. I've been crying a lot."

My Linh told the ABC she was detained in 2012 at the Vietnamese border and interrogated for five days before being released.

My Linh Do says Hiep Tran's arrest reminded her of her own traumatic incident. (Supplied)

She said authorities intimidated her, tried to access her Queensland state government email account and even tried to recruit her to provide intelligence back to the Vietnamese government.

"They didn't use the term 'work as a spy', but they said they want me to report any suspicious activity by a Vietnamese in Australia who is involved in anything," she told the ABC.

DFAT officials 'continue to engage'

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) did not say if they had been granted consular access to Mr Tran.

"Australian officials in Vietnam continue to engage with the Vietnamese government," they said.

DFAT's official travel advice for Vietnam warns that people can be detained for "perceived involvement with non-state-sanctioned political organisations or groups perceived by the Government of Vietnam to be associated with dissident groups".

Allegations 'unfounded and misleading'

Vietnam's embassy in Canberra told the ABC that the allegations of forced abduction were "unfounded and misleading."

"In Viet Nam, arrests and prosecutions are carried out in accordance with the law, as in other countries," a spokesperson said in a statement.

The spokesperson also denied that Vietnamese Australians were treated inappropriately when travelling to the country.

"The steady growth in Australian visitors to Viet Nam, reaching a record half a million last year — including thousands of Australians of Vietnamese origin — reflects Viet Nam's appeal as a travel destination and the growing people-to-people ties between our two countries," they told the ABC.

Cambodia's embassy in Canberra did not respond to the ABC's questions.

World.title: Wallaroos believe 'possibilities are endless' ahead of 2029 World Cup
World.content:
Like every Test rugby player, Wallaroos lock Kaitlan Leaney knows a team cannot be defined by anything less than an 80-minute performance.

But on the recent WXV Global Series tour of Great Britain and France, Leaney feels the Wallaroos gave glimpses of the team they can be ahead of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.

The Wallaroos' 48-15 loss to England in Salford last month is a case in point.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

The final scoreline suggests a thrashing, but it does not tell the story of the first half when the Wallaroos held the upper hand over the world champions.

England did not hit the front on the scoreboard until the 46th minute after the Wallaroos led 10-5 at half-time.

"That first half just showed the potential that we have as a squad," Leaney told ABC Sport.

"I don't think it came down to England being rusty, or us having a few more games under our belt before we played them.

"I think it came down to us having that pure intent. We knew the way we wanted to play.

"We were physical on both sides of the ball. We spoke about winning the collision, and I think that we definitely did that."

The Wallaroos' Allana Sikimeti (right) takes on England's defence last month. (Getty images: Lewis Storey)

It was not just the Wallaroos' brute force that gave them the advantage, but also their intelligent strategy.

Faliki Pohiva's 31st-minute try came after the Wallaroos identified weaknesses in England's defensive formation and line-out.

"England is the best in the world and we took it to them for 45 minutes," said Leaney, who has been among the Wallaroos' most consistent players in 2026.

"We're definitely not happy with just that. We want to be able to come away with wins, but I think it just shows the growth and the capabilities we have."

Kaitlan Leaney has been one of the Wallaroos' best players this year. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A 29-26 defeat to world number four France in Aix-en-Provence the following week also provided encouraging signs, although the match was there for the taking.

The seventh-ranked Wallaroos failed to land the decisive blow, having squandered a 19-0 lead against a French side reduced to 11 players at one stage during the first half.

They rebounded seven days later to defeat Scotland 30-10 in Edinburgh; however, Leaney and her teammates were dissatisfied with their display after trailing 10-5 at half-time.

"In the first half, I think we let ourselves down in terms of discipline and missing some key opportunities that we created," Leaney said.

'Possibilities are endless'

The establishment of a full-time Wallaroos program is in progress, and will be a game-changer for women's rugby in Australia.

England invested wisely when it first offered full-time contracts in 2019, and it is little surprise the Red Roses have not lost a match in four years.

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A veteran of 43 Tests, Leaney knows the Wallaroos will improve immensely once they are no longer semi-professional.

"I think once we have that and we're together full-time, you'll see the results come from that," she said.

"I think the possibilities are endless in that space."

Wallaroos lose star for Scotland Test The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos' immediate focus is tomorrow's WXV Global Series Test against Scotland in Sydney.

It is the first of two Tests against the Scots on Australian soil, with the second match to be played in Canberra on October 23.

Winning is the obvious goal, but Leaney is also determined that the Wallaroos produce a complete performance across both halves.

"That's something we're working on for this weekend and making sure we're firing from the get-go and sticking to our game plan," she said.

"Because when we do, it works. We just need to do it from the start.

"We just haven't reached that 80-minute performance yet."

World.title: Councillor told woman it was a 'pity' she wasn't bashed, investigator finds
World.content:
A NSW Mid North Coast councillor is under pressure to resign after an independent investigator found he told a woman on social media it was a pity she had not been "bashed".

Kempsey Shire Council hired consulting firm Centium to investigate following complaints about a post on the personal social media account of Noel Selby in April this year.

The post, made in response to a comment from a woman alleging a man was violent towards multiple partners, said "pity he hadn't bashed you".

Cr Selby has maintained his account was hacked and that he did not post the comment.

But in an outcome statement obtained by the ABC, lead investigator Jennifer Perry "formed the view that Cr Selby did post the comment from his Facebook account".

She also found that the comment "generated significant public commentary" that identified him as a Kempsey Shire councillor.

The ABC approached Ms Perry for comment about the report but was referred to the council.

She declined to provide details about what methods were used to reach the conclusion that Cr Selby was responsible for the Facebook comment.

Noel Selby declined to comment until the matter was discussed at the October council meeting. (Supplied: Kempsey Shire Council)

The full report and its findings will be considered at a council meeting on October 20.

Cr Selby declined to comment on the report until after the meeting.

Calls for resignation

June Wilson, the executive officer of the domestic violence service Kempsey Families, contacted the council with concerns after seeing Cr Selby's comments.

"I think the only option is for him to resign," she said.

"It undermines the work we do.

"It comes back to people holding someone to account, and that's the work we do in the [area of] men's behaviour change — you actually have to hold the mirror up and look at it."

June Wilson says comment such as Cr Selby's undermine the work of advocacy groups. (Supplied: June Wilson)

According to the latest NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research statistics, domestic violence rates in Kempsey are almost three times the state average.

Ms Wilson said the council should seize the opportunity to take a firmer position against domestic violence and to strengthen relationships with domestic violence organisations.

Kempsey Shire Council did not respond to questions about calls for Cr Selby's resignation, or about developing a domestic violence policy for staff and councillors.

In a statement, the council said it rejected "all forms of violence, including family and domestic violence".

Centium's outcome statement also found the comment breached council's code of conduct for intimidation and harassment and had "the capacity to damage the council's reputation".

It was recommended that Cr Selby be formally censured.

That would involve a public reprimand but would not allow for councillors to be stood down or suspended.

A spokesperson for the NSW Office of Local Government said the government was "progressing reforms to strengthen councillor accountability and establish a more effective framework for dealing with serious misconduct".

Sherele Moody shared Noel Selby's comments on social media. (Supplied: Sherele Moody)

Multiple complaints

Cr Selby's comment was publicised by domestic violence and femicide researcher Sherele Moody, who shared it on social media.

She said actions promoting violence against women should be grounds for immediate dismissal from public office.

"I don't know what the form of their censure will be, but it will need to be a response that recognises the gravity of the impact of his words," Ms Moody said.

"I would like to see him retire from council.

" I don't think it's at all appropriate for a man in a prominent position to make comments that normalise gendered violence in Australia and retain their public-facing role. "

Hannah Moreno says she's "sick to death" of seeing a lack of consequences for aggressive behaviour towards women. (Supplied: Hannah Moreno)

Sydney-based domestic violence survivor and advocate Hannah Moreno said she was not from Kempsey Shire but felt compelled to submit a complaint to the council after seeing the comment.

"[Cr] Selby's paid out of the public purse. He votes on decisions that shape women's lives and that makes him every Australian's business," she said.

Ms Moreno said the consequences for such a breach should be tougher and considered grounds for "immediate suspension".

"I'm just sick to death of powerful men seeing no consequences for their violent words and actions inflicted on women," she said.

World.title: De Minaur falls to world number one Zverev in Shanghai
World.content:
Top-ranked Alexander Zverev said he felt good on court after beating Alex de Minaur 6-4, 6-4 at the Shanghai Masters.

Behind his impregnable serve, Zverev, who is guaranteed to end the year as the top-ranked men's player after a season-ending injury to Jannik Sinner, enjoyed his most clinical match of the tournament after struggling with foot problems in earlier contests.

Zverev made 80 per cent of his first serves and saved all five of the break points he faced as he set up a semifinal meeting with Alejandro Davidovich Fokina.

"I felt both of us were playing really, really well. I was a lot of times out-hitting Alex, which is difficult to do from the baseline because he is so fast and he loves this kind of court speed here," Zverev said.

"I felt good, and I'm happy with the step up from the last couple of matches."

World number nine de Minaur, one of the best returners in the game, managed to eke out five break points over two key games, one in each set, but was then thwarted by Zverev's delivery.

After being broken for 3-2 in the opening stanza when the German unleashed a series of monster forehands, de Minaur immediately hit back in the next game by carving out three break points, only for Zverev to pound down five unreturnable serves in a row.

Having wrapped up that set in 37 minutes, Zverev then found himself under pressure from the Sydneysider in the second stanza as de Minaur earned two break points, sniffing an opportunity to move into a 4-2 lead.

Again, though, Zverev rescued the situation with fine serving and immediately broke a deflated "Demon'' in the next game to effectively seal the deal, earning his ninth win over the Australian, this time with 10 aces and 14 searing winners.

It continued de Minaur's depressing record against the German, having beaten Zverev only four times in team competition but never in an individual tournament.

The consolation for de Minaur, though, is that he ends another promising tournament by improving his chances of reaching the end-of-season, eight-man ATP Finals for the third straight year as he has moved up to seventh in the live Race to Turin standings.

That leaves him sixth overall, with Sinner's season already over because of his knee injury.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Wells says gender ‘debates’ would not be policed in reforms; Trump administration will not livestream firing squad execution
World.content:
Communications Minister Anika Wells says gender “debates”, including around transgender rights, will not be policed under Labor’s digital reforms, but could not provide more clarity on how the government would determine what constituted a hostile attitude towards women.

She said debate around transgender issues would not be captured by the legislation, but content that displays a hostile attitude towards women would.

“A hostile attitude example that I used at the National Press Club is material that says to young boys that consent doesn’t matter,” the minister told ABC’s 7.30 last night.

Communications Minister Anika Wells at the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen

But she could not provide further clarity on the scope of the definition, and said the eSafety Commissioner would produce and publish regulatory guidance that would determine whether the intent of online content was hostile.

“The reason that that provision is in the bill is because we had more than 20 women’s groups and teachers, teachers’ coalitions from across the country ask us to incorporate that because they’ve noticed that young boys coming through the education system have these hostile attitudes,” Wells said.

“The regulatory guidance that was published around what reasonable steps were for the social media minimum age, that’s similarly going to be instructive for how big tech has to assess the risks on its platform against that detail.”

World.title: ‘Monster-like’: Woman alleges Russell Brand posed for photos moments before sudden rape
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeCourts ‘Monster-like’: Woman alleges Russell Brand posed for photos moments before sudden rape David Crowe Updated October 16, 2026 — 6:45am ,first published 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Warning: Graphic content London: A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand has told a court the actor underwent a sudden change in manner as they talked in her hotel room, demanding she take photographs of him before pushing her onto a bed. The woman told jurors that Brand became suddenly “monster-like” after they had talked for hours on the night they met in September 1999, leaving her in pain after he forced himself on top of her and raped her. The 1999 photographs of Russell Brand that were tendered as evidence in court at his rape trial on Thursday (UK time). Metropolitan Police “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe,” she told the court, saying she was pinned down by the actor’s weight. “I know I said ‘No’.”



Brand, 51, is facing trial in London on three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has insisted he never engaged in non-consensual sex. The woman, described as the first complainant among six women alleging sexual assault and rape, said she thought Brand was gay because of his “effeminate” manner when they met at a cabaret where he was appearing on the sidelines of a Labour conference in Bournemouth. Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court on Thursday (UK time). Jordan Pettitt/PA via AP They spoke about her ideas for a play about forced marriage, she told the court, and went to her hotel room to continue the conversation because she was not drinking and did not want to go to a pub because it would be hard to hear. She said that after she suggested Brand make a coffee while she went to the bathroom, she returned to find him “prancing” around the room “like an ostrich” without his shirt, and that he then demanded she take photographs of him with her camera.



In key evidence produced in court, jurors were shown two photographs of the actor, who was 24 at the time, staring at the camera with a mirror and small wash basin behind him. In one image he appears to gesture to the camera. Related Article Graphic content

Courts Russell Brand a ‘ruthless sexual predator’, prosecutor alleges as rape trial opens The woman, who was in her late 20s at the time, said that Brand became aroused while she was taking photographs and that she saw this clearly at one stage because he was in his underpants, which she referred to as “budgie smugglers”. In a video interview with police that was shown to the court, the woman said Brand forced her onto the bed and pulled her trousers and underwear down. He kissed her in a “lizard-like” way and put his fingers in her mouth, making it hard for her to breathe. “He knew I didn’t want it. He put himself straight in. It was hurting. He was having sex, pushing, pushing.” She said she had her eyes shut and could not do anything because of his weight.



Her statements in the police interview were challenged by Brand’s counsel when the woman appeared in court to give direct evidence, after the video was shown. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial The defence counsel, Ian Winter, KC, said the photographs were at odds with the woman’s statement to police because they showed Brand was wearing white pants rather than being in his underwear as she had said. The woman rejected those doubts by saying she had kept taking photographs even if some did not turn out, and she was adamant that he had been in his “budgie smugglers” at one stage – and that she had become scared. When Winter asked the woman in cross-examination why she did not leave the hotel room when Brand took off his clothes, she replied that she had nowhere to go and there were no staff at the hotel late in the night.



Winter suggested to the woman that she had allowed Brand to persuade her to have sex, telling her: “It wasn’t rape.” He then said: “It’s your right to have a one-night stand if you want.” The woman said: “He did not persuade me.” She said she could have had one-night stands if she chose, but she did not want sex with Brand. “I didn’t find him attractive,” she said. Brand with his wife, Laura, outside court on Monday. AP Photo/Kin Cheung The trial has made headlines in Britain this week because of the six claims against Brand, who shot to stardom two decades ago as a host on MTV before appearing on reality television shows and appearing in movies such as Get Him To the Greek and Forgetting Sarah Marshall. Brand married singer Katy Perry in 2010, but they divorced two years later. In 2017, he married author Laura Gallacher, who has supported him against the allegations and appeared alongside him on the first day of the trial.



With the question of consent dominating the second day of the trial, Brand’s counsel suggested that the first complainant only came forward because she had seen part of a 2023 documentary that cited unnamed women who accused Brand of sexual assault. Winter said this made the woman think that Brand raped her – a suggestion she vehemently rejected in testimony. At times, she became tearful as she spoke of being ashamed over what had taken place. The judge presiding over the trial at Southwark Crown Court, Justice Joel Bennathan, interrupted the cross-examination when Winter suggested that the woman did not say “No” during the alleged rape. The judge checked the transcript from the video interview and noted that the woman told police she had said to Brand: “What are you doing? No, no.” Prosecuting barrister Riel Karmy-Jones, KC, also highlighted parts of the police interview when the woman said she had told Brand to stop.



“I did say ‘No’,” the woman told the court. The sex took about five minutes, she said, and she felt she could not do anything and it was better for it to end quickly. “He did rape me,” she said. The woman testified in court behind a screen so she was visible to the judge and jury, but not to the media to Brand, who sat in a glass dock paying close attention to the testimony. Brand sat upright throughout the day in court, thanking attendants briefly at times. The woman told the court that Brand left quickly after the alleged rape and told her that he remembered he needed to see his mother. After he left, she said, she spent hours washing herself in the hotel bathroom. “I remember banging my head against the wall,” she said.



Those making sexual assault accusations have the right to anonymity under British law. This masthead seeks to avoid reporting details that might identify witnesses in the trial. The trial is expected to continue for at least six weeks. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: ‘As if the sky had fallen’: School roof collapse kills at least 34 children and a teacher
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy ‘As if the sky had fallen’: School roof collapse kills at least 34 children and a teacher Riaz Khan and Hritam Mukherjee Updated October 16, 2026 — 6:29am ,first published 6:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Peshawar: The roof of a private school collapsed in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar, killing at least 34 children and a teacher and injuring more than 50 other people in the deadliest building collapse ever in the country, authorities and a hospital official said. Most of the children killed or injured at Al-Khair school on Thursday were between 6 and 12 years old, while the oldest was 14, Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said. Some of the injured were in critical condition, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded. Hours after the collapse in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, emergency services spokesperson Bilal Faizi said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews had cleared debris.



He said the roofs of two classrooms collapsed when second- and third-grade children were in them with their teachers. Faizi said ambulances and disaster management personnel arrived from a nearby facility within five minutes of being alerted. Nearly 100 rescuers eventually joined the operation, he said. Panicked, grieving parents were trying to help when crews arrived, Faizi said. He credited the rapid evacuation with saving at least 40 lives. More than a dozen children suffered minor injuries, he said. Mourners attend funeral prayers for children killed when the roof of a school, in Peshawar, Pakistan, collapsed. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs. One teacher said it felt as though the sky had fallen



Hundreds of mourners later gathered at Rehman Baba cemetery for mass funeral prayers as grief gripped the neighbourhood and announcements echoed from mosque loudspeakers, urging residents to join in prayers for those killed. Residents said most of the children killed lived in the Dir Colony neighbourhood, where the school is located, leaving them unsure which bereaved family to visit first to offer condolences. A rescue worker gestures toward roof as he searches through the rubble. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair Ambulances were seen leaving the hospital to bring the children’s bodies home as mourners wept and wailed. Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said the school had about 1200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She said she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.



Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children. According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighbourhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene. A man shows a picture of his young relative who was killed in the roof collapse. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom for a drink of water. Another resident, Mohammad Khan, said that rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.



Officials offer condolences and promise investigations Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school’s owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak. However, following his arrest, the owner, Mohammad Khan, blamed recent rains for weakening one of the roofs, according to police, who said the investigation was still underway. The provincial government said a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse of the three-storey building. The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.



In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements. “The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow,” Zardari said. He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies. World.title: The LNP is adamant Brisbane 2032 will be delivered within budget. Here’s what voters think
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics The LNP is adamant Brisbane 2032 will be delivered within budget. Here’s what voters think Cameron Atfield October 16, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nearly two-thirds of Queenslanders doubt the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games can be delivered within its set budget, according to exclusive polling conducted for this masthead. The state LNP government has long insisted its 2032 delivery plan, jointly funded by the Commonwealth, would be delivered within the agreed $7.1 billion funding envelope. Most Queenslanders have little confidence in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games being delivered on budget. Graphic: Marija Ercegovac But the Resolve Political Monitor survey of 434 Queensland voters, conducted between October 6 and 10, found the Crisafulli government’s messaging had failed to assuage voter concerns about cost blowouts over the next six years. Just 24 per cent are confident the Games would stay on budget, compared with 63 per cent who are not. The remaining 13 per cent are unsure.



The divide is even more stark among those with stronger feelings about the Games budget. Only 4 per cent are “very confident” the Games will be delivered on budget, while 36 per cent are “not at all confident”. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership When confronted with the polling, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie insisted voters had nothing to be concerned about. “Unlike [former Labor premier and current opposition leader] Steven Miles’ flip-flopping, fake plan and repeated budget blowouts, we’re focused on delivering the infrastructure Queensland needs with financial discipline and transparency,” he said. “Venues will be delivered within the $7.1 billion funding envelope, as agreed with the federal government.”



The Miles government scrapped an earlier Labor plan to rebuild the Gabba in favour of having the Queensland Sport and Athletics Centre as Brisbane 2032’s main stadium. Shortly after its election, the Crisafulli government conducted a 100-day review to eventually settle on a new stadium at Victoria Park. Overall, the Resolve polling shows confidence in the state’s ability to deliver the 2032 Olympics within or close to its $7.1 billion budget remained low across all major voter groups. The most sceptical respondents were One Nation supporters, of whom 74 per cent expected the Games to go over budget. It also had the largest cohort of not-at-all confident voters, at 50 per cent. Just 15 per cent of One Nation voters expected the Games to come in on budget – 6 per cent were very confident, and 9 per cent were fairly confident. The most optimistic respondents were largely from the left side of politics, with 29 per cent of Labor and Greens voters expressing confidence – the same percentage as uncommitted voters – closely followed by LNP voters on 28 per cent.



Of those confident Labor voters, only 6 per cent were very confident, with the remaining 23 per cent “fairly confident”. A quarter were not very confident, but the single biggest cohort – 30 per cent – had no confidence whatsoever. Among Greens supporters, about 29 per cent were confident the Games would be delivered on or close to budget (6 per cent very confident, 24 per cent fairly confident). However, 60 per cent were not confident, including 34 per cent who were “not at all confident”. Premier David Crisafulli with Tourism Minister Andrew Powell, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and junior Australian Rules players at Brisbane Stadium’s ceremonial sod-turning in June. Cameron Atfield Even among supporters of the governing LNP, sceptics outnumbered believers more than two to one. Twenty-eight per cent expressed confidence the Games would be delivered within budget, but just 3 per cent were “very confident”, while 25 per cent were “fairly confident”. A clear majority, 61 per cent, were not confident, including 29 per cent who were devoid of confidence. In marginal seats, 64 per cent expected costs to soar above $7.1 billion, with 41 per cent “not at all confident” costs could be reined in. Just 23 per cent thought expenditure would stick to budget.



Former premier Campbell Newman, who shared a cabinet table with Crisafulli and Bleijie during his time in the state’s top job, has long warned of potential cost blowouts at the Victoria Park site. Former premier Campbell Newman has been a vocal critic of his former party’s Victoria Park plans. Cameron Atfield Newman said the poll numbers showed “the public seem to get” it would be difficult to deliver the Games on budget. “I find it quite remarkable that self-identified LNP voters don’t believe they’re going to deliver on budget – that’s very telling,” he said. “I would have been horrified when I was in political office, whether it be City Hall or the state, if that was the view of me and my government.



“We’re entitled to expect better, a lot better, and an LNP government should be absolutely committed to being responsible with our dollars.” Newman said Queensland’s recent credit downgrade was a direct result of the government “abandon[ing] any sense of fiscal responsibility” when it came to the Games. Miles also cited the credit downgrade when asked about the poll numbers. “S&P Global warned David Crisafulli that an Olympic blowout would result in a further credit rating downgrade, costing Queenslanders millions of dollars in extra interest payments,” the opposition leader said.



“The premier must release the true cost of the Olympics after promising to be open and transparent before the election.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return Victoria Ward Updated October 16, 2026 — 5:54am ,first published 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There were selfies and fist bumps, chit-chat about the British weather and group hugs. Meghan said it was “wonderful” to be back in the UK, compared wedding rings with a fan and was given a healing crystal amid armfuls of flowers and balloons. Britain’s Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on Thursday. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska Prince Harry beamed as he bounced along high-fiving local school children, asking which year they were in and which lessons they were missing. To seasoned royal watchers, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s first joint appearance since returning to Britain was straight out of the Buckingham Palace playbook. This time, however, the couple were on their own manoeuvres, entirely independent of the monarchy.



Whether or not that matters will continue to be a subject of much debate. But to the 150-strong crowd who turned out to greet them on Thursday (UK time) at the Community Recording Studio (CRS), a youth charity in Nottingham, it was irrelevant. Margaret Langdon, 67, from Carlton, said their visit showed “it’s not all about London” and “small cities matter as well”. “I’m a big fan,” she said. “They’ve come to Nottingham to see us so the least we could do is come out and see them.”



Among those whose efforts were rewarded with warm hugs from Harry and Meghan was Irene Hardman, 90, from Roddington, who was brandishing a framed photograph of herself meeting the couple in December 2017. “Oh my gosh how sweet is that” gushed Meghan as she clasped her hands to her mouth. “That was our very first walkabout. Oh my gosh, what a great memory. I remember this day so well, that is so special.” Meghan holds a bouquet of flowers from the crowd. Getty Images The Duke and Duchess of Sussex meet members of the public as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio in Nottingham. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska



The duchess, clad in British designs, including a belt from Marks & Spencer, told another fan: “It’s great to be back.” Related Article Royal family ‘Slipped into depression’: Prince Harry on leaving the UK and grieving for his mother One school boy asked if she had come in a Rolls-Royce, prompting laughter. The less glamorous reality was that the couple were 10 minutes late after getting stuck in traffic following the morning school run. No blue light police escort for these two yet, despite Prince Harry’s ongoing efforts. Inside, there was plenty of inspirational chat and messages of support.



The duchess joined a group of girls from Bluebell Hill Primary School for a “confidence-building and bracelet-making session”, noting that drawing could be “very calming” and revealing that her daughter, Princess Lilibet, 5, loved gymnastics. “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I cook,” she said. “I love to cook, do you? Experimenting?” Meghan poses for a selfie with a member of the public. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska At another table, Meghan discussed the importance of complimenting others. “Sometimes we have to remember to talk to ourselves like we talk to our best friends, really,” she said. “You have to remember to be just as kind to yourself.” Before leaving, she gave each of the girls each a handwritten card inscribed with a motivational quote.



The couple also watched an acting workshop led by actor André Squire. “That was great,” Meghan told the young people involved, asking the group: “Did you find the characters relatable?” As the duke and duchess left, they were accosted by more fans. “We’ve got to go. I’ve got to take her,” a proud Harry said of his wife, as one lady shouted: “You’re lovely, you’re just like your mother.” Later, Trevor Rose, CRS chief executive and co-founder, said Prince Harry, who first visited the studio in 2013, always had a big impact. “For him to want to bring Meg as well and to hear that she wanted to find out more about what we are and what we do is incredible,” he added.



“In the end, there’s a lot of young females in here and they need people who understand them and Meghan has definitely made a point of asking about what they do, what they’re about and what the challenges are. Related Article Epstein fallout Raids on Andrew’s homes in hunt for Epstein ties were unlawful, police admit “To say to them that she’s coming here to meet you – they were speechless. I’ve seen a few tears in peoples’ eyes. That’s what it’s about. I take it as a great stepping stone that they’re still here, we can still reach out to them and they still care.” He added: “They don’t just say they’ll visit every year – they ring up every couple of months, they ask what we’re doing and monitor progress and give us suggestions.” Asked if CRS users look up to the couple, he said: “100 per cent.” The Sussexes later visited the Himmah food bank where Meghan said it felt “really meaningful” to be reunited with some of the women from the Grenfell Hubb Community Kitchen.



The couple washed their hands before helping to prepare lunch, with Harry joking that he had been allocated washing up duties. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub. Getty Images Meghan was warmly welcomed to Himmah Hub. Getty Images The Sussexes concluded their day at Epic Partners, a youth charity Harry has supported for 13 years, where they played pool and decorated cupcakes. World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace culture McKinsey leader steps down from charity board days after controversial ‘glass cliff’ comments Colin Kruger October 16, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. One of McKinsey & Co’s most prominent partners, Sydney-based Chris Bradley, has resigned from his board role at Opportunity International Australia just days after the global consulting giant dumped him a leadership role at its high-profile research arm over online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. “Chris Bradley has offered to resign from the Board of Opportunity International Australia, and we have accepted his resignation,” the charity said in a post on its website on Thursday evening. McKinsey partner Chris Bradley questioned the existence of the glass cliff. Peter Rae “For more than 25 years, Chris has passionately and ably supported our mission in empowering more than 10 million women and their families to lift themselves out of poverty with dignity. “We are grateful for his support of our mission and thank him for his work as a Board member.”



McKinsey removed Bradley from his board role at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit, this week. Bradley remains a board member of Sydney-based conservative think tank, The Centre for Independent Studies and remains a senior partner at McKinsey. The decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth last month with one of the authors of a new book that discusses the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. The term glass cliff was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered chief executive officer jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode.



Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. Bradley also wrote in the recent LinkedIn exchange that “we once had a problem of female advancement to CEO, but now we have a new problem that the jobs they get are too hard? Is this actually a thing?” Walking on Broken Glass co-author Julia Carreon. Vanessa Kay Julia Carreon, a former Wall Street executive and co-author of the book Walking on Broken Glass: Navigating the Aftermath of the Glass Ceiling, commented on Bradley’s LinkedIn post, saying: “Aren’t people from McKinsey & Company supposed to know these things?



“I understand you ARE the establishment, but this is surprising.” In response to Carreon, Bradley said: “I am not going to start researching glass cliffs as I don’t think it ranks in the top 1000 problems of the world.” Related Article Updated

Workplace culture McKinsey strips Australian partner of leadership role after ‘glass cliff’ comments Bradley was defended by a senior fellow at the Centre for Independent Studies, Parnell Palme McGuinness, in a column for this publication. “There are a couple of issues here. The first is the slavering cowardice of the management consultancy in responding to the incident by relieving a highly competent leader of a role he was demonstrably succeeding in because of what should have been a reasonably innocuous social media dispute,” she said.



“Another is whether the concept of the glass cliff is based on such rock-solid evidence that it is uncontestable.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

Fontaines DC’s new album completes their transition to stadium-rock stars. Fontaines DC, Dopamine Chamber ★★★★ Just two years ago, Fontaines DC’s arena-rock pivot Romance turned them into the prevailing band for middle-aged dads eager to prove they listen to new music. The Irish rockers, once the snarling soldiers of Dublin city, expanded their frantic guitar-attack with synthy atmospherics, Smashing Pumpkins-style orchestration and stadium-ready pomp. If that outlined their heady ambition, then Dopamine Chamber completes the band’s journey from the streets of Dublin to outer space. Opener Six Shot Morning, with its motorik propulsion, ping-ponging lasers and frontman Grian Chatten’s Ian Curtis-esque bark now a calm baritone croon (ever vague, his lyrical snatches lament Silicon Valley, environmental collapse and the folly of resistance), envelops us in the inevitability of cosmic doom.



Fontaines D.C.: From the streets of Dublin to outer space. Ewen Spencer Apparently inspired by the Epstein files and subsequent protests in London, the band’s members have taken to turning up to interviews with dog-eared copies of Brave New World in their coat pockets. Such precious self-seriousness could leave early fans wondering if the DC now stands for “Doing Coldplay”, if not for the fact their songs are still underpinned by their nervy post-punk. On highlights Mimesis, Happy For You and single Marianne, chiming guitars and synth melodies pluck their way from the expansive, reverb-drenched haze. And then there’s the fairly remarkable centrepiece Where Is Gone?, a swooning duet with Spanish icon Rosalia that plays like Lee Hazlewood and Nancy Sinatra reunited at the end of the world, complete with timpani rolls, swelling strings, Western guitars and a stirring melody that’s been living in my head for a week. You’d imagine these guys could have a Bond theme in their future if they believed the future was even a plausible possibility. Robert Moran



Effortless guitar-pop from Newcastle’s all-conquering Vacations. Vacations, Pursuit of Anything ★★★ On their fourth album, Pursuit Of Anything, all-conquering Newcastle band Vacations sound more settled than ever. That’s despite the backdrop of the album’s creation, with various members settling down and/or relocating to various parts of the world. It’s enough to throw any group off their axis, but that’s not the case here. The album finds lead singer Campbell Burns musing on getting older, with these thoughts pressed up against beds of warm, lush guitar-pop. Pursuit of Anything doesn’t demand anything of the listener except to absorb it. Songs such as Yesterday and I See Myself In You sound utterly effortless, with the band totally in sync.



It might be the biggest issue with the album. In asking almost nothing of the listener, Burns’ laconic vocal delivery risks masking his strong lyricism. On opening track Congratulations, he sings “Scared to death/As the world stands still/Time marches on/When you don’t have the will” – but rather than entering with a bang, the band winds up slowly, like awaking from a deep slumber. Pursuit of Anything proves Vacations have mastered the art of swaying guitar-pop. However, at times, it all threatens to wash into itself. Ben Madden Want more music stories and reviews? Communications Minister Anika Wells says gender “debates”, including around transgender rights, will not be policed under Labor’s digital reforms, but could not provide more clarity on how the government would determine what constituted a hostile attitude towards women.

She said debate around transgender issues would not be captured by the legislation, but content that displays a hostile attitude towards women would.

“A hostile attitude example that I used at the National Press Club is material that says to young boys that consent doesn’t matter,” the minister told ABC’s 7.30 last night.

Communications Minister Anika Wells at the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen

But she could not provide further clarity on the scope of the definition, and said the eSafety Commissioner would produce and publish regulatory guidance that would determine whether the intent of online content was hostile.

“The reason that that provision is in the bill is because we had more than 20 women’s groups and teachers, teachers’ coalitions from across the country ask us to incorporate that because they’ve noticed that young boys coming through the education system have these hostile attitudes,” Wells said.

“The regulatory guidance that was published around what reasonable steps were for the social media minimum age, that’s similarly going to be instructive for how big tech has to assess the risks on its platform against that detail.”

World.title: ‘Monster-like’: Woman alleges Russell Brand posed for photos moments before sudden rape
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeCourts ‘Monster-like’: Woman alleges Russell Brand posed for photos moments before sudden rape David Crowe Updated October 16, 2026 — 6:45am ,first published 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Warning: Graphic content London: A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand has told a court the actor underwent a sudden change in manner as they talked in her hotel room, demanding she take photographs of him before pushing her onto a bed. The woman told jurors that Brand became suddenly “monster-like” after they had talked for hours on the night they met in September 1999, leaving her in pain after he forced himself on top of her and raped her. The 1999 photographs of Russell Brand that were tendered as evidence in court at his rape trial on Thursday (UK time). Metropolitan Police “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe,” she told the court, saying she was pinned down by the actor’s weight. “I know I said ‘No’.”



Brand, 51, is facing trial in London on three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has insisted he never engaged in non-consensual sex. The woman, described as the first complainant among six women alleging sexual assault and rape, said she thought Brand was gay because of his “effeminate” manner when they met at a cabaret where he was appearing on the sidelines of a Labour conference in Bournemouth. Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court on Thursday (UK time). Jordan Pettitt/PA via AP They spoke about her ideas for a play about forced marriage, she told the court, and went to her hotel room to continue the conversation because she was not drinking and did not want to go to a pub because it would be hard to hear. She said that after she suggested Brand make a coffee while she went to the bathroom, she returned to find him “prancing” around the room “like an ostrich” without his shirt, and that he then demanded she take photographs of him with her camera.



In key evidence produced in court, jurors were shown two photographs of the actor, who was 24 at the time, staring at the camera with a mirror and small wash basin behind him. In one image he appears to gesture to the camera. Related Article Graphic content

Courts Russell Brand a ‘ruthless sexual predator’, prosecutor alleges as rape trial opens The woman, who was in her late 20s at the time, said that Brand became aroused while she was taking photographs and that she saw this clearly at one stage because he was in his underpants, which she referred to as “budgie smugglers”. In a video interview with police that was shown to the court, the woman said Brand forced her onto the bed and pulled her trousers and underwear down. He kissed her in a “lizard-like” way and put his fingers in her mouth, making it hard for her to breathe. “He knew I didn’t want it. He put himself straight in. It was hurting. He was having sex, pushing, pushing.” She said she had her eyes shut and could not do anything because of his weight.



Her statements in the police interview were challenged by Brand’s counsel when the woman appeared in court to give direct evidence, after the video was shown. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial The defence counsel, Ian Winter, KC, said the photographs were at odds with the woman’s statement to police because they showed Brand was wearing white pants rather than being in his underwear as she had said. The woman rejected those doubts by saying she had kept taking photographs even if some did not turn out, and she was adamant that he had been in his “budgie smugglers” at one stage – and that she had become scared. When Winter asked the woman in cross-examination why she did not leave the hotel room when Brand took off his clothes, she replied that she had nowhere to go and there were no staff at the hotel late in the night.



Winter suggested to the woman that she had allowed Brand to persuade her to have sex, telling her: “It wasn’t rape.” He then said: “It’s your right to have a one-night stand if you want.” The woman said: “He did not persuade me.” She said she could have had one-night stands if she chose, but she did not want sex with Brand. “I didn’t find him attractive,” she said. Brand with his wife, Laura, outside court on Monday. AP Photo/Kin Cheung The trial has made headlines in Britain this week because of the six claims against Brand, who shot to stardom two decades ago as a host on MTV before appearing on reality television shows and appearing in movies such as Get Him To the Greek and Forgetting Sarah Marshall. Brand married singer Katy Perry in 2010, but they divorced two years later. In 2017, he married author Laura Gallacher, who has supported him against the allegations and appeared alongside him on the first day of the trial.



With the question of consent dominating the second day of the trial, Brand’s counsel suggested that the first complainant only came forward because she had seen part of a 2023 documentary that cited unnamed women who accused Brand of sexual assault. Winter said this made the woman think that Brand raped her – a suggestion she vehemently rejected in testimony. At times, she became tearful as she spoke of being ashamed over what had taken place. The judge presiding over the trial at Southwark Crown Court, Justice Joel Bennathan, interrupted the cross-examination when Winter suggested that the woman did not say “No” during the alleged rape. The judge checked the transcript from the video interview and noted that the woman told police she had said to Brand: “What are you doing? No, no.” Prosecuting barrister Riel Karmy-Jones, KC, also highlighted parts of the police interview when the woman said she had told Brand to stop.



“I did say ‘No’,” the woman told the court. The sex took about five minutes, she said, and she felt she could not do anything and it was better for it to end quickly. “He did rape me,” she said. The woman testified in court behind a screen so she was visible to the judge and jury, but not to the media to Brand, who sat in a glass dock paying close attention to the testimony. Brand sat upright throughout the day in court, thanking attendants briefly at times. The woman told the court that Brand left quickly after the alleged rape and told her that he remembered he needed to see his mother. After he left, she said, she spent hours washing herself in the hotel bathroom. “I remember banging my head against the wall,” she said.



Those making sexual assault accusations have the right to anonymity under British law. This masthead seeks to avoid reporting details that might identify witnesses in the trial. The trial is expected to continue for at least six weeks. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy ‘As if the sky had fallen’: School roof collapse kills at least 34 children and a teacher Riaz Khan and Hritam Mukherjee Updated October 16, 2026 — 6:29am ,first published 6:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
