Peshawar: The roof of a private school collapsed in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar, killing at least 34 children and a teacher and injuring more than 50 other people in the deadliest building collapse ever in the country, authorities and a hospital official said. Most of the children killed or injured at Al-Khair school on Thursday were between 6 and 12 years old, while the oldest was 14, Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said. Some of the injured were in critical condition, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded. Hours after the collapse in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, emergency services spokesperson Bilal Faizi said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews had cleared debris.



He said the roofs of two classrooms collapsed when second- and third-grade children were in them with their teachers. Faizi said ambulances and disaster management personnel arrived from a nearby facility within five minutes of being alerted. Nearly 100 rescuers eventually joined the operation, he said. Panicked, grieving parents were trying to help when crews arrived, Faizi said. He credited the rapid evacuation with saving at least 40 lives. More than a dozen children suffered minor injuries, he said. Mourners attend funeral prayers for children killed when the roof of a school, in Peshawar, Pakistan, collapsed. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs. One teacher said it felt as though the sky had fallen



Hundreds of mourners later gathered at Rehman Baba cemetery for mass funeral prayers as grief gripped the neighbourhood and announcements echoed from mosque loudspeakers, urging residents to join in prayers for those killed. Residents said most of the children killed lived in the Dir Colony neighbourhood, where the school is located, leaving them unsure which bereaved family to visit first to offer condolences. A rescue worker gestures toward roof as he searches through the rubble. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair Ambulances were seen leaving the hospital to bring the children’s bodies home as mourners wept and wailed. Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said the school had about 1200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She said she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.



Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children. According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighbourhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene. A man shows a picture of his young relative who was killed in the roof collapse. AP Photo/Muhammad Zubair A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom for a drink of water. Another resident, Mohammad Khan, said that rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.



Officials offer condolences and promise investigations Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school’s owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak. However, following his arrest, the owner, Mohammad Khan, blamed recent rains for weakening one of the roofs, according to police, who said the investigation was still underway. The provincial government said a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse of the three-storey building. The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.



In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements. “The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow,” Zardari said. He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies. World.title: The LNP is adamant Brisbane 2032 will be delivered within budget. Here’s what voters think
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics The LNP is adamant Brisbane 2032 will be delivered within budget. Here’s what voters think Cameron Atfield October 16, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nearly two-thirds of Queenslanders doubt the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games can be delivered within its set budget, according to exclusive polling conducted for this masthead. The state LNP government has long insisted its 2032 delivery plan, jointly funded by the Commonwealth, would be delivered within the agreed $7.1 billion funding envelope. Most Queenslanders have little confidence in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games being delivered on budget. Graphic: Marija Ercegovac But the Resolve Political Monitor survey of 434 Queensland voters, conducted between October 6 and 10, found the Crisafulli government’s messaging had failed to assuage voter concerns about cost blowouts over the next six years. Just 24 per cent are confident the Games would stay on budget, compared with 63 per cent who are not. The remaining 13 per cent are unsure.



The divide is even more stark among those with stronger feelings about the Games budget. Only 4 per cent are “very confident” the Games will be delivered on budget, while 36 per cent are “not at all confident”. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership When confronted with the polling, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie insisted voters had nothing to be concerned about. “Unlike [former Labor premier and current opposition leader] Steven Miles’ flip-flopping, fake plan and repeated budget blowouts, we’re focused on delivering the infrastructure Queensland needs with financial discipline and transparency,” he said. “Venues will be delivered within the $7.1 billion funding envelope, as agreed with the federal government.”



The Miles government scrapped an earlier Labor plan to rebuild the Gabba in favour of having the Queensland Sport and Athletics Centre as Brisbane 2032’s main stadium. Shortly after its election, the Crisafulli government conducted a 100-day review to eventually settle on a new stadium at Victoria Park. Overall, the Resolve polling shows confidence in the state’s ability to deliver the 2032 Olympics within or close to its $7.1 billion budget remained low across all major voter groups. The most sceptical respondents were One Nation supporters, of whom 74 per cent expected the Games to go over budget. It also had the largest cohort of not-at-all confident voters, at 50 per cent. Just 15 per cent of One Nation voters expected the Games to come in on budget – 6 per cent were very confident, and 9 per cent were fairly confident. The most optimistic respondents were largely from the left side of politics, with 29 per cent of Labor and Greens voters expressing confidence – the same percentage as uncommitted voters – closely followed by LNP voters on 28 per cent.



Of those confident Labor voters, only 6 per cent were very confident, with the remaining 23 per cent “fairly confident”. A quarter were not very confident, but the single biggest cohort – 30 per cent – had no confidence whatsoever. Among Greens supporters, about 29 per cent were confident the Games would be delivered on or close to budget (6 per cent very confident, 24 per cent fairly confident). However, 60 per cent were not confident, including 34 per cent who were “not at all confident”. Premier David Crisafulli with Tourism Minister Andrew Powell, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and junior Australian Rules players at Brisbane Stadium’s ceremonial sod-turning in June. Cameron Atfield Even among supporters of the governing LNP, sceptics outnumbered believers more than two to one. Twenty-eight per cent expressed confidence the Games would be delivered within budget, but just 3 per cent were “very confident”, while 25 per cent were “fairly confident”. A clear majority, 61 per cent, were not confident, including 29 per cent who were devoid of confidence. In marginal seats, 64 per cent expected costs to soar above $7.1 billion, with 41 per cent “not at all confident” costs could be reined in. Just 23 per cent thought expenditure would stick to budget.



Former premier Campbell Newman, who shared a cabinet table with Crisafulli and Bleijie during his time in the state’s top job, has long warned of potential cost blowouts at the Victoria Park site. Former premier Campbell Newman has been a vocal critic of his former party’s Victoria Park plans. Cameron Atfield Newman said the poll numbers showed “the public seem to get” it would be difficult to deliver the Games on budget. “I find it quite remarkable that self-identified LNP voters don’t believe they’re going to deliver on budget – that’s very telling,” he said. “I would have been horrified when I was in political office, whether it be City Hall or the state, if that was the view of me and my government.



“We’re entitled to expect better, a lot better, and an LNP government should be absolutely committed to being responsible with our dollars.” Newman said Queensland’s recent credit downgrade was a direct result of the government “abandon[ing] any sense of fiscal responsibility” when it came to the Games. Miles also cited the credit downgrade when asked about the poll numbers. “S&P Global warned David Crisafulli that an Olympic blowout would result in a further credit rating downgrade, costing Queenslanders millions of dollars in extra interest payments,” the opposition leader said.



“The premier must release the true cost of the Olympics after promising to be open and transparent before the election.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘It’s wonderful to be back’: Harry and Meghan on first outing since UK return Victoria Ward Updated October 16, 2026 — 5:54am ,first published 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There were selfies and fist bumps, chit-chat about the British weather and group hugs. Meghan said it was “wonderful” to be back in the UK, compared wedding rings with a fan and was given a healing crystal amid armfuls of flowers and balloons. Britain’s Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex in Nottingham on Thursday. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska Prince Harry beamed as he bounced along high-fiving local school children, asking which year they were in and which lessons they were missing. To seasoned royal watchers, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s first joint appearance since returning to Britain was straight out of the Buckingham Palace playbook. This time, however, the couple were on their own manoeuvres, entirely independent of the monarchy.



Whether or not that matters will continue to be a subject of much debate. But to the 150-strong crowd who turned out to greet them on Thursday (UK time) at the Community Recording Studio (CRS), a youth charity in Nottingham, it was irrelevant. Margaret Langdon, 67, from Carlton, said their visit showed “it’s not all about London” and “small cities matter as well”. “I’m a big fan,” she said. “They’ve come to Nottingham to see us so the least we could do is come out and see them.”



Among those whose efforts were rewarded with warm hugs from Harry and Meghan was Irene Hardman, 90, from Roddington, who was brandishing a framed photograph of herself meeting the couple in December 2017. “Oh my gosh how sweet is that” gushed Meghan as she clasped her hands to her mouth. “That was our very first walkabout. Oh my gosh, what a great memory. I remember this day so well, that is so special.” Meghan holds a bouquet of flowers from the crowd. Getty Images The Duke and Duchess of Sussex meet members of the public as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio in Nottingham. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska



The duchess, clad in British designs, including a belt from Marks & Spencer, told another fan: “It’s great to be back.” Related Article Royal family ‘Slipped into depression’: Prince Harry on leaving the UK and grieving for his mother One school boy asked if she had come in a Rolls-Royce, prompting laughter. The less glamorous reality was that the couple were 10 minutes late after getting stuck in traffic following the morning school run. No blue light police escort for these two yet, despite Prince Harry’s ongoing efforts. Inside, there was plenty of inspirational chat and messages of support.



The duchess joined a group of girls from Bluebell Hill Primary School for a “confidence-building and bracelet-making session”, noting that drawing could be “very calming” and revealing that her daughter, Princess Lilibet, 5, loved gymnastics. “I feel most like myself when I’m with my family and also when I cook,” she said. “I love to cook, do you? Experimenting?” Meghan poses for a selfie with a member of the public. AP Photo/Maja Smiejkowska At another table, Meghan discussed the importance of complimenting others. “Sometimes we have to remember to talk to ourselves like we talk to our best friends, really,” she said. “You have to remember to be just as kind to yourself.” Before leaving, she gave each of the girls each a handwritten card inscribed with a motivational quote.



The couple also watched an acting workshop led by actor André Squire. “That was great,” Meghan told the young people involved, asking the group: “Did you find the characters relatable?” As the duke and duchess left, they were accosted by more fans. “We’ve got to go. I’ve got to take her,” a proud Harry said of his wife, as one lady shouted: “You’re lovely, you’re just like your mother.” Later, Trevor Rose, CRS chief executive and co-founder, said Prince Harry, who first visited the studio in 2013, always had a big impact. “For him to want to bring Meg as well and to hear that she wanted to find out more about what we are and what we do is incredible,” he added.



“In the end, there’s a lot of young females in here and they need people who understand them and Meghan has definitely made a point of asking about what they do, what they’re about and what the challenges are. Related Article Epstein fallout Raids on Andrew’s homes in hunt for Epstein ties were unlawful, police admit “To say to them that she’s coming here to meet you – they were speechless. I’ve seen a few tears in peoples’ eyes. That’s what it’s about. I take it as a great stepping stone that they’re still here, we can still reach out to them and they still care.” He added: “They don’t just say they’ll visit every year – they ring up every couple of months, they ask what we’re doing and monitor progress and give us suggestions.” Asked if CRS users look up to the couple, he said: “100 per cent.” The Sussexes later visited the Himmah food bank where Meghan said it felt “really meaningful” to be reunited with some of the women from the Grenfell Hubb Community Kitchen.



The couple washed their hands before helping to prepare lunch, with Harry joking that he had been allocated washing up duties. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub. Getty Images Meghan was warmly welcomed to Himmah Hub. Getty Images The Sussexes concluded their day at Epic Partners, a youth charity Harry has supported for 13 years, where they played pool and decorated cupcakes. Meghan was introduced to the card game Dobble and signed an autograph for 12-year-old Kelsey with the words: “Keep shining! All my best, Meg.”



She later blushed with pride as she watched her husband successfully pot every ball in a pool challenge; declining requests to get involved herself. In the kitchen, however, it was a different story as she rolled up her sleeves to neatly ice some cakes. The duke, on the other hand, took a rather more haphazard approach to the challenge, licking the icing off his fingers. Pete Bewley, the chief executive, said the Sussexes’ support provided “long-term, sustained impact” and said Megan was a “positive role model” for young girls. The Telegraph, London Read more royal news:

World.title: McKinsey leader steps down from charity board days after controversial ‘glass cliff’ comments
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace culture McKinsey leader steps down from charity board days after controversial ‘glass cliff’ comments Colin Kruger October 16, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of McKinsey & Co’s most prominent partners, Sydney-based Chris Bradley, has resigned from his board role at Opportunity International Australia just days after the global consulting giant dumped him a leadership role at its high-profile research arm over online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. “Chris Bradley has offered to resign from the Board of Opportunity International Australia, and we have accepted his resignation,” the charity said in a post on its website on Thursday evening. McKinsey partner Chris Bradley questioned the existence of the glass cliff. Peter Rae “For more than 25 years, Chris has passionately and ably supported our mission in empowering more than 10 million women and their families to lift themselves out of poverty with dignity. “We are grateful for his support of our mission and thank him for his work as a Board member.”



McKinsey removed Bradley from his board role at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit, this week. Bradley remains a board member of Sydney-based conservative think tank, The Centre for Independent Studies and remains a senior partner at McKinsey. The decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth last month with one of the authors of a new book that discusses the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. The term glass cliff was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered chief executive officer jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode.



Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even existed. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. Bradley also wrote in the recent LinkedIn exchange that “we once had a problem of female advancement to CEO, but now we have a new problem that the jobs they get are too hard? Is this actually a thing?” Walking on Broken Glass co-author Julia Carreon. Vanessa Kay Julia Carreon, a former Wall Street executive and co-author of the book Walking on Broken Glass: Navigating the Aftermath of the Glass Ceiling, commented on Bradley’s LinkedIn post, saying: “Aren’t people from McKinsey & Company supposed to know these things?



“I understand you ARE the establishment, but this is surprising.” In response to Carreon, Bradley said: “I am not going to start researching glass cliffs as I don’t think it ranks in the top 1000 problems of the world.” Related Article Updated

Workplace culture McKinsey strips Australian partner of leadership role after ‘glass cliff’ comments Bradley was defended by a senior fellow at the Centre for Independent Studies, Parnell Palme McGuinness, in a column for this publication. “There are a couple of issues here. The first is the slavering cowardice of the management consultancy in responding to the incident by relieving a highly competent leader of a role he was demonstrably succeeding in because of what should have been a reasonably innocuous social media dispute,” she said.



“Another is whether the concept of the glass cliff is based on such rock-solid evidence that it is uncontestable.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Fontaines DC, rock music’s latest saviours, swoon into the apocalypse
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Fontaines DC, rock music’s latest saviours, swoon into the apocalypse Ben Madden Robert Moran and October 16, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Fontaines DC’s new album completes their transition to stadium-rock stars. Fontaines DC, Dopamine Chamber ★★★★ Just two years ago, Fontaines DC’s arena-rock pivot Romance turned them into the prevailing band for middle-aged dads eager to prove they listen to new music. The Irish rockers, once the snarling soldiers of Dublin city, expanded their frantic guitar-attack with synthy atmospherics, Smashing Pumpkins-style orchestration and stadium-ready pomp. If that outlined their heady ambition, then Dopamine Chamber completes the band’s journey from the streets of Dublin to outer space. Opener Six Shot Morning, with its motorik propulsion, ping-ponging lasers and frontman Grian Chatten’s Ian Curtis-esque bark now a calm baritone croon (ever vague, his lyrical snatches lament Silicon Valley, environmental collapse and the folly of resistance), envelops us in the inevitability of cosmic doom.



Fontaines D.C.: From the streets of Dublin to outer space. Ewen Spencer Apparently inspired by the Epstein files and subsequent protests in London, the band’s members have taken to turning up to interviews with dog-eared copies of Brave New World in their coat pockets. Such precious self-seriousness could leave early fans wondering if the DC now stands for “Doing Coldplay”, if not for the fact their songs are still underpinned by their nervy post-punk. On highlights Mimesis, Happy For You and single Marianne, chiming guitars and synth melodies pluck their way from the expansive, reverb-drenched haze. And then there’s the fairly remarkable centrepiece Where Is Gone?, a swooning duet with Spanish icon Rosalia that plays like Lee Hazlewood and Nancy Sinatra reunited at the end of the world, complete with timpani rolls, swelling strings, Western guitars and a stirring melody that’s been living in my head for a week. You’d imagine these guys could have a Bond theme in their future if they believed the future was even a plausible possibility. Robert Moran



Effortless guitar-pop from Newcastle’s all-conquering Vacations. Vacations, Pursuit of Anything ★★★ On their fourth album, Pursuit Of Anything, all-conquering Newcastle band Vacations sound more settled than ever. That’s despite the backdrop of the album’s creation, with various members settling down and/or relocating to various parts of the world. It’s enough to throw any group off their axis, but that’s not the case here. The album finds lead singer Campbell Burns musing on getting older, with these thoughts pressed up against beds of warm, lush guitar-pop. Pursuit of Anything doesn’t demand anything of the listener except to absorb it. Songs such as Yesterday and I See Myself In You sound utterly effortless, with the band totally in sync.



It might be the biggest issue with the album. In asking almost nothing of the listener, Burns’ laconic vocal delivery risks masking his strong lyricism. On opening track Congratulations, he sings “Scared to death/As the world stands still/Time marches on/When you don’t have the will” – but rather than entering with a bang, the band winds up slowly, like awaking from a deep slumber. Pursuit of Anything proves Vacations have mastered the art of swaying guitar-pop. However, at times, it all threatens to wash into itself. Ben Madden Want more music stories and reviews? World.title: Migrant advocacy group says NZ First has adopted its policy
World.content:
Audio player for " Migrant group backs Peters' proposed visa changes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1940991%2Fmigrant-advocacy-group-says-nz-first-has-adopted-its-policy

Migrant group backs Peters' proposed visa changes Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The Migrant Workers Association is welcoming a policy change by New Zealand First, which echoes proposals from pro-migrant advocates for many years.

New Zealand First says migrants would not be tied to an employer under a proposed replacement to the accredited employer work visa.

The Migrant Workers Association says that's a good first step, as it allows workers to more easily move on from exploitative jobs.

But it also questioned the motivation behind the policy given recent remarks by party leader Winston Peters and deputy Shane Jones about Indian and Chinese migrants, which had been labelled racist.

Association president Anu Kaloti said on the surface, it seemed like an improvement on the status quo, and it was something it had called for in previous public consultations.

"We were also proposing similar, that the bottom line basically is that any kind of bondage must stop - tying migrant workers to single employers is where most of the exploitation is happening," she said.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ/Nick Monro

But if it was introduced, it might be too little, too late, she said, as exploitation had become rampant in recent times and now increasingly included human trafficking and money-laundering.

"We also keep suggesting that unions, maybe they should be given a greater role to play here. I know when I say mandatory unionisation of migrant workers, most people probably get very nervous when I use those two words, but I think that needs to be trialled."

Kaloti said while NZ First's policy was "possibly better than the current situation", it would not reverse some voters' unhappiness with Peters' other views.

"Unless Winston, Shane Jones, and generally New Zealand First address their racism and xenophobia, announcements like this are not really going to pacify any of the migrants. It just seems, it just sounds a bit rich coming from them."

Struggling businesses

Immigration adviser Arunima Dhingra said the immigration system could not be overhauled every election cycle, as businesses, advisers and migrants needed certainty about processes.

"It would be like putting an axe through the heart of the immigration system. It is one of the core temporary visa policies. And this is what New Zealand employers have taken many, many years to get used to. And they've introduced systems in their businesses to be compliant with immigration.

"There are so many layers within the instructions and the policies and the processes and you cannot responsibly propose dismantling an entire framework without understanding those intricacies and identifying precisely where the problems have been."

Immigration adviser Arunima Dhingra. RNZ / Liu Chen

The current accredited employer work visa framework had many of the safeguards New Zealand First was calling for, she said, including labour market testing.

"When an employer has been through a lot of steps to actually hire a migrant worker, then to decouple the employer from that person (the migrant) is potentially disadvantaging the employer. I think there's a real clear balancing act here. It's not just about protecting that individual person, but also protecting and looking after New Zealand businesses."

NZ not a 'labour-hire company'

New Zealand First has not responded to requests for comment, either about the policy rationale, or its similarity to proposals put forward by pro-migration supporters.

Peters wants work visas to be tied to migrants' occupation and region instead of a specific business.

At a public meeting announcing the proposal, he said the current work visa was being used as a routine recruitment channel, a "back door" to bring in friends and family, or a way of making money by exploiting staff.

"We are a country with an immigration system, not an international labour-hire agency with a flag," he told a Dunedin public meeting.

"The policy will put New Zealand workers first, lift confidence in the immigration system, protect migrant workers from exploitation, and preserve a clear route for employers who genuinely cannot find critical skills here."

World.title: Kiwis lose Kalyn Ponga to injury in major setback for Kiwis after loss to Australia
World.content:
Audio player for " Sports update " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/sport/1944909%2Fkiwis-lose-kalyn-ponga-to-injury-in-major-setback-for-kiwis-after-loss-to-australia

The Kiwis could be without fullback Kalyn Ponga for the rest of the Rugby League World Cup after he suffered an injury in the opening game in Sydney.

Ponga eventually left the field with a suspected broken arm in the Kiwis 24-22 loss to Australia.

He scored two of the Kiwi's three tries and then bravely battled on for 20 minutes with the suspected fracture, before being forced to leave the field late in the game.

"Yeh he's a tough bugger," Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris said afterwards. "Obviously a lot of pride in the black and white jersey and he didn't want to let his team mates down."

Ponga was playing his first game for New Zealand after a change in the international eligibility rules made him available for selection for the World Cup.

He was one of the NRL's top players this season helping Newcastle to the grand final.

"He did an outstanding job, a freakish player but he's also one of those tough players and feeling for him right now but fingers crossed," Fisher-Harris said.

The Kiwis next game is against Cook Islands on October 25, while the final is four weeks away.

World.title: How much does it cost to run an election?
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1940993%2Fhow-much-does-it-cost-to-run-an-election

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

How much does it cost to run an election?

This year, the answer is about $180 million.

Putting aside the cost to candidates and political parties to run their campaigns, which runs to millions of dollars, the Electoral Commission has given a breakdown of what it expects to spend getting New Zealanders to the polls this year.

It said the biggest costs were the temporary workforce employed for the election, then property, paper, printing and postage. "These are all things we need to set up and run an election where all New Zealanders have the opportunity to enrol and vote."

It said this year there would be 22,000 temporary staff, 2321 election day voting places and nine million voting papers printed.

It has budgeted $94.7m for staff costs, $17.9m for communications, $11.6m for IT, $3.1m for travel and catering, $23.1m for property costs and $25.5m for printing and post. Other costs come in at just under $6m.

University of Otago professor Andrew Geddis said the Electoral Commission had to put in a request to the Minister of Justice outlining what funding it expected to need to run the election.

"The physical getting of votes and the associated advertising around it to tell people there is an election coming up and you've got an obligation to vote.

"In the end it is up to the minister to decide whether or not to take that bid into the budget-setting process to the Ministerof Finance, and say 'this is what I am going to need in order to fund the election properly' and the Minister of Finance to then go 'yep, okay, I'm going to include that in the Budget'. There is no statutory formula, or anything like that."

He said the 90 percent enrolment had been steady over the years and turnout in the high 70s was good by international standards.

Andrew Geddis is a law professor at University of Otago. Supplied

But he said the Electoral Commission was facing a bigger problem in how much of its interaction with voters happened through the post.

"That is becoming more and more of a problem because the postal service has just started to fall apart. The Electoral Commission was given some money in the most recent Budgets … to try to start modernising everything and do work to try to bring more of those enrolment services online, in recognition that the postal service just isn't going to manage in the future."

This year, many voters will get their Easy Vote cards via email rather than post.

He said ultimately how much the commission was given to run the election was up to the government. There was a case that went to the Court of Appeal in the mid-1990s regarding the Māori electoral option, where it was argued the government wasn't doing enough to publicise the Māori roll option.

"The Court of Appeal said the government has provided a sum of money and the government has met its obligations. The Court of Appeal also said that there is a implied duty on central government to make sure that essentially the electoral system is properly funded, and that people are appropriately told about their democratic rights and so on ... but it's up to the government to put a dollar figure on it.

"You could see a world in which if a future government ever did try to essentially starve the electoral system, you could use that case to go to court and get a court to order the government to put more money into the system."

He said while all political parties had a strong interest in how the system worked, he was not aware of any party ever having claimed the government was not doing enough to fund elections.

"Whatever concerns we might have about a government not appropriately funding democracy, it's the sort of thing that if it was happening you could imagine the opposition parties being very vocal about it. The fact they haven't been is perhaps an indication that on this one the government is [doing] what it should."

Victoria University associate professor Lara Greaves said the amount the Electoral Commission was given should at least increase with inflation each election and potentially jump further because of demographic changes.

Victoria University associate professor Lara Greaves. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

"We have got more ethnically diverse populations and those populations have relationships to government where they might need a different way of being reached and so that costs money."

She said the post was a problem. "The other thing is that people don't necessarily have their physical addresses up-to-date anymore as much.

"So one of the things in the electoral law changes in this term were not only to make it so people couldn't enrol in the advance voting period, but they also did change some of the provisions to allow for data matching across agencies to be able to manually update addresses, to enrol people automatically ... they haven't really made an investment in that at this point.

"That actually needs quite a decent chunk of IT investment to be able to link those data up."

She said it had been suggested a live digital roll mark-off would speed up the vote count but that would also require significant investment.

She said there was not enough money being made available for the process.

"What I would do if I I wanted to downgrade our democracy, if I wanted to let it erode a bit would be not fund at least at inflation but also not fund those kinds of projects that update the system, take it out of the 1950s which has been what's been needed for quite some time."

World.title: Mother heartbroken toddler's cancer treatment delayed by Starship Hospital staff shortages
World.content:
Audio player for " Mother speaks out after son's cancer treatment is delayed " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/1942123%2Fmother-heartbroken-toddler-s-cancer-treatment-delayed-by-starship-hospital-staff-shortages

Mother speaks out after son's cancer treatment is delayed Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The mother of a toddler whose cancer treatment was delayed due to staff shortages at Starship Hospital says often her son was screaming and writhing in pain while they tried to get help from a nurse.

She said she was heartbroken and doubted the health minister's assurances the jobs were being recruited for.

Some chemotherapy and bone marrow treatments have been delayed at the children's hospital for up to seven days due to lack of staff.

Tanya Lapu'aho's two-and-a-half year old son Cillian was diagnosed in January with high-risk neuroblastoma.

He's since had multiple stays at Starship for rounds of chemotherapy and two bone marrow transplants, and is moving on to radiation and immunotherapy.

Lapu'aho said timing is everything with cancer treatment - but her son's second bone marrow transplant was delayed at least a week because there were not enough specialist nurses to carry out the treatment.

She said babies were bearing the brunt of delays.

Lapu'aho said and her son had been in Starship Hospital many times with the two longest stays lasting just over a month and it was obvious that the nursing staff were under a huge amount of pressure.

Initially they thought delays to her son's surgery were for medical reasons but they were then told it was due to staffing shortages, she said.

"On a day to day basis it looked like our son screaming and writhing in pain and us calling for our nurse and her wanting to come straight away but her not being able to because she had too many other things to do - you know duties to carry out, other patients to take care of - to the point where it was taking on average about 20 minutes, half an hour on a really busy day for a nurse to come to the room and respond to you pressing the nurse call button.

"And most of the time we were pressing that button for pain relief because our boy is in so much pain from the cancer, from the chemo, from everything."

She said it was evident that the pain was severe because when they were finally able to get help her son was put on oxycodone and ketamine.

Lapu'aho's son had to wait for chemotherapy lines to be changed and medication to be administered, and said available nurses would apologise because they were not yet qualified for those tasks.

Once her son's pain medication ran out completely and there was no nurse available to top it up again, she said.

It took the nurse 24 minutes to come to change the pain pump containing the medicine which had run out, she said.

"Another time it took over half an hour for the nurse to get someone from the pain relief team to come and have a look at upping the dose because it wasn't enough to kill the pain for Cillian.

"He's screaming, we can't put him down, he's writhing you know, like he's only two years old, the cancer feels like fire inside his bones, it's so unfair that that guilt and responsibility gets put on the nurses, you know they keep apologising 'I'm so sorry, we're just so short staffed' and we know it's not their problem and we feel horrible that they even feel that it is."

She said it was obvious that there were not enough nurses to do the work.

"When you take a step out of your hospital room and look at the ward there's just not that many nurses and the ones that are there, they're running around working as hard as they can and it just feels like a hopeless and helpless situation really."

Despite the fact that her son had a very high risk diagnosis he is now in complete remission "and that's only thanks to the amazing medical professionals that we have access to at Starship Hospital, it's so unfair what's happening to them" she said.

Tanya with her young son in hospital. Supplied

Lapu'aho said staff were overworked and under-resourced, and a charge nurse had told her there was a hiring freeze.

Health Minister Simeon Brown insisted all eight vacant paediatric haematology/oncology roles had been filled or recruited for.

Health NZ since confirmed it would be three months before the ward was fully staffed, with seven nurses due to start over that period.

A spokesperson in Brown's office denied any hiring freeze and said the vacancies were the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement.

But Lapu'aho said those could be planned for months in advance.

She said it was tough trying to advocate for her child because there was nothing the nurses themselves could do about the shortage.

Other parents were scared about complaining because they did not want to risk receiving poor care, Lapu'aho said.

Tanya says babies are bearing the brunt of delays. Supplied

Nurses Organisation says better workforce planning needed

Nurses Organisation Kaiwhakahaere Kerri Nuku told Morning Report the situation was not a surprise as there had been nursing workforce shortages for years.

"We have known that this ward has been understaffed for months, we should have had strategies in place long before we were needing to compromise the care of young children."

Audio player for " Nurses Organisation responds to Starship treatment delays " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/1942123%2Fmother-heartbroken-toddler-s-cancer-treatment-delayed-by-starship-hospital-staff-shortages

Nurses Organisation responds to Starship treatment delays Morning Report Download MP3 6m

There may be activity now to recruit because of the staffing crisis, but it should never have been that way, she said.

The Tertiary Education Commission has told organisations to limit the number of nurses it trains next year due to a shortage of student nursing placement spots.

"It's all about workforce and evolving around the workforce planning," she said.

"This is not the solution to reduce the amount of nurses that you are putting through because we certainly are having shortages in the workforce already. What it does mean potentially is that we look to internationally qualified nurses... to fill gaps as experienced nurses."

New Zealand should be training recruiting and its own domestic supply of nurses and having to recruit overseas once again indicated a failure of planning, she said.

She said there should be enough room for the increased number of nursing enrolments and the required placements.

"If we had a fully functioning system that is well staffed then absolutely we should be able to accommodate the students and their experience for placements.

World.title: Why is the price of petrol rising while oil prices are falling?
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1940990%2Fwhy-is-the-price-of-petrol-rising-while-oil-prices-are-falling

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

Why is the price of petrol at the pump going up even while the crude oil price falls?

The price of Dubai crude oil in New Zealand dollars has fallen from $210 a barrel mid-September to $192.

At the same time, the weekly adjusted retail fuel price of petrol has increased from about $3.15 to more than $3.50 a litre, according to Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment data.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said MBIE's estimates also suggested that over the past few weeks, importer costs had been rising, reflecting a divergence between oil prices and refined output prices.

"We saw a similar, more pronounced, example in March and April this year, when diesel prices surged far more than crude prices would have implied.

"It might also be that Dubai oil prices are currently not the best indicator of what is flowing through into our retail operations, given the disruption to supply from the Middle East, which has meant that Asian refineries have been forced to source oil from elsewhere."

He said there seemed to have been a lag between international oil prices rising and petrol pump prices rising.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold agreed there were a few reasons that the prices might have diverged.

"We don't use Dubai crude to give us the best indication. We use Singapore Mogas, which I realise sounds like gobbledygook but basically Mogas is essentially the wholesale version of petrol. So when they distill oil into different things, one of the things they get is called Mogas, which is petrol, and Gasoil, which is diesel."

He said there could be situations where the diesel price went up but Mogas did not, and both could work differently to the price of crude oil.

He said there was also usually a lag effect between oil prices and Mogas moving and the retail price that drivers paid changing.

"It takes two or three weeks before whatever's happening in the wholesale marekts and the exchange rate will flow through to what you see at the pump.

"I do half expect that there might be a fall in petrol prices coming, or at least some kind of stabilisation because I have noticed that some of these refined fuel prices have fallen back a bit in the last week or so. The exchange rate is still quite low but it isn't really moving … so that's not putting any additional pressure on."

He said the wholesale price of Mogas had stabilised over the last couple of weeks and the exchange rate was about the same, so there was no additional pressure going on fuel prices.

But he said there was also not a lot of evidence that they should fall much, either.

"I suspect that if the Dubai price is falling it may be something a bit more specific to Dubai itself."

He said Middle East companies had also been offering discounts for crude oil because they wanted people to pick it up and transport it out of the region. "That's quite expensive right now because the Iranians are shooting at people. You could understand how there might be some kind of additional transportation costs associated with that."

World.title: 30,000 people in Wellington region fail to pay first Tiaki Wai water bill
World.content:
Audio player for " Unpaid Tiaki Wai bills add to Wellington water price debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions/1942429%2F30-000-people-in-wellington-region-fail-to-pay-first-tiaki-wai-water-bill

Unpaid Tiaki Wai bills add to Wellington water price debate Morning Report Download MP3 4m

More than 30,000 people across the Wellington region have not paid their first Tiaki Wai bill, with the second round due to arrive soon.

Second bills from the water agency will be sent to Wellington, Lower and Upper Hutt and Porirua residents and businesses from late October.

They come as debate ramps up over whether Tiaki Wai's prices should be capped, and as Wellingtonians stare down a future of price increases which a budget advisor says is causing people in the community deep stress.

Numbers revealed to RNZ show 30,116 residential and commercial customers haven't paid bills for the first quarter yet - 18.5 percent of all accounts.

It shows $21 million in total invoiced bills for the first quarter has not yet been paid.

Chief executive Michael Brewster said Tiaki Wai had received $89.5m of the $110.5m it had invoiced. An extra $3.6m had been paid by people ahead of new bills coming.

Payments had been received from 82.2 percent of residential accounts, 71.2 percent of business accounts, and 76.4 percent of non-profit, community and government organisations, he said.

Brewster said the agency wasn't imposing fines yet on people who hadn't paid, though it was vital the company collected the money needed to fix ageing water networks.

A burst pipe on Willeston Street in Wellington's CBD in June this year. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In a briefing to city councillors this week, Tiaki Wai board chair Will Peet said there had been some initial "teething issues" for payments which he expected to settle in time, and those struggling could access the agency's hardship policy.

"Our message to anybody is that if you can't pay, if you've got issues, the sooner you get in touch with us the better we will be able to do that."

In a written response to RNZ, Tiaki Wai said nearly 500 customers spoke to the agency about financial hardship, and nearly 50 customers owing nearly $45,000 collectively had formally entered hardship arrangements.

Tiaki Wai said it did not know how many people were simply refusing to pay their bill in the future.

In comparison, Wellington City Council said it had collected about 95 percent of its rates over the same period - with around $10m outstanding.

Wellingtonian's water bills under Tiaki Wai are increasing by about 13.3 percent this year, in an average total annual bill of $2390.

Forecasts of bills reaching over $6000 per year in a decade has shocked some residents, prompting backlash and protests against the agency in August.

Peet said warned there would be consequences if people were opting out in protest.

"There is a very small group of people who have decided they don't want to pay, I can't see cutting people off as a viable thing.

"Debt collection is probably the next... that would be the step."

Wellington has a history of burst pipes and reoccurring leaks. Here a burst water main flooded a major Wellington street in August 2024. RNZ / REECE BAKER

Christine Tawhara, a budget advisor in Canon's Creek, said the threat of rising bills was worrying renters coming into the Porirua Whānau Centre.

"Their landlords are looking at a rent increase and that will be to cover the water rates, and the tenant knows that.

"It's real hard for them because then they're going to have to chop back on something if there's a rent increase ... and it's always food, it's always food they chop back on."

Tawhara said the pensioners she was seeing could pay this year's increase, but were stressed about the severity of future bills.

They were currently already avoiding repairs on their house to keep bills down, Tawhara said.

Commerce Commission chairperson John Small told Nine to Noon on Thursday Tiaki Wai's costs - including the debt it had inherited, and the extent of faulty infrastructure it needed to fix - far exceeded the money it currently collected from Wellingtonians.

He was asked whether the company was "technically insolvent".

"I wouldn't say that no, but I do know the directors had that issue in mind before the company was constituted on the 1st of July," Small replied.

"It's ultimately their job to maintain a solvent enterprise."

Small said the commission was imposing extra performance rules to monitor Tiaki Wai was making progress on its plans to upgrade or fix infrastructure.

But he said it would not cap bills right now.

"Right or wrong, affordability is not something that is within our mandate. What our mandate is, is to make sure that the assets are being managed properly and that prices are not out of line with costs."

Wellington mayor Andrew Little said the pressure would now increase on the government to fix its local water done well policy as other regions start to receive their own "extraordinary" price rise projections.

Local government minister Simon Watts recently told RNZ the government had imposed the stronger oversight by the Commerce Commission, giving ratepayers a better picture of performance and applying independent scrutiny.

"Wellington's water infrastructure problems are well known and have built up over decades, and while local Water Done Well has increased the long term financial stability of Wellington's water, the position they've started from has meant the overall costs Wellington ratepayers face have been higher than many other entities stood up through the scheme, some of which have actually reduced expected water charges from what they predicted last year."

World.title: Hobart stadium facing 'cost pressures' as price tag remains unclear
World.content:
The head of the government body tasked with delivering a new stadium in Hobart has acknowledged that "cost pressures" could impact the final price tag of the project.

The construction of a 23,000-seat, roofed stadium is a key requirement for the entry of the Tasmania Devils into the AFL and AFLW competitions in 2028.

The project is currently budgeted at $1.13 billion, but that estimate is now more than a year old.

Builder chosen for Hobart's stadium The company that built a 30,000-seat arena in Christchurch, New Zealand, has been selected to construct Hobart's new roofed stadium.

Since then, construction costs have increased significantly because of the war in the Middle East.

Macquarie Point Development Corporation chief executive Anne Beach said further work would now be done to finalise the cost before the contract is signed by the end of the year.

"Through this next stage an important part of that is moving from the target construction sum to actually locking down the lump sum that will go into the contract," Ms Beach said.

"The stage two process will end in around mid-November.

" We'll then go through an assessment, and that's when we'll be coming back to government to discuss that cost. "

Loading...

On Thursday, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder of the stadium.

Ms Beach said "cost pressures" would play a part in the outcome.

"We'll need to consider, as we go through this process, cost pressures that are in the market and the cost to build as at today.

"We'll be continuing to analyse that, and we'll provide an update once we can after stage two."

At a press conference, Jeremy Rockliff did not take up the chance to promise Tasmania's input to the stadium would be limited to $875 million. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the final cost would be publicly revealed shortly before the contract is signed.

But when asked whether he could promise the state's input would be limited to $875 million, as previously flagged, he repeatedly skirted the question.

"We're working through a very rigorous process," Mr Rockliff said.

"We're at stage one, and we're working through and continuing that to get to stage two and, of course, signing the contract.

" And I'm not going to detail costs — they are being, they continue to be, worked through. "

Work is being done at the Macquarie Point site in preparation for the stadium construction. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Cost will be 'quite north' of $1.13b, MLC says

The state government's $875 million funding cap was part of its agreement with independent MLC Bec Thomas, who voted in favour of the development in December last year.

As part of that agreement, any further funds required to build the stadium would either be clawed back via "value management", a reduction in scope, or be sought from either the federal government, AFL or Cricket Australia.

The Greens remain sceptical the stadium can be built within the current funding envelope.

"We don't trust the premier and his commitment to stick to $875 million," Greens MP Vica Bayley said.

"That's why it's incumbent upon him to be transparent about where the additional money is going to come from and how parliament is going to be involved."

Vica Bayley says the state government needs to be transparent about where extra funds could come from. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Independent MLC Meg Webb said it would be "naïve" to think the cost of building the stadium won't be more than envisaged last year.

"I think all of us can look at the world's events since then, can look at other costs that have clearly gone up and imagine that now we're looking at a full cost for this stadium that's somewhere quite north of $1.13 billion."

She urged the government to disclose the cost to parliament before the contract is signed.

"We know that Tasmanians would like there to be transparency around that cost and now that a builder has been announced, there's no reason for the state government not to come clean and be really open and transparent and give us the expected full cost of the stadium."

Meg Webb says it's clear the full cost of the stadium will be far more than the current $1.13 billion figure. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Expert says Middle East conflict likely 'having impacts'

Kirr Parr is a construction industry advocate and senior fellow at the University of Melbourne Law School who lectures in the delivery of major projects.

She said it was common for large-scale construction projects to go over budget because of external factors and long timeframes that can significantly affect costs.

"An external war that drives up prices that's happened since you did your budget won't have been factored into that original budget," Ms Parr said.

"So, it's exactly the kind of external factor that major projects are exposed to and it likely is having impacts on the budget.

" The exact nature of how it all plays out over the next three or four years is unknown. "

BESIX Watpac built Christchurch's new 30,000-seat stadium at a cost of just over $530 million. (Supplied: One New Zealand)

Ms Parr saidthe key was to limit the scale of any potential cost overruns through good management.

"It's the importance of working very, very hard on your projects to resolve problems as early as possible and not allowing them to escalate," she said.

"The importance of experts, people who have experience on major projects."

The stadium is due for completion by the end of 2030.

World.title: How the joy of Pride is 'a form of resistance' against queer discrimination
World.content:
GWS player Tilly Lucas-Rodd says AFLW Pride Round is important to keep celebrating and championing while harmful attitudes towards queer people persist.

Lucas-Rodd, who is non-binary, said the joy and pride of the moment is an important counter to the discrimination queer people can still face in sport.

"I feel like we were getting to a place of more acceptance and now we're going backwards, and there's more discrimination, and more homophobia, and transphobia," Lucas-Rodd told ABC Sport.

First current AFLW player undergoes gender affirming top surgery Over the AFLW off-season, Hawthorn's Tilly Lucas-Rodd underwent top surgery, a gender-affirming procedure that involves the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

They said this is evident particularly if you look at comment sections online that contain discriminatory rhetoric towards queer people, including at times AFLW posts on social media.

"People are coming out of the woodwork and they're proud and happy to have these opinions, and they think it's okay, which is why I think it's so important that we still have Pride round, and show up and represent community and challenge these dangerous beliefs with joy," they said.

"There's a time and place to be reflective on the harm and the negative parts in terms of like the discrimination we face and truly reflect on that and sit in that and be like 'this is not okay'.

"But there's also a time to use joy and pride and celebration as a form of resistance."

They have seen the impact representation can have on lives.

Last year, Lucas-Rodd went public with having had gender affirming chest surgery in an exclusive with the ABC Sport.

The top surgery was a procedure that involved the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd in the Pride guernsey that GWS will wear for the club's home game during Pride round. (Supplied: GWS Giants)

They received many messages from people after the story came out, with people sharing it had opened up conversations with family members, and gave a better understanding of the gender diverse and trans experience.

"A parent at my school that I taught at was like, 'You being so visible shows that for young trans (and) gender diverse kids you can be successful, because they're often so hard on themselves and they don't see a future that's bright,'" they said.

"They see hardship, they see discrimination, they see transphobia as their future, but then they see someone being successful, being championed, being celebrated publicly, and they could see a way forward for themselves.

This year, making Pride round even more special for Lucas-Rodd, is that it coincides with their 100th game.

Over the past 11 seasons, Lucas-Rodd has played for four different clubs, including Carlton (2017-2020), St Kilda (2020-2022), Hawthorn (2022-2025) and now GWS.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd was an inaugural player for Carlton. (Getty: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

"It is so funny," Lucas-Rodd laughed, noting in particular the shaved sides and bun years at Carlton. "There's been so many eras.

"I've changed completely as a person and it was guided by AFLW. All I've ever known (as an adult) is AFLW and all I've ever really been overly passionate about in my 20s is AFLW," they said.

The environments of the league helped shape them, which again they say, is why Pride round is so important because the welcoming rooms they've been in aren't the same for everyone in sport.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd moved from Hawthorn to GWS ahead of the 2026 season. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

They did a video with men's GWS player Tom Green earlier this week for the club's channel for Pride round, where he asked Lucas-Rodd if they ever struggle with using their platform.

It made them reflect on how they use their social media accounts — quite often championing trans and gender diverse people playing sport and playing footy — and how it has created a two-way dialogue with more people in the community.

"When I speak to people or hear from people's actual lived experience in community sports, it's not safe," they said.

"And I was like, that's something I've only ever learned through more conversations around Pride round."

AFLW Pride Round The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch wants to see the power of the AFLW's dedicated Pride Round harnessed and extended across the whole code.

Lucas-Rodd sometimes thinks, "Oh, this is probably getting old, people are probably bored of it", when they speak about their LGBTQ+ experience.

"But then I have someone message me being like, 'Oh, my parents read this, they heard this, they watched your video, and that made the conversation easy for me.'

"And it takes you back to that's why it's so important that we still have Pride round.

"That's why it's so important that we have visibility and representation and keep talking about it over and over again because it helps make other people's lives easier out there in community."

World.title: Quick hits: Walsh vomits after try, Ponga shines then suffers in epic duel
World.content:
Australia and New Zealand have set a high standard for the 17th edition of the Rugby League World Cup, opening the 2026 tournament with an all-time classic.

Young Kiwi Casey McLean defied gravity, and debutant Aussie Jack Bostock won the match for the Kangaroos,

Meanwhile, a vomiting Reece Walsh and a broken-armed Kalyn Ponga produced one of the great fullback duels.

Here are the quick hits from the opening match.

1. McLean defies gravity in all-time finish

Casey McLean is Kiwi superman.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

After a towering bomb from Jahrome Hughes was batted back by Ronaldo Mulitalo, Isaiah Papali'i threw what could best be described as a one-handed chuck, collected by McLean on the blind side.

With no space to work in, and Kangaroos halfback Mitchell Moses smothering him while directing him towards touch, McLean went airborne.

Somehow, seemingly in slow motion, as his body hovered horizontally over the sideline, McLean grounded the ball in the corner.

ABC Sport expert commentator Luke Lewis described it as "one of the best finishes you will see in this game."

And just four minutes into this World Cup, a contender for try of the tournament was born.

2. Long-range intercepts put Kangaroos on top

The Kiwis dominated the first half at the Sydney Football Stadium.

The New Zealanders had 59 per cent of the ball, made 300 more metres running, and had 66 fewer tackles.

But they went into the break level after the Kangaroos scored two 90-metre intercept tries.

The first Kangaroos score came from debutant Jack Bostock, who rushed out of the defensive line to grab a looping pass by Kiwi halfback Jahrome Hughes.

If that ball got over his head, it would have been a try for the Kiwis. But the Australian winger took the ball cleanly, broke the grasp of a Kiwi, and ran for the goal-line.

Incredibly, an almost identical play happened for Australia's other winger Tom Trbojevic on the other side of the field.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean gave a pass meant for his unmarked winger, but Trbojevic stuck his arm in the way and caught the footy.

Trbojevic then showed the speed he was known for at the start of his career, beating the cover tackle attempt of Kodi Nikorima and streaking away.

3. After first half denial, Ponga breathes fire

The duel of the opposing fullbacks was one of the most hyped heading into this game, featuring two of the most electric talents in the game.

Kalyn Ponga was a standout for the Kiwis, before leaving the game with a suspected broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

And it produced everything fans could hope for.

Kiwis' custodian Kalyn Ponga came into the tournament off the back of a breathtaking season for the Knights, while the Kangaroos' number one Reece Walsh was considered a somewhat controversial selection, preferred over the Roosters' Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco.

After being kept relatively quiet for most of the first half, Ponga burst to life on the left, dancing, darting, and taunting the Kangaroos.

He slipped past Staggs and tried to sidestep Walsh, who produced a scintillating try-saver, bundling Ponga into touch.

It was one for the purists, in shades of Scott Sattler's tackle on Toddy Byrne in the 2003 NRL grand final.

Ponga shook it off after the break, and the Kiwis debutant was on the end of some slick passing from the Kiwis for a straightforward finish for his first try.

His second was better, a 40-metre vintage Ponga effort.

With his shorts pulled halfway down his legs, he still managed to power past Walsh with a classic step, sending the sizeable Kiwi contingent in Sydney into delirium.

4. Walsh plunders then chunders, Ponga goes off

The Kangaroos were staring down a rare defeat to their arch-rivals in this arena, when Walsh responded to his opposite number's heroics, and left the Kiwis in his dust.

Reece Walsh struggled to re-gain his composure after scoring his try. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Deep in their own half and trailing by six, Bostock slipped a clever flick pass behind his back, and the Broncos superstar swooped.

He swerved past defenders, running 60 metres to go over in the corner.

But he gave everything in the effort, and as he prepared to take the conversion, he was interrupted by his exhaustion.

He threw up and was unable to take the kick, with Lattrell Mitchell stepping up instead.

Walsh continued to dry retch, and looked completely spent. But he managed to keep it together (and inside) to stay on the field and see out the game.

But it was a horrible end to the game for Ponga; his night ended early with a suspected broken arm — a huge blow for the Kiwis' title hopes.

Ponga had nursed his left arm after a tackle on Cam Munster early in the second half.

He stayed out there, but appeared to hit his arm again in a collision with teammate Hughes in an attempt to tackle Walsh.

5. Bostock hat trick

Jack Bostock had already made his mark on international rugby league with his 90-metre intercept try in the first half.

But he was not done scoring, and it proved a match-winning performance.

His second try came in the 57th minute, with the Aussies trailing by six points.

Kangaroos five-eighth Cam Munster put up a pinpoint kick for Bostock to chase.

The Australian went up against his Dolphins teammate Jamayne Isaako, beat him in the air, and scored a fantastic try to help level the scores.

But Bostock had an even better effort to win the game.

Down by two with less than four minutes to play, it was Munster again who put up a high kick for Bostock to chase.

Isaako was in a much better position this time, and appeared to have caught the footy.

But Bostock ripped the ball out of the Kiwi's arms, in turn, ripping the game away from New Zealand.

World.title: A-League star in fiery exchange with reporter over suspension loophole
World.content:
Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.

Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.

Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.

That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.

The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.

In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".

Loading Instagram content

"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.

"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"

Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.

"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.

"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.

"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."

Auckland FC are the reigning A-League Men champions. (Getty Images: New Zealand Herald/Alyse Wright)

The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.

"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.

An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.

"You know what football's like in this country, mate? We f***ing work hard to get it good. You bring it down with shit like that," Cosgrove said, prompting a chuckle from the reporter.

"What are you laughing for? We'll just f*** you off. You won't get back here again."

In a podcast episode posted on Tuesday, Cosgrove said he was relieved when news of the rule's workaround became public so he could "finally stop lying about it".

"It was a poor challenge in oppressive heat and late in the game, but the two-game suspension was a little bit harsh," he told The Unused Subs podcast.

"We were trying to get that reduced, and the power of lawyers and legal teams these days, they managed to find a way to sign me up with the Auckland reserves."

The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday, before an away trip to face Western Sydney Wanderers on October 24.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Aussies win all-time World Cup classic, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm
World.content:
Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

The Kiwis, trying to inflict a first home defeat on the Kangaroos in 11 years, dominated much of the game but a trio of long-range tries, including a pair of 90-metre intercepts, lifted Australia to a stunning win.

Kiwi fullback Kalyn Ponga, playing his first match for New Zealand, suffered a suspected broken arm after starring with two second-half tries and putting the Kiwis on the verge of victory.

But Bostock's three-try performance, including the match-winner with less than four minutes to play, sunk the Kiwis.

The Kangaroos have injury concerns of their own, with halfback Mitchell Moses limping off just moments into the second half.

World.title: Wallabies show faith in rookie fly half for final All Blacks Test
World.content:
Declan Meredith will start at fly half against the All Blacks for just the fourth time in his young Test career, as the Wallabies make changes for Saturday's final Bledisloe Cup clash at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Meredith, who made his Test debut against France in July, replaces Ben Donaldson in the number 10 jersey.

Donaldson was ruled out with a minor upper leg injury in the wake of the 50-19 thrashing dished out by the All Blacks at Auckland's Eden Park last Saturday night.

Back-up fly half Harry McLaughlin-Phillips will make his Test debut if he comes on as a reserve in Sydney.

He is joined on the bench by reserve scrum half Kalani Thomas, who is yet to play a Bledisloe Cup Test.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

It will be a tough initiation for Meredith, although he will be playing outside Brumbies teammate and scrum half, Ryan Lonergan.

The 27-year-old got his first taste of playing the All Blacks after coming on as a reserve at Eden Park last weekend.

Meanwhile, the Wallabies have moved Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres.

He started on the wing in the Wallabies' past two Tests, but the absence of Len Ikitau (concussion) forced Wallabies coach Les Kiss to shift the ex-NRL star back to the midfield.

He will partner Isaac Henry, who switches from outside to inside centre, while Harry Potter will start on the wing.

Ikitau is a massive loss for the Wallabies, who are also missing Hunter Paisami (suspension) from their midfield options.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted back to the centres for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Elsewhere in the Wallabies' match-day squad, former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead prop, alongside hooker Josh Nasser.

Ross replaces Angus Bell, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa (rested) made way for Nasser.

Hooker Billy Pollard, lock Josh Canham, openside flanker Carlo Tizzano and utility back Filipo Daugunu have returned to the Wallabies' squad as reserves.

Wallaroos lose star for historic 'quadruple header' The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

"We got a clear picture last weekend of where we need to be better," Kiss said in a Rugby Australia statement.

"We've said all along we'll continue to work hard and grow our game, and the squad has been impressive in the way they have prepared this week."

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who retained his place alongside Jeremy Williams in the second row, will appear in his 50th Test.

The Bledisloe Cup Test will cap off a historic "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos play Scotland earlier in the day, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams meet New Zealand and Fiji respectively.

It is the first time all four national teams have featured on the same match-day schedule.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Aidan Ross, Josh Nasser, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter, Isaac Henry, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright
