World.title: Wallaroos lose star but regain experience for historic 'quadruple header'
World.content:
The Wallaroos have been forced to leave out star fullback Caitlyn Halse for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Halse is unavailable for the WXV Global Series Test due to concussion symptoms.

The 20-year-old's withdrawal is a blow but the Wallaroos have regained experienced winger Maya Stewart, who returns to the starting XV.

Stewart, a 27-Test veteran with the Wallaroos, was named after recovering from an Achilles tendon injury.

Her inclusion sees Desiree Miller move from the wing to fullback in place of Halse.

Wallaroos 'got some work to do' Ending a run of six straight defeats was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

In the forward pack, captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona and Pia Tapsell swap positions in the back row, starting at blindside flanker and number eight respectively.

Eva Karpani and Cecilia Smith have returned to the match-day squad on the reserves bench, which also features fresh faces Allana Sikimeti and Piper Simons.

"We have maintained considerable selection consistency throughout the WXV, strategically strengthening our cohesion and combinations," Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, said in a statement.

"During the WXV we have layered specific areas of our game to build stronger performances each Test.

"We have selected a balanced 23 armed with leadership, power, strength and speed."

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona will play at blindside flanker against Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland.

In their most recent Test, the Wallaroos triumphed 30–10 in Edinburgh late last month.

The two sides meet in Sydney and Canberra (October 23) to conclude their WXV Global Series campaigns.

Saturday's match is part of a rugby "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the final Bledisloe Cup Test, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams are also appearing.

The world champion Australian women's team plays arch rivals New Zealand, while the men's squad faces two-time Olympic champions Fiji.

It is the first time all four national rugby teams will be playing on the same match-day schedule.

Reserves: Tania Naden, Allana Sikimeti, Eva Karpani, Jemma Bemrose, Emily Chancellor, Lily Bone, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith

World.title: Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
World.content:
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.

Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.

The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.

Australia's 2017 World Cup win was the last game before the women's game changed forever. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.

Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.

These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.

The women's World Cup will again be held alongside the men's tournament. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.

Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.

In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.

Unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign Jessica Skinner once doubted her coaching style was elite. Now she believes it's exactly what the top level needs, and her journey from rural NSW has shaped why.

The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.

They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.

State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.

The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.

Tamika Upton has won three of the last four Dally M medals. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.

Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.

As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.

Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.

Samoa will be making its World Cup debut. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.

It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.

The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.

One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.

The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.

Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.

England was humiliated in its last meeting with Australia. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.

Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.

If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.

That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.

But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.

New Zealand shape up as the only side with a realistic chance of taking down Australia. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.

Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.

A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.

The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.

But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.

This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

Tech.title: Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta announced the Muse Spark Open AI model today, claiming that it’s the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” But the company also says that it’s the “the first model in its class” that can “run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.”

Meta and Apple, typically rivals, worked together on the launch and are publicly supporting each other.

“Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on X.

“Congrats to the team!” new Apple CEO John Ternus said in a reply. “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”

“We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said to Axios, who also noted that the companies have been collaborating over several months.

The new model is a “natively multimodal model” with 816 billion total parameters that “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” according to Meta. Apple also published a new technical post about MLX, an “array framework” for ML tasks on Apple Silicon, Muse Spark Open, and two other open models.

Tech.title: Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell.

All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD (Direct Stream Digital) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise.

The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference.

What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated.

This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

Tech.title: Volvo will use Nvidia’s tech for hands-free, point-to-point driving
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan, said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge.

Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future.

By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt.

Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars.

“Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.”

Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead, including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality.

Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.”

Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

Tech.title: Google is making inline links more prominent in AI responses
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Google is updating its AI search results to make inline links appear “higher up in responses more frequently,” according to a blog post. The company’s search results from AI Overviews and AI Mode give you answers in a customized view instead of the traditional list of links, but there are concerns that the format reduces traffic to publishers. Google says it’s been making “continued and substantial increases to the presence of inline links in our AI experiences,” and this new change will help ensure “ensure key sources are easily clickable right when you need them.”

The company is announcing several other changes to highlight links and publishers within its AI results. For sites that are among a few for a specific task or certain information — an example image from Google highlights a query about an airline refund — Google is testing showing the relevant links at the top of a response with context. For “timely” articles, the company is now rolling out the link carousels announced in May to more locations and languages. Google is making links at the end of a query “more engaging and prominent, with image thumbnails and a more clickable design.” And it’s now testing clickable links in AI mode to search profiles for publishers and creators.

An image from Google showing relevant links to a query about getting a refund. Image: Google

Google also says that more than 400 publishers are participating in its “News AI” pilot program, which it announced in December. The licensing program pays publishers for “the delivery and use of enhanced content to develop new AI features,” including “in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages,” and Axios, CNN, and the Financial Times are among the partners that are newly onboard, according to Google.

Tech.title: Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents
Tech.content:
There’s a growing trend in the consumer tech world: gadgets designed to spy on everything and everyone around you, regardless of whether or not anyone else actually consented to it. Now, with the advent of “AI personal assistants” like Meta’s Muse, you’re being cheerfully asked not just to give up your own data, but also the information of your friends, family, the person you went on a Hinge date with five years ago — and virtually anyone else you’ve ever come in contact with.

Since Muse was released last month, the agent has already been downloaded millions of times and hit No. 1 on Apple’s App Store. With the help of its creepy virtual avatar — a Temu Labubu-esque creature with a disarming grin — the app requests and encourages users to grant access to bank accounts, passwords, contacts, chat logs, and anything and everything that might help it to do the user’s bidding.

“These systems are advertised as autonomous helpers, genies, or servants who do what you need before you ask, seamlessly,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of the Signal Foundation, makers of the popular encrypted messaging app, told The Verge. These autonomous actions are applied “not just to the person who installed Muse on their device, but also to everyone that person communicates with, as extrapolated from their most intimate information — emails, messages, contacts, photos, and more.”

With AI agents, tech companies are letting consumers automate their everyday tasks by extending their omnivorous style of mass surveillance to massive amounts of sensitive data. It’s the same Faustian tradeoff Silicon Valley has been offering us for decades: your private data in exchange for a little bit of convenience. And for many people, the idea of having a virtual assistant that does menial tasks like filling out invoices and sending emails is compelling — especially if they don’t realize how much data they’re actually giving away in return.

“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge regarding other people’s data shared with Muse. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” Roberts pointed to Muse’s opt-in process and various options and settings that will “help people make the privacy choices that are right for them.”

“The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late.”

But not everyone has been able to navigate these options and settings. Already, users are describing incidents that are both alarming and entirely predictable. Some have reported the virtual assistant making all sorts of trouble, like grabbing millions of text messages they believed were off limits. Meta has disputed that the assistant has the ability to access text messages without permission, again attributing the incident to misconfigured app permissions and describing Muse’s ability to read text messages as “entirely opt-in.” On Threads, Meta executive David Singleton responded to a user directly, claiming that on a Mac, Muse can only gain access to the messages if the user grants the app full disk access.

In another incident, Muse gave out a tech reviewer’s home address and summoning a stranger to his apartment. In this case, the reviewer in question had given Muse permission to access that data, but simply didn’t realize it.

Eva Galperin, the director of cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says these incidents are no surprise, given that AI agents like Muse are designed to confuse people into giving up as much data as possible.

“The most important takeaway is that people don’t understand what kind of data they’re handing over,” Galperin told The Verge. “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late. It’s using dark patterns, and as a result you end up with Muse doing things that people don’t want.”

Because of the huge breadth of data AI agents like Muse are ingesting, this also means that users risk leaking not only their own sensitive information, but the information of everyone else they’ve had digital contact with.

And just like with Meta’s infamous “pervert glasses”, there’s no meaningful way to opt out — even if you’re constantly monitoring for signs that your data is compromised or your privacy is being violated. Your friends can now simply feed all of your private conservations to their virtual chatbot servants, and you’d have no way of knowing it happened.

After security researchers extracted Muse’s operating instructions, they discovered an internal process that compiles and updates profiles of every single person in a user’s life on an hourly basis. The goal of collecting all this data is to build an intimate and detailed portrait of a person’s life that forms the basis of the app’s personalized recommendations. The app tracks and measures each of the user’s private relationships, including “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now,” and uses that data to make personalized suggestions, Wired reported.

“Meta says Muse only remembers what you choose to share. But the idea that people are making an informed choice in this case is laughable,” said Whittaker. “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it, or the creepy dossiers that are being compiled about those they know and communicate with.”

Whittaker argued that this mirrors how tech companies have used privacy policies and terms of service since the 1990s: placing the onus of privacy on the consumer, and then avoiding responsibility for the consequences while reaping the benefits of the advertising model it helped create.

“Such broken consent systems are much older than AI and serve as the bedrock for the surveillance advertising industry,” said Whittaker. “More info about users allows better ad targeting, and the pernicious feedback loop at the heart of the surveillance business model was set in motion. Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”

“The idea is to place these impossible burdens on ordinary people, and then use that to argue, whether it’s in court or legislation or in the public, that [this is] what people have chosen,” Neil Richards, a professor of privacy law and codirector of Washington University’s Cordell Institute, told The Verge. “We already place so many burdens on consumers, [who are] overworked, facing a cost-of-living crisis, and may not understand the technologies behind the tool. I don’t think it’s fair to place a burden of monitoring a highly complex agentic tool on a consumer when its own company’s executives have confessed before Congress that they don’t even know how it works at a certain level.”

“There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it.”

In this way, AI assistants like Muse are creating a new spin on a classic privacy problem that has been around since the creation of Gmail and social media platforms writ large: Even if you avoid using AI agents, there’s no guarantee someone you know won’t share your private conversations, address, personal history, and other sensitive data with Meta’s virtual assistant, or one of its competitors.

“If I am not storing my stuff in Gmail, Google doesn’t have the plaintext of all the emails I’ve ever sent. But three-quarters of the emails I’m sending are being sent to Gmail accounts,” explained Galperin. In other words, if anyone you’re communicating with uses data-hungry tech platforms or has bad security practices, they can expose everyone’s communications. “The problem is not new, but the scale is new, and one reason we’re seeing this push toward wearables and always-on recording is because we now have the computational capacity to take that enormous amount of data and analyze it in a reasonable amount of time. That is the technical breakthrough that has brought us to this shitty moment.”

Meta claims that all of the information shared with Muse is placed in a text file inside a dedicated virtual machine, which supposedly prevents the AI model from talking to other agents. But the company has never hid the fact that it can access this data, and like other models created by its competitors, Muse has been discovered escaping its virtual cage to perform all manner of unauthorized shenanigans. Meta has confirmed that just prior to its release, the AI model had broken containment and hacked a third-party company. The incident followed the infamous Hugging Face attack from earlier this year, where OpenAI’s model exploited a previously unknown security flaw to gain unauthorized access to credentials on four other external services. Anthropic reported in July that its model had also gained unauthorized access to external systems on three separate occasions.

Even if they don’t hack everything in sight, the potential dangers of using a data-hungry AI agent extend far beyond the individual end user. Whittaker warned that in a world where AI agents are able to freely access and utilize private communications, companies and governments can effectively gain the ability to access private data by circumventing encryption without breaking it. That can spell disaster for activists and community organizers who use encrypted comms to protect themselves from police and the government, but also for anyone with sensitive communications — which these days can include virtually everyone.

“Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”

“If software reads a message after it is decrypted on your device and sends it to a cloud service, the encryption can work exactly as intended at the level of the application, which the developers control. However, the purpose of this encryption is ultimately nullified by invasive third-party apps like Muse that are selling convenience in the headline while demanding massive data access in the fine print,” Whittaker explained.

Like with smart glasses and other wearable ambient recording devices, experts say that the solution must be a combination of legal fixes, technical safeguards, and good old-fashioned shame.

“I think we should point the shame upstream onto the companies. Privacy should not be a right you can exercise only with the privilege of technical knowledge, or after throwing a jerk wearing Meta glasses out of a party,” said Whittaker. “Legally, the burden has to move from the person who clicked on a consent prompt to the companies that built these underlying systems.”

In the meantime, consumers will have to consider more carefully the impacts their individual choices to use this tech are having, both on themselves and others — and whether the convenience these companies are offering is even worth it.

“I think we need to treat agentic agents and AI more generally as an ultra-hazardous product for which strict liability is the rule,” said Richards. “There’s no reason to engage in what to my mind is a reckless privacy, mental health, cybersecurity, and financial risk experiment on the entire population.”

Tech.title: E Ink upgraded the screen found in most color e-readers
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Other E Ink technologies, like its Gallery 3 display found in the Remarkable Paper Pro, use colored pigments that move around to form full-color images, but Kaleido 3 employs a color filter over an e-paper panel with just black and white pigments. That approach results in color e-paper screens with fast refresh rates, but it generates color images at a lower resolution with a limited palette that tends to make them look desaturated. The extra color filter also leaves plain text looking darker than it does on e-readers with only a black-and-white E Ink screen.

E Ink claims its new Kaleido 4 display tech doubles the “color gamut volume” of its predecessor, which should improve how color images look. However, the technology is still limited to producing just 4,096 colors (modern LCD and OLED displays can produce millions) and, as with Kaleido 3, at a lower resolution than black-and-white text is displayed. But Kaleido 4 does increase white reflectance by 15 percent and boosts contrast by 50 percent, so plain text will potentially look less muddy than it often does with Kaleido 3.

The reason that E Ink’s seemingly superior Gallery 3 technology hasn’t been used in more devices is because those displays have a slow refresh rate that can often feel frustrating to use. Kaleido 3 refreshes much faster, and thanks to a new oxide TFT backplane (that sounds similar to what the Kindle Colorsoft uses), Kaleido 4’s performance is even faster with refresh rates up to 18fps, making the screens capable of playing back video.

Image: E Ink

Companies like Amazon and Kobo haven’t yet announced any new devices that will feature Kaleido 4 screens, but Hanvon Technology will be the first to adopt the new technology in its upcoming M10C II tablet. It will only be available in China, but the M10C II will feature a Kaleido 4 display with a micro-etched tempered-glass surface designed to reduce glare while providing a more authentic paper-like feel when taking notes using its battery-free pen.

Tech.title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
Tech.content:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.

The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.

“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”

Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.

Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.

METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.

“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.

METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.

Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

Tech.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more
Tech.content:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.

The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform, which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.

These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.

Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.

Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.

Image Credits:Bluesky

“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”

When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.

To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”

That network today has 47 million registered users, though it’s seen a decline in engagement, as some users who tested it out later returned to X.

Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.

“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

Tech.title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
Tech.content:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.

Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.

The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.

“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.

Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.

“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”

He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”

While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.

All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.

“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

Tech.title: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US
Tech.content:
SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.

Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.

NAND flash chips are primarily used in solid-state storage drives, which are employed in everything from laptops and smartphones to AI data centers. But the global component shortage, thanks to skyrocketing demand for AI data centers, has driven up prices for everything that goes into data centers, including high-speed RAM chips and SSDs. Research firm TrendForce expects NAND prices to rise 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter.

Reuters cited its sources as saying that Solidigm wants to install more chipmaking equipment in spare space at SK Hynix’s Dalian factory in China to boost NAND chip production.

SK Hynix told TechCrunch it is not seeking to expand capacity at its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The chip giant added that the equipment installation is being carried out in consultation with and under authorization from the U.S. government.

Washington first imposed sweeping restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment exports to China in October 2022, citing national security concerns, and further tightened the rules in 2023. Then in September 2025, the Trump administration revoked special export exemptions for certain SK Hynix, Samsung, and Intel facilities in China. The U.S. has since granted an annual license to Samsung and SK Hynix for sending chipmaking equipment to their plants in China.

The U.S. has also been pushing foreign chipmakers to build and expand their manufacturing facilities in America. In July, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said he wanted Samsung and SK Hynix to build chip plants in the country and that he was in talks with both companies.

Solidigm is said to be preparing for a 2027 U.S. IPO that could raise around $10 billion and value it at up to $100 billion.

Tech.title: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
Tech.content:
Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic.

“That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage.

Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December.

But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music).

Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news.

“Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said.

As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy.

“There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful.

“You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said.

Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users.

For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device.

Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

Tech.title: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI
Tech.content:
Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation.

The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.

Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.

The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.

The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.

Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.

“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.

Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.

The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.

As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.

Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.

“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”

— With additional reporting from Connie Loizos

Tech.title: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US
Tech.content:
Google on Thursday said “Universal Cart,” a tool that lets users collect and monitor products they find across search and in the Gemini app, is now available to U.S. users. The company first previewed the tool at Google I/O in May.

The idea is to make online shopping easier to manage. Find something you like, save it to your cart, and move on. When you return later, your items and shopping progress are still there, so you don’t have to hunt down the same products or start over. Universal Cart can collect items from multiple retailers, turning it into a central hub for browsing and keeping track of potential purchases.

Google says the cart can also help shoppers stay on top of deals and availability. The tool can send notifications when a saved product’s price drops or when an out-of-stock item becomes available again.

The tool is also designed to offer more tailored help during the shopping process. Google says it can take credit card perks into account when helping users choose how to pay, and also surface relevant promo codes.

Checkout is tied to Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP, an open standard the company introduced earlier this year. UCP is designed to help AI agents and retailers work together across different parts of the shopping journey, including checkout.

Google is already deeply invested in AI-powered shopping, and Universal Cart is its latest effort to make the experience more convenient. It joins features such as conversational product discovery in Search’s AI Mode and Google’s “Let Google Call” tool, which uses an AI agent to contact nearby stores and check whether an item is in stock.

Google isn’t the only company bringing AI into e-commerce. Amazon, OpenAI, and other rivals have added agentic commerce features as companies look for ways to make chatbots useful beyond answering questions.

Tech.title: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Was an Affiliate Marketer for a Fitness MLM
Tech.content:
Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.

A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online resume shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”

Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications advisor at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.

Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.

On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, was identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)

Tech.title: Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV
Tech.content:
“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”

Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.

The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.

Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”

“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.

We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”

Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.

Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”

Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.

When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.

“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

Tech.title: Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Tech.content:
If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.

Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.

Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads, doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.

The company’s cofounder and chief product officer Tanyella Leta tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”

Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”

Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.

It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps child development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.

AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation, but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.

Michael Robb, head of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb believes YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”

A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.

Tech.title: Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy
Tech.content:
As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.

In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent the GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”

The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.

“In a world where there is no shame, it’s hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn’t involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”

The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.

The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.

“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”

Tech.title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
Tech.content:
On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.

Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.

“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”

The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.

During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)

Tech.title: The Best Permanent Outdoor Lights (2026): Govee, Eufy, Cync
Tech.content:
Permanent outdoor lights are the perfect solution to a holiday season's worth of lights, and will last you for years to come. The name suggests exactly what they are: a type of string light designed to stay up all year instead of coming down after the occasion you hung them for, whether it's the holiday season or a big party that inspired you to deck out your front porch.

Whether these lights are truly “permanent” is up to you, since you can choose to anchor them to your home with either screws or adhesive. Note that they may not be a fit for every home's architecture—you will need eaves, and preferably flat ones, to hide the thick cords. Our favorite options are from Govee ($300, 100 feet) and Eufy ($350, 100 feet); both are great sets you can cut and splice to customize to your home's roofline. My favorite affordable set is from Cync ($117, 100 feet)—it's easy to use and install and has lots of great color options.

No matter which set you choose, these lights are made for year-round enjoyment, though they shine best in the holiday season. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck uses hers in the post-holiday season to display her husband’s favorite sports team colors, while I'm currently using mine to backlight the giant spiderweb spread across my balcony for Halloween. We're both looking forward to switching over to Christmas color schemes soon, and you can too after picking up one of our favorite sets below.

Updated October 2026: I've updated this guide with current pricing as we head into the holiday season, and added a new section about the lights we're testing next.

What Are Permanent Outdoor Lights?

Permanent outdoor lights are exactly what they sound like: outdoor lights meant to be permanently affixed to your home, so you don't have to go up and down a ladder every Halloween and Christmas season. They're similar to smart Christmas lights like those from Twinkly ($125) and Philips Hue ($220), and other smart lighting options like Philips Hue's smart bulbs ($90), in that they connect to an app and have custom color control.

The lights we recommend below are all DIY-friendly, but you can also hire a professional to affix them to your home. Some higher-end brands, like JellyFish and Gemstone, are for professional installation only. Hiring an installer is recommended either way if you have harder-to-reach eaves or a trickier home design, which may add considerably to the overall cost.

Tech.title: Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission
Tech.content:
For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.

Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.

In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.

Tech.title: Grand Theft Auto 6: The Release Trailer You’ve Been Waiting For
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games is taking one of the last steps on a very long road: The Grand Theft Auto 6 launch trailer arrived Thursday. In an incredibly popular but chaotic series, the new trailer hits different from the rest, complete with a new, haunting track from Justice, featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard. We’re obsessed with it all.

Judging from the trailer, it seems like the wait has been worth it. The launch trailer hits a beat that the other games haven’t seemed to quite elevate to. It was almost a year ago that Rockstar Games announced it would be releasing GTA 6, and now we’re getting closer to its Nov. 19 release date for the Xbox Series X, Series S and PlayStation 5.

The story centers around a character named Jason, who used to be in the army, but admits he “got into some trouble,” and that they “don’t give loans to people like me.” When he gets a call from the other central character, Lucia, the story begins, and we’re swept into the adventure and chaos that this game is trying to bring to the table.

More from CNET

GTA has always been a choose-your-own-adventure type of game. Personally, I’ve never played through the storylines, instead preferring the open-world nature of doing anything you want in an extensive setting. But this trailer has me intrigued and wanting to know what happens to our main characters.

The new background track is dynamic and sad, suggesting that the story that will unfold won’t be your typical smash-and-bash game.

GTA 6 has been in development for an extremely long time — GTA 5 came out in 2013 — and we’re about to see just what the fruits of Rockstar Games’ labor are all about. Get ready for a new ride that should bring old GTA lovers and newcomers on board.

Tech.title: You Can Now Play Battlefield 6 and More on Xbox Game Pass
Tech.content:
Xbox Game Pass subscribers can jump into huge battles now in Battlefield 6. That’s good because, Microsoft removed one of CNET’s best games of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, from the service. Maybe Battlefield 6 and the other games arriving this month will have what it takes to fill the Clair Obscur-sized hole in my heart.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. With a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ($23 a month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass in the first half of October 2026.

More from CNET

Battlefield 6

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

CNET’s David Lumb called this installment in the popular Battlefield series a “riveting shooter.” It’s full of huge multiplayer battles, close-quarters combat and loads of gunfights and explosions. While most people will gravitate towards multiplayer, there is a single-player campaign if you want a break from the online mayhem.

Valor Mortis

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

In this first-person soulslike game, you’re a soldier in Napoleon’s army who dies. No worries, because you’re back from the dead with a handful of supernatural abilities that you wield in your left hand, like in the almost 20-year-old game BioShock. You’ll use these skills to battle monsters and uncover a conspiracy that could threaten all of humanity.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps proves that not every game coming to Game Pass has to be full of action. You’ll unwind and explore Bluey’s world while taking photos in areas familiar to anyone who’s seen the popular children’s show – let’s be honest, this show’s also popular with adults. You can take photos on your own, or play with a partner, friend or your kid as you turn in-game moments into fun.

Other games coming to Game Pass soon

Those are a few of the games Microsoft is bringing to Game Pass in October. Here are the rest of the games you’ll see on the service soon.

Echo Weaver: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Forever Ago: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Neon Abyss 2: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Deep Dish Dungeon: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Chained Beasts: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Beyond These Stars: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 16.

Games that left Xbox Game Pass

Microsoft also removed nine games from Xbox Game Pass, including the award-winning Clair Obscur. So you’ll have to buy these games separately now if you still want to play them.
