Tech.title: I’ve Tested Echo Shows and Nest Hubs. Here’s How Apple’s HomeView Display Stacks Up
Tech.content:
The HomeView, announced Tuesday and available on Nov. 13, is Apple’s first-ever smart home display and a new way to control smart home devices or interact with Siri AI. But Apple has significant catching-up to do in this space, because its top competitors have been in the game for a while.

I’ve been testing Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays since they first launched in 2017, and started trying out Google Nest Hubs – originally the Google Home Hub – in 2018. Since then, both brands have released multiple smart speaker models, adding and ditching various features. (And sometimes canceling entire lines – anyone remember the Facebook Portal?)

Apple HomeView See at CNET Preorders

That means the stylish HomeView has a chance to learn from past smart display mistakes and differentiate itself in buyers’ eyes, including the Echo Show 11 and the 10-inch Google Nest Hub Max I use at home. Now that we have details and I’ve tried out the Apple HomeView in person, I have several thoughts for anyone considering which smart display to buy.

More from CNET

Nuts and bolts: Apple’s stylish display faces a challenge

Apple

The HomeView looks great. It immediately reminds me of the Echo Show 11, with the screen mounted on a low-set, domed base housing the speakers. With the discontinued Echo Show 10, Amazon tried an auto-rotating base that followed people as they moved, but it frequently bumped into things, which annoyed me. So I’m glad to see this display is stationary.

At 7 inches, the HomeView is also tiny.

CNET Smart Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar, who tested out the HomeView at a press briefing, reported that others at Apple’s event complained that the screen was too small. Based on my experience with smart displays, I wholeheartedly agree: It’s significantly smaller than any competitor models made for the same spaces. I’m confused as to why Apple added a screen better suited to a bedroom smart clock than to a tabletop display.

Those Liquid Retina details and colors look great, and maybe a screen this size was the only way to keep the price below $300. But it also hampers some of the best uses of a smart display, like making video calls and watching movies. Apple may have demonstrated Pluribus playing on the HomeView, but I can guarantee you won’t want to watch it on a 7-inch screen from halfway across the kitchen. You won’t be able to catch many details of those Siri “Start Cooking” instructions or FaceTimes with the family, either.

There’s a reason both Amazon and Google have been steadily inched up the size of their flagship smart displays. They’re useful as second TVs or video guides and they need the screen real estate to pull it off. I know from experience that screens under 8 inches don’t cut it unless you’re about a foot or two away.

The wall-mounted HomeView looks remarkably good. Ajay Kumar/CNET

But wait — there are also wall-mounting options. Google Nest falls way behind here, but you can buy the HomeView as a wall mount version, and Amazon offers a few wall-mounted Echo Shows, too. Kumar said the wall-mounted version of the HomeView looks good, but it also requires professional installation to hide the wired power connection, which will drive your bills well beyond $300. While the result looks amazing, the wired plug-in model may be more practical. Keep in mind that the cheapest wall mount Apple sells with the HomeView costs an additional $60.

I’m also worried about the size of the display on a wall mount, too. The Echo Show 21 ($500) offers a 21-inch touchscreen for your home, as well as a built-in Fire TV platform for watching shows. That much screen real estate still feels more useful than a 7-inch display, which seems more like a security system and lighting hub than an all-purpose station.

The battle of voice assistant AIs — I still think Amazon’s is better

The HomeView will tap into information from your personal apps. Apple

I’ve pitted the big three voice assistants against each other in the past, and recently tested which can predict the weather best. Gemini for Home is fine, if a little boring, and very accurate. Siri is snappy when controlling Apple Home devices, but falls behind elsewhere. Alexa Plus, however, is my favorite for smart display use.

Alexa Plus is chatty by nature, but also offers several different personalities to choose from, an option other voice assistants don’t have. Amazon’s integration with Echo Shows has numerous benefits, like showing you the previous details of your conversation so you can keep it going more easily, or displaying extra information on request. Alexa AI is overconfident and sometimes insists it can do things it can’t, but this is an issue with many LLM chatbots.

My favorite Alexa Plus ability is integration with third-party apps, an area where other voice assistants haven’t caught up yet. You can use an Echo Show and Alexa Plus to order food from GrubHub or Uber Eats without lifting a finger, or arrange for an Uber ride from across the room. You can also buy tickets on Ticketmaster or make reservations with OpenTable via Alexa, and Amazon continues to add new integrations for me to test.

Alexa Plus now offers compatibility with some very useful apps, both new and returning. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

There’s no indication that Siri AI includes such third-party app support on the HomeView. Apple says, “HomeView supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone,” but doesn’t give many details, and I haven’t seen signs that the HomeView/Siri AI combo will support services or bookings like Alexa Plus can.

But Siri’s AI does win on some accounts, carving out capabilities that Alexa Plus and Gemini for Home don’t have. From the examples Apple showed, it looks like Siri can naturally search your email and texting apps to bring up messages, recipes or other info, something the other voice assistants can’t (Gemini only does this on phones, with the right permissions). You can also customize Siri AI in unique ways, like speeding up or slowing down the voice, which I really like for ease of use and accessibility.

I still prefer Alexa Plus overall, with its chatty asides, personalities to play with and connections to useful third-party apps. I’m looking forward to testing Siri AI on the HomeView to see just what it can do and if Apple adds further integrations. Pricing could also work in Siri AI’s favor, depending on what iCloud Plus subscription is needed to enable all features. If you’re not an Amazon Prime member, Alexa Plus costs a steep $20 a month to fully enable, and Gemini for Home is priced similarly, so Apple could step ahead if Siri AI costs are low.

Smart home controls are where Apple’s ecosystem shines

Just like an Apple Watch: You can customize the look of your HomeView, depending on your preference, from standard clocks to a calendar to a family to Snoopy. Apple

While Kumar explored how the HomeView worked, he noted that he used an Echo Show to control his smart home and said that, “the result is… functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.”

It’s not an uncommon frustration with the Matter standard and home hubs. Linking multiple smart devices to Alexa or Google hubs and using smart displays for control can be challenging. Interfaces are sometimes wonky, and you can’t always find the settings you want. Devices disappear and need to be reconnected or updated to work again. Voice assistants may not recognize commands that previously worked.

Here, Apple’s tightly knit ecosystem and careful management of the Apple Home app offer a distinct advantage. Kumar saw how the HomeView could effortlessly find and pair with compatible devices, which he compared to setting up a new pair of AirPods. Siri AI can also offer personalization based on facial recognition or manual profile creation, with speedy customization options.

As with HomePods, you can also hand off content between iPhones and the display. Other little Apple tricks, like an instant Find My map displayed to locate missing Apple items, are also included. It already feels more seamless than both the past smart display experiences Kumar and I have had, which is enticing.

The only issue is device support, which tends to be more limited for Apple than other platforms. The company has come a long way in addressing this with its new line of security cameras, a smart lock, and a smart thermostat announced at the Welcome Home event, all clearly made to work with Siri AI and Apple Home. Third-party smart locks also tend to be highly compatible with Apple. Other devices like smart plugs, smart bulbs and third-party security cameras still lag behind, so you may have to look harder to find Apple-friendly models.

Keep in mind that competition also plays a role. Google allows some products, like my Nest cameras and Nest Learning Thermostat 4, to work on Echo Shows with Alexa, but there’s no Apple support. Amazon brands like Ring and Blink will only work with Alexa, not Google or Apple platforms. Choosing the Apple smart home may come with self-imposed limitations.

Always double-check your streaming capabilities

Apple’s streaming support is a huge question mark for the HomeView. Apple

Equipped with two custom full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, the HomeView’s audio proved “significantly more impressive than I expected,” according to Kumar, but not quite as good as a full-size HomePod. For reference, the Echo Show 11 has two full-range drivers and a woofer but no passive radiators, and the Nest Hub Max has two 10-watt tweeters and a 30-watt woofer.

All three can fill a standard room with sound, but in my experience, the most important part by far is whether they support the music streamers you use.

Apple Music is a given for the HomeView, but again, Apple is light on integration details and intent on pulling people into all things Apple. While Apple mentioned the new HomePod Mini 2 supports TuneIn Radio, iHeartRadio, and Audacy, it doesn’t mention any specific services for the HomeView, so if you rely on other apps, you may want to check for confirmation. Based on Apple’s past HomePod support, only Deezer and Pandora have been easy to add in addition to the listed services.

Alexa and Google Home’s audio streaming options are extensive. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Meanwhile, my Echo Show supports not only Amazon Music and Apple Music but also Deezer, Spotify, Tidal, Pandora and SiriusXM. Likewise, my Google Nest Hub supports not only YouTube Music, but Apple Music, Deezer, Spotify, Pandora, Amazon Music, TuneIn Radio, and iHeartRadio. As you can see, for maximum music streaming options, you may want to choose a smart display other than the HomeView, or wait to see if other apps add compatibility.

If you don’t mind the small screen, the same caveat applies to video streaming services, but even more so. The HomeView is highly focused on Apple TV, and I don’t know what other streaming apps will be available, if any.

Video options also appear much broader on Echo Shows and Nest Hubs. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Google’s Nest Hubs, meanwhile, can handle a variety of apps through Google Casting, including Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu, Paramount Plus (I assume Skydance support will be included), Sling, Viki, Starz, Tubi and others. That makes it one of the best smart display choices for watching videos.

My Alexa app is currently a mess and desperately needs redesigning, but through my Echo Show touchscreen, I can access Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, YouTube, Peacock, TikTok, Disney Plus, HBO Max and many more. Larger Show models gain native support for Fire TV, which enables all kinds of streaming apps, too.

Pricing is comparable, but Apple’s display will still cost the most

Echo’s wall-mounted models are the only options that cost more than the HomeView. Chris Monroe/CNET

Some of Apple’s home prices shocked me. $400 for a floodlight security camera is wild when competitors charge around half as much for similar capabilities. But aside from the small screen, HomeView’s $299 price is in line with other current flagship smart displays. Amazon’s Echo Show 11 starts at $250, but sees discounts around the holidays, something Apple is more averse to. Bumping up to wall-mounted Show 21 brings costs to $500. Google’s Nest Hub Max, while increasingly hard to find these days (I’m hoping Google will release a new Hub soon) is available from around $230 to $250 at various stores.

So while you’ll pay more for a HomeView, it’s not as huge a jump as you see with some other Apple products.

One more thing: Don’t forget about iPads

The iPad is an alternative screen for your home. Sarah Tew / CNET

Of the big three display brands, Apple has by far the most complete support for its tablet computers across the various iPad lines. That introduces an alternative I must bring attention to: You could just use an iPad.

Add a prop cover as a stand, and an iPad could serve many of the same roles as a HomeView on various counters and tables, but with a much larger screen and much more compatibility with apps you already use. Plus, you can pack it away or switch it to other purposes, like serving as a small laptop or a workout companion, when you’re at home.

Two downsides to the iPad approach. First, they cost a lot more, starting around $750 for the iPad Air and $600 for the iPad Mini. Second, unless you’re an AirPods owner or have a HomePod to connect to, sound will always be better on a HomeView.

I’ll provide more details as we get to testing the HomeView and Apple’s other new home products in the coming months, but for now, you should have enough to decide whether you want one for the holidays or are prepared to wait.

Tech.title: Can the Shark Tank Water Bottle Really Keep Drinks Cold for 36 Hours? I Tested One to Find Out
Tech.content:
The universal push for better hydration has produced a seemingly endless supply of water bottles that promise to keep H2O cold for hours, days, even months. Admittedly, “months” is a stretch, but given recent advances in insulation technology, that milestone may not be far off.

Fresh off Stanley’s early-2020s hype, a new water bottle contender, Coldest, piqued my interest with its bold, brazen name alone. The company’s line of bottles and tumblers, which come in a range of sizes, styles and limited-edition designs, was featured on ABC’s “Shark Tank” and promises to keep beverages cold for 36 hours.

The design is reminiscent of Stanley’s mug. Joey Skladany/CNET

Coldest also operates out of my hometown of Naples in Florida (which I didn’t realize until I researched it), and I welcome any opportunity to support a local small business. But did it ultimately live up to its hype, the thousands of positive reviews and the praise from national media outlets?

More from CNET

The test

For comparison, I grabbed my go-to $30 Owala water bottle and filled it with equal amounts of water (three cups) and ice (one cup). This model is a different size and shape than the 46-ounce Coldest, which means the liquid and ice were more condensed in the compartment.

That said, despite the lack of error-free, controlled-environment analysis, the primary goal was to determine whether the Coldest water bottle lived up to its 36-hour promise.

I put Coldest’s claims to the test. Joey Skladany/CNET

The results

After only a few hours, both water bottles delivered refreshing, ice-cold agua, with Owala consistently beating Coldest by a couple of degrees. Using a meat thermometer, here is a breakdown of the reading times and temperatures across 36 hours:

After 3 Hours

Coldest: 52°F

Owala: 50°F

After 7 Hours

Coldest: 54°F

Owala: 52°F

After 15 Hours

Coldest: 57°F

Owala: 56°F

After 18 Hours

Coldest: 58°F

Owala: 57°F

After 24 Hours

Coldest: 60°F

Owala: 59°F

After 36 Hours

Coldest: 63°F

Owala: 63°F

While water certainly remained cool after the experiment concluded, it was by no means teeth-chattering cold. Though I can hardly imagine anyone waiting this long to drink a beverage, it’s still worth noting since this is a major part of Coldest’s marketing claim.

Coldest performed on par with Owala in my chill test. Joey Skladay/CNET

Owala’s water bottle, though smaller in volume, yielded a consistently colder liquid, likely because of its smaller surface area and greater exposure to the stainless steel interior. But after 36 hours, both bottles tied in temperature, giving Coldest a slight edge because of its significantly larger size.

The Verdict

My feelings towards Coldest were essentially neutral. While I appreciate the company’s ability to retain a cult-like following with monthly limited-edition design drops, I didn’t feel its water-cooling technology was any more superior than the models I currently own (including the Owala).

The Coldest bottle kept things chilled, but it comes at a steep price. Joey Skladany

It’s clear that this was introduced to disrupt Stanley’s virality and market share, though I’m not entirely sure if I’d cough up the cash to make it part of my must-have accessory rotation. I didn’t dislike it, by any means, and applaud the founders on their early success, but even loyalty points and an affiliate program wouldn’t incentivize consistent buys, despite my obsession with staying hydrated and color-coordinating my outfits.

Best Reusable Water Bottles We've Tested See at CNET

Those who collect water bottles like Pokémon will certainly think otherwise, as the impressive range of designs can be exciting. They are one-of-a-kind, often glow in the dark, and reflect current seasons and holidays, which is undeniably adorable. If that’s your thing, then great. But if your main concern is quenching thirst, you’re likely thinking less about style and more about substance, so any popular drinking vessel will do.

Tech.title: Europe’s Largest Airline Wants Predictive AI Models to Nip Airport Meltdowns in the Bud
Tech.content:
If there’s one thing that’s unifying across the world, it’s that we can all agree that a canceled or delayed flight is a massive headache at best. Ryanair – the largest airline in Europe by fleet size, global passenger volume and total flights, and the second-largest airline in the world by global passenger volume – has implemented proprietary predictive AI models to help prevent airline disruptions before they lead to widespread cancellations or diversions.

The AI models were developed by Ryanair Labs, the Ireland-based airline’s tech innovation hub launched in 2014, to more quickly and efficiently predict when weather delays, airport curfews and issues with airline crew hours are likely to disrupt passengers’ journeys.

I spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland, the governmental economic development agency, before the International AI Summit in Dublin to discuss how the airline is using these AI models. The goal, Wilson said, is not to replace Ryanair’s core of human operators, but to give his employees advanced tools to manage and handle operational complexities across Ryanair’s 96 operational bases and its more than 3,800 flights per day.

More from CNET

“And that, by making us efficient,” he said, “translates into lower fares, better operational performance — same boring, virtuous circle, you know, ’cause that’s what the airline industry is like.”

Predictive models in practice

Wilson said there are a lot of variables in making sure a plane is in the right place, at the right time: weather, an airplane going out of service, an airport closing to meet curfews, staff and crew showing up.

For instance, say a crew on a plane is about to exceed the hours they’re allowed to work due to a weather delay and they’re not going to make it back to their base, yet are scheduled to work the next day. The Ryanair model is designed to recognize the disruptions this will cause and to take appropriate action.

CNET spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland before the International AI Summit in Dublin. Macy Meyer/CNET

“If you know they’re not going to be able to do the flights the next day, there’s no point in waiting for them to come back the next morning for them to tell you that they’re out of hours,” Wilson said. “But if the model is running, it reassigns somebody else to do it, or it may just reassign them to do a flight later the next day, and you pair up the crew in a different way, that’s all.”

AI is starting to take a larger role in airline and airport operations. In September, the Federal Aviation Administration rolled out a trial program for a new system, Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, around Washington, DC, airports, to use AI to mitigate delays and congestion caused by air traffic control staffing shortages. Some carriers, like American Airlines, are now using AI for flight rebooking, while others, like United, Delta and JetBlue, have partnered with third-party weather predictors, such as Tomorrow.io, to use AI systems to address route or delay issues and quickly calculate solutions.

The future of AI in airline operations

Looking ahead, Wilson said he thinks the next major impact AI will have on airlines is in distributing flights. Specifically, as more people adopt personal AI agents – like OpenAI Dots or Meta’s Muse, both introduced just in the last few weeks – he’s thinking about whether a customer tells an agent “book me a flight” and the potential negative, costly impact that the agent books a more expensive flight due to an airline paying to be prioritized by that AI model.

Ultimately, though, Wilson doesn’t suspect that AI is drastically changing the airline industry – at least not rapidly. “Everything changes and nothing changes, right?” he said.

Wilson says that Ryanair’s strategy will be to find “the killer applications” of AI to better serve customers and gain a competitive edge, but, really, the humans who “execute the real stuff in flight” are the key to smooth operations.

“The actual nuts and bolts of our industry won’t change,” Wilson said.

“In the AI world that’s coming, we just see this as a new set of tools for fine-tuning work processes and efficiencies in doing the core model of what we’ve been successful at.”

Editor’s note: Macy Meyer’s travel costs for the International AI Summit were covered by Enterprise Ireland. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Xreal’s New High-End Display Glasses Get a Brightness Boost
Tech.content:
The quality of plug-in display glasses has gotten seriously good lately, if you can put up with the idea of resting your monitor on your face. The price for good glasses has been dropping (down to $299 for some notable ones), but the pricier top-end models have advantages.

The new $599 Xreal One Pro Plus glasses, available now, offer a few subtle upgrades to last year’s model. I’ve been trying a pair out and the experience is largely the same, just a bit better (namely, brighter).

The lenses on these wearable displays still stick out a bit. (I also have prescription inserts added on them here.) Scott Stein/CNET

What’s new: Brightness, a few new visual modes

The previous Xreal One Pro display glasses were one of my favorite pairs around, along with the Viture Beast ones. In the past, Xreal’s design was thinner and lighter than Viture’s, but they had a notably dimmer display. That’s been fixed now with the One Pro Plus, which have 1,200 nits of brightness (versus 700 for the One Pro display glasses). There are also a few more visual settings, including “Reading,” which seems to move the virtual display a bit closer.

More from CNET

The One Pro Plus also have a smoother AI 3D conversion mode that turns any 2D image or video (or connected game) into 3D. The effect runs at a smoother frame rate than before, but the conversion still feels imperfect and gimmicky and compromises the frame rate too much compared with leaving it off.

But the rest of these glasses are similar to their predecessor. They still need to be tethered via USB-C cable to whatever laptop, phone or game console you have around, and they still project their displays down from the top of the glasses through half-mirror lenses that make the display feel overlaid in front of your eyes. They’re not any more portable or differently designed than before, and still resemble odd sunglasses. (They do pack up easily into an included case, though.) They have the same onboard chip that can pin displays in place when you turn your head, along with the same ability to change the size and perceived distance of the virtual display, including widescreen modes for connected computers.

The included nose pads are slightly more comfortable, and the arms can still bend at different angles for a proper fit.

Connecting to Steam Deck is still my favorite thing to do with these types of glasses. Scott Stein/CNET

Wearing the Xreal One Pro Plus

I’ve been wearing the One Pro Plus with prescription lens inserts while writing this story on a MacBook, and the differences are subtle. But I appreciate the extra brightness, and the electrochromic dimming seems to block out room light even better. Together, those improvements make the glasses much more effective in brightly lit rooms or outdoors.

I also watched some of the indie horror movie Buddy on my iPhone, and the more vivid display made the glasses feel like a more effective personal cinema.

I played Star Wars Galactic Racer on Steam Deck with these on my face, too, and had a blast. The display is crisp and vivid, although after swapping back and forth with the Viture Beast, I prefer the Beast slightly for its larger-feeling display.

The audio on the speaker arms sounds fine, but isn’t any better than the Xreal One Pro’s audio. When I wear them, I prefer to use AirPods for audio.

The Xreal One Pro Plus (left) versus the Viture Beast (right). The Beast glasses are clearly a bit chunkier. Scott Stein/CNET

I liked the Viture Beast for their bright, micro-OLED display and their stepped-up screen resolution, which has an aspect ratio that works better for gaming (1,900×1,200). The 1,250 nits on the Beast are pretty close to Xreal One Pro Plus, though.

My issue is that Xreal has so many display glasses options now that it’s getting confusing, including a pair made with Asus, a more affordable pair released earlier this year and a mixed reality computer-glasses system called Xreal Aura that was made with Google, costs $1,279 and is arriving later this fall.

With the One Pro Plus, Xreal has made the best display glasses I’ve ever worn next to Viture Beast, and their smaller on-face feel is more comfortable. But if you’re looking to see what glasses tech has in store next, you might want to see what the Xreal Aura offer. I’ll be reviewing them soon.

Tech.title: The $2,000 Duo: Who Is Apple’s First Folding iPhone Actually For?
Tech.content:
Apple’s first swing in the foldables market, the iPhone Duo, has already made a huge splash before it’s even available to buy.

The foldables segment has been overrun by Android devices, and all eyes have been patiently waiting for Apple to make its move. And the Duo’s design confirms the popularity of Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 and Google’s original Pixel Fold: Shorter and wider seems to be the sweet spot, as opposed to the more traditional taller folding phone designs we see with something like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

But this is Apple we’re talking about, and the iPhone Duo is more than just an iOS version of the Galaxy Fold and Pixel Fold — it has a lot going for it. We had a lot of things to say about it during our hands-on with the device, and while personally, it seems like the best foldable I’ll never buy, it certainly will be delivered into the pockets of some discerning customers who want the Apple level of polish (or who can’t stand green message bubbles).

More from CNET

So who needs the iPhone Duo? Who is it best suited to? We know that the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max is for photography enthusiasts and those who want the best battery ever in an iPhone, but the Duo doesn’t provide that. It’s an oddly-shaped but good-looking device that fills a new space in Apple’s lineup.

Is the iPhone Duo actually for anyone in particular? There are a few crowds that are more likely to gravitate toward this foldable over others. Your grandparents likely aren’t going to run out and grab the Duo, but here’s who likely will.



Early adopters, power users and professionals

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

There are likely plenty of Apple fans who have been waiting for its first foldable, but a lot of people also likely won’t pick up a first-generation device, preferring to wait until the second or third version so that Apple works out any kinks. (On the other hand, Apple has patiently waited and watched the foldable market, so its first swing might not feel like a first-generation foldable full of finicky foibles at all. It’s probably going to be great.)

But there will be some early adopters and tech enthusiasts who won’t care and plan to get this phone anyway.

Power users and those looking essentially for a foldable iPad Mini are going to love the iPhone Duo. You’ll likely be able to resize apps side by side, similar to how you would on any iPad, making it a dream for those who want an iPad experience with an iPhone form factor that fits right in your pocket. Still, we’ll need to see just how well multiple apps work on the inner screen simultaneously. It might not be as elegant as you’d get on an iPad, but it’s close.

The other group that might really want to get their mitts on the Duo is the professional crowd. The larger inner screen makes way for easier work apps that would be more cumbersome than even the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Editing Excel or Google Sheets spreadsheets, Google and Word docs, checking emails and sending work chats will be a far smoother experience on the wider display. Throw in a wireless keyboard, and you might have a pocket iPad-like productivity suite of your dreams.

Fashionistas

Apple products are synonymous with style, and this is a crowd that will happily gravitate toward this phone.

The new “it” item will be in the pockets of celebrities and content creators who want to make sure they’re seen with Apple’s newest device. It’s also an expensive phone, like all foldables, making it a status symbol that maintains the cool and pretentious vibe that Apple products give off.

The sexiest Kindle replacement

The iPhone Duo has a typical but useful foldable feature of showing a preview of what the rear cameras are shooting to help with selfies. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Avid readers may also want to pick up the iPhone Duo, since it’s virtually the perfect e-reader size. Not only that, but you’ll also get access to the App Store, which doesn’t limit you just to Amazon’s Kindle Store or e-reader apps.

That type of flexibility on top of the power of iOS and the A20 Pro chip makes this a killer Kindle or e-reader replacement. While it is very expensive to replace a Kindle, its style, form and functionality would make it a worthy consideration for some people.

Who isn’t the iPhone Duo for?

If your priorities are camera features, battery life and durability, your first choice shouldn’t be the iPhone Duo. What you’re looking for is the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It checks all of those boxes, and you shouldn’t be swayed by the novelty of the Duo.

It’s not that the Duo isn’t alluring, but it’s both nearly double the price of the latest iPhone 18 Pro handsets and likely significantly less durable. The iPhone Duo costs about as much as a new iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad combined.

Like most foldables, the iPhone Duo doesn’t ship with issues, just compromises. That’s something that really needs to be considered when making your purchasing decision. This device is a marvel of engineering, wrapped in luxurious style, but 90% of people spending money on new phones are not going to buy this one.

Tech.title: Popular Norwegian Kitchen Brand Lands in the US with 7 Sleek Small Appliances
Tech.content:
Wilfa, a Norwegian brand known for kitchen appliances and minimalist Scandinavian designs, is officially launching in the US today with seven new appliances.

Although we haven’t put the new lineup through testing just yet, a few have caught our eye.

Blending and mixing

The Probaker NXT, Wilfa’s most expensive new appliance, features a 7.4-quart stainless steel bowl, 20 speed settings and a hefty price tag of $999.

That is by far the most expensive stand mixer we’ve seen, but we’d love to do a side-by-side comparison with the Ooni Halo Pro Spiral Mixer, which we previously gave high marks to, as they feature similar designs and features.

Other launches include the Powerfuel XL Blender, which is a heavy-duty blender with a Tritan plastic, 60-ounce jug, a digital-knob design and three presets — soup, ice crushing and smoothie — plus an included tamper. The Prostick, an immersion blender with multiple attachments, is the final new blending option.

Best Blenders of 2026 See It

Coffee

Wilfa is also launching three new drip coffee makers and an electric coffee grinder.

Coffee connoisseurs may already be familiar with Wilfa, as we’ve reviewed earlier versions of the brand’s coffee maker and grinder, the Wilfa Performance and the Uniform coffee grinder, in 2023 when both were available in partnership with Lardera Coffee.

The three new drip makers and grinders share similar designs but are expected to differ.

From left, the Zense Alux Coffee Maker ($299), the Zense Alux Thermo Coffee Maker ($349) and the Performance Thermo Coffee Maker ($399). Wilfa/CNET

When we get our hands on these new launches, we plan to run the new coffee makers through their paces as well to see if one, or multiple, can perform well enough to make it on our best coffee makers list.
